and adaptation to Climate Change (CC). Productivity growth has been uneven, with 
higher gains in crop farming (56%) than in livestock (40.3%), and wide regional and 
producer-level disparities. Similarly, access to support services such as technical 
assistance and credit is heterogeneous. These issues particularly affect the Northeast 
and North regions, which are the poorest areas of the country.

characterized by family farming, which accounts for approximately 87% of rural 
establishments, though it contributes only 38% of the region‚Äôs gross agricultural 
production value, reflecting low relative productivity (IBGE, Agricultural Census 2017). 
Most of these family farms operate areas smaller than 10 hectares and rely on family 
labor, with limited access to technology, technical assistance and credit. In this 
context, rural poverty remains a structural challenge: more than 60% of the rural 
population in the Northeast live below the poverty line, with this figure exceeding 70% 
in states such as Maranh√£o and Piau√≠ (IPEA, 2021). Additionally, nearly 90% of the 
region are considered semi-arid, facing severe water scarcity and soil degradation: 
more than 45% of soils show signs of desertification or erosion (MMA, 2017), 
worsened by overgrazing, deforestation, and unsustainable farming practices.

biome ‚Äî already exceeds 46% of its original coverage (Funda√ß√£o Joaquim Nabuco,

2020). In light of this situation, the main challenges include increasing family farm 
productivity through semi-arid-adapted technologies; reducing rural poverty through 
targeted public policies; conserving natural resources and strengthening climate 
resilience via agroecological practices and improvement in water use efficiency.
3.4Brazilian Amazon. The agricultural sector in the Brazilian Amazon also relies 
primarily on family farming, representing 84% of rural establishments but only 24% of

mechanization and limited access to technical assistance: only 13% of family farmers

biodiversity loss: approximately 17% of the Amazon biome has already been

temperature increase of 2¬∞C to 3.5¬∞C by 2050 and up to a 20% drop in crop yields

extreme events such as prolonged droughts and changing rainfall patterns are already 
disrupting traditional agricultural cycles. In this context, the main challenges include 
sustainably increasing productivity, reducing rural and indigenous poverty through 
inclusive policies, and promoting climate-resilient agroecological systems while 
protecting the natural resources of the Amazon biome.

which may request loans for programs contributing to the achievement of the 
multisectoral objectives in one or more of the CCLIP‚Äôs sectors. The sectors are: 
(i) agricultural services; (ii) basic and productive infrastructure; and (iii) environment

sub-loans for specific investments.

delivered within the framework of the IDB Group‚Äôs Amazon Forever Program,

(iii) Bioeconomy and Creative Economy.

institutional capacity, support policy reforms, and foster sustainable agricultural and

Deforestation and Poverty Reduction Fund (LCA Fund)3, financed by the United 
Kingdom‚Äôs Department of Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA). The LCA

with the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock, to finance technical assistance in LCA

of the ABC+ Plan in the state of Par√° (BR-T1577). In order to promote rural

implemented in partnership with the Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change: 
Conservation, Restoration and Sustainable Management in the Caatinga, Pampa and

bioeconomy (BR-T1567), with a focus on regulating the National Policy on Payments

IV. Description of activities/components and budget
4.1Component 1: Technical and operational support for project implementation 
(US$325,000). This component will finance targeted technical assistance to 
strengthen the institutional and operational capacities of the main state-level executing 
and co-executing agencies responsible for the implementation of IDB-funded projects 
in the areas of agriculture and rural development in the states of Piau√≠, Para√≠ba, and 
Bahia. This support will aim to improve the efficiency, effectiveness, and sustainability 
of project implementation, addressing both cross-cutting and sector-specific 
challenges. Key areas of support will include: (i) Project management and planning, to 
enhance coordination, execution capacity, and alignment with project objectives; 
(ii) Procurement and financial management, with a focus on compliance with IDB 
policies, preparation of terms of reference, bidding documents, and contract 
management; (iii) Design and supervision of rural infrastructure works, such as water 
supply systems, rural sanitation, and access roads; (iv) Environmental and social 
safeguards, to ensure that projects meet IDB standards and national regulations, with 
attention to risk management and mitigation measures; (v) Monitoring, evaluation, and 
results measurement, including support for the design and application of baseline 
studies, indicators, and data systems; (vi) Gender and diversity mainstreaming, 
through the implementation of inclusive approaches that promote the participation and 
empowerment of women, youth, indigenous peoples, traditional communities, and 
LGBTQ+ populations; and (vii) Technical assistance in key thematic areas such as 
value chain development, access to rural credit and financial services, promotion of 
sustainable and low-carbon agricultural practices, and land regularization and tenure 
security. This comprehensive support package is expected to enhance the 
performance of public institutions and contribute to the successful achievement of the 
development goals set out in the Bank‚Äôs rural and agricultural portfolio in these states.
4.2Component 2. Sustainable agriculture public policies and knowledge 
management (US$75,000). This component will finance the development of studies 
on agricultural policy at both the national and subnational levels in Brazil, building on 
previous analytical work conducted in partnership with state governments based on 
the OECD Producers Support Estimate methodology. The component will finance the 
collection and analysis of data on public support to agriculture, institutional 
arrangements, and the effectiveness of existing policies. It will promote the use of 
standardized methodologies to allow comparability across states and with national-
level trends. The work will: (i) inform decision-making processes; (ii) contribute to more 
transparent and efficient policy design; and (iii) enhance the capacity of national and 
state level government to monitor the progress of their agricultural policies in terms of 
social and environmental sustainability. Special attention will be given to identifying 
best practices and regional differences in support strategies to the agricultural sector. 
Findings will be discussed with national and state authorities, producer organizations, 
and civil society. The studies will also support impact evaluations of agricultural public 
policies. The component will be implemented in coordination with federal and selected 
state governments. Such policy analysis provides the private sector with comparable 
and up-to-date data on Producer Support Estimates (PSE), enabling agribusinesses 
- 7 -
and investors to assess agricultural policy incentives, risks, and opportunities across 
Latin America and the Caribbean to make more informed investment decisions.
4.3 The TC expected results are: (i) improved capacities at states levels to implement 
Bank‚Äôs rural and agricultural portfolio; (ii) improved projects‚Äô implementation 
performance; (iii) updated technical and sectorial analysis available for public policy 
makers in the fields of agriculture and rural development.
4.4 The total budget for this TC is US$400,000, financed by the Ordinary Capital Strategic 
Development Program Window 2 Sustainability (W2A).

V. Executing agency and execution structure
5.1 The beneficiaries of this Technical Cooperation (TC) will be the states of Piau√≠, 
Para√≠ba, and Bahia, depending on the needs identified. At the request of the 
Government, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) will act as the executing 
agency. Execution by the Bank is justified due to procedural and budgetary 
management constraints at the state level across the three states, which could 
significantly delay implementation and jeopardize the achievement of the TC‚Äôs 
objectives. Furthermore, some of the requesting state-level entities have limited 
institutional capacity for operations and procurement, as their resources are currently 
fully dedicated to the execution of IDB-financed loan programs. Implementing this TC 
at the state level would divert these limited resources and compromise the timely and 
effective execution of the TC‚Äôs activities.
5.2 PTI/ARD team based in Brazil will be leading the execution, in collaboration with other 
divisions that could be related to specific topics. The execution of this TC will also be 
coordinated with CSD/ACU to guarantee adequate links with other initiatives in the 
Amazon. The UDR will be CBR.
5.3 Supervision and monitoring will be carried out in accordance with ‚ÄúThe Technical 
Cooperation Monitoring and Reporting System (OP-1385-4). The Project Team will 
prepare an evaluation report at the closure of the TC, which identifies the 
achievements and lessons learned, and will serve as a reference for related 
operations.
5.4 All procurement to be executed under this Technical Cooperation have been included 
in the Procurement Plan (Annex IV) and will be hired in compliance with the applicable 
Bank policies and regulations as follows: (a) Hiring of individual consultants, as 
established in the regulation on Complementary Workforce (AM-650) and (b) 
- 8 -
Contracting of services provided by consulting firms in accordance with the Corporate 
procurement Policy (GN-2303-33) and its Guidelines.
5.5 As per the request of the beneficiary, the IDB will be the executing agency, considering 
its experience in executing technical cooperation in the natural resources sector in 
Brazil. In addition, the fact that the TC will be executed directly by the Bank means 
that the procurement processes will not depend on factors that affect government 
execution mechanisms, and financial execution will not depend on the availability of

section_text:
II. Objective and Justification
2.1 The general objective of this Technical Cooperation (TC) is to enhance the 
understanding of the socio-economic significance of Trinidad and Tobago's Carnival 
on the tourism sector and the country's economy. Its specific objectives are: (i) to 
support the development and implementation of a methodological framework for 
assessing both the direct and indirect socio-economic significance of Carnival to the 
tourism and creative sectors, and (ii) to assist in applying the developed framework to 
determine Carnival's direct and indirect socio-economic contributions to tourism and 
creative sectors.
2.2 As one of the largest and most culturally significant events in the Caribbean, Carnival 
represents a major pillar of Trinidad and Tobago‚Äôs tourism offering and overall 
economic driver.  However, there is limited quantifiable data available to fully 
 - 2 - understand its direct and indirect economic contributions, particularly to the tourism 
and creative sectors, associated industries and the wider economy. This Technical 
Cooperation (TC) is therefore essential to evaluate the full economic significance of 
Carnival, shedding light on its impact on local economies, businesses, employment 
generation, and its growing potential as an exportable cultural product. By supporting 
the development and implementation of a comprehensive methodological framework, 
this initiative will not only assess the direct and indirect contributions of Carnival to the 
tourism sector but also explore its role in driving the growth of micro, small, and 
medium enterprises (MSMEs) across various industries. It will also examine Carnival‚Äôs 
influence on the international stage‚Äîincluding the export of cultural goods and 
services such as music, fashion, and performance‚Äîrevealing untapped socio-
economic opportunities. This in-depth analysis will serve as a tool for policymakers 
and industry stakeholders, providing actionable policy recommendations to foster 
sustainable growth in the creative tourism sector. Ultimately, the findings will inform 
about the impact on the country's economy vis a vis other traditional sectors of 
development and will inform policy strategies that harness Carnival‚Äôs full socio-
economic potential, supporting long-term economic resilience for the people of 
Trinidad & Tobago.

significance of Carnival in Trinidad and Tobago. It begins with a review of global and 
local studies and the development of a theory of change to map Carnival‚Äôs multi-
sectoral impacts. The framework will then be implemented through targeted data 
collection, fieldwork, and stakeholder consultations. Findings will guide a final 
evaluation and inform future policy and strategic planning.

VI. Project Risks and Issues
6.1 No significant risks are identified. However, potential risks include: (i) Poor 
coordination between the different public authorities with shared competency 
regarding Carnival. To mitigate this risk, the Bank will directly execute the main 
activities of TC, ensuring continuous monitoring of the process; (ii) Limited data 
availability and quality in Trinidad and Tobago pose a challenge, as gaps in existing 
studies or restricted access to reliable data could hinder an accurate assessment of 
Carnival‚Äôs socio-economic impact, ultimately affecting the evaluation‚Äôs credibility and 
the framework‚Äôs robustness. To mitigate this risk, a competitive and rigorous selection 
process will be implemented to identify a qualified consultant or firm with expertise in 
socio-economic impact analysis. Preference will be given to a local expert with 
extensive sector experience. Additionally, efforts will be made to strengthen data 
collection and validation by leveraging existing tourism and economic datasets, 
collaborating with relevant agencies, and integrating primary research methods to 
address data gaps, ensuring a comprehensive and reliable assessment of Carnival‚Äôs 
socio-economic impact.; and (iii) Low stakeholder engagement as difficulty in securing 
active participation from key stakeholders, including government bodies, private sector 
actors, and local communities, could delay the project or result in insufficient buy-in for 
policy recommendations and findings. To mitigate this risk, the IDB team will work 
closely with the selected consultant or firm, serving as a liaison with local stakeholders 
to ensure effective engagement. A structured approach will be implemented, including 
collaborative workshops and regular updates, to build trust, secure stakeholder buy-in, 
and foster a shared sense of ownership over the project‚Äôs outcomes and policy 
recommendations.

II.	Objective and Justification
2.1	The specific objectives of the TC are: (I) To analyze the composition, functioning, and performance of the implementation models used in health infrastructure projects; (II) To identify best practices, common challenges, and critical factors affecting the efficiency and effectiveness of the hospital infrastructure implementation models; and (III) To assess the link between implementation performance and the achievement of health governance and service delivery outcomes, particularly in the development of health integrated networks.
2.2	The portfolio of Health, Nutrition and Population (HNP) projects that finance infrastructure has been increasing in the several years. Fifty-six percent of health projects now include hospital infrastructure. Best practices and lessons from implementation experience of hospital infrastructure and integrated health networks have not been systematized at portfolio level. 
2.3	Almost all projects with hospital infrastructure experience delays during implementation. There are different implementation models for the hospital infrastructure.  An analysis of the functioning of the different models used by HNP's projects will draw lessons to improve project design, supervision, and execution of infrastructure works. The analysis of the implementation mechanisms of infrastructure projects will focus on the composition and functioning of the three most common implementation models: (i) self-contained executing agencies; (ii) executing agencies that depend on other units (either internal or external) for the execution of activities; and (iii) external management entities. Delays of infrastructure works and good practices to avoid delays have not been systematized. 
2.4	Projects that finance or have financed health networks have encountered challenges in achieving outcome indicators and in achieving targets related to health governance, which are critical for the establishment and strengthening of health networks. While these projects have developed tools to support executing agencies in the analysis of health networks, there has not been a systematization of the tools used and important gaps remain in understanding the effectiveness of the interventions, limitations, and challenges associated with how the networks are functioning.  
Strategic alignment. This TC is aligned with the objectives of IDB Group's Institutional Strategy: Transformation for Greater Scale and Impact (CA-631) by: (i) reducing poverty and inequality by supporting the capacity to learn from operational experiences to improve project execution and project preparation. The TC also aligns with the following areas of operational focus: (i) sustainable, resilient and inclusive infrastructure; (ii) gender equality and inclusion of diverse groups, by taking into consideration these groups in the service provision analysis to determine how projects are addressing specific challenges faced by women and diverse populations; (ii) institutional capacity, rule of law and citizen security, through the analysis of alternatives to better evaluate of institutional capacity of executing agencies to execute hospital infrastructure projects to strengthen their capacity for project execution; and (iii) social protection and human capital development, as it aims at promoting effectiveness in projects of these areas.
2.5	This TC is part of stream T2 "Strategic knowledge of factors driving development effectiveness" of the Development Effectiveness Impact Fund (DEIF) 2025. This project has been selected for DEIF under a rigorous competitive process involving VPS, VPC, and SPD. The DEIF initiative supports projects that generate knowledge and address strategic gaps in development effectiveness through impact evaluations, analysis of execution factors, and  efective enhancement iniatives. Following the OC-SDP framework, this initiative is aligned with Window 2, under the priority area '5' Inclusive Social Development.

section_title: Objectives and Justification of the TC
section_text:
II. Objectives and Justification of the TC 
2.1 The general objective of this Technical Cooperation (TC) is to enhance agricultural 
productivity and innovation, strengthen climate change resilience, and promote food 
security by supporting the governments of the Latin America and Caribbean (LAC) 
region through the following specific objectives: (i) improving the efficiency and 
effectiveness of agricultural policies and identifying innovative opportunities to mitigate 
the environmental impact of agricultural practices; (ii) implementing and monitoring 
- 2 -
agricultural policies and programs; and (iii) designing policies that recognize and 
quantify the value of ecosystem services within agricultural systems.
2.2 The beneficiaries of the TC are the Ministries of Agriculture and the Agricultural 
Innovation Institutes, as well as the private actors of the agricultural sector of the 
countries included in the TC.
2.3 Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) stands at a critical juncture where agricultural 
development and environmental sustainability must be addressed in an integrated 
manner. Agriculture remains a vital economic driver in the region, contributing nearly 
7% of total GDP, above the global average. The region is home to several of the 
world‚Äôs most biodiverse ecosystems, including the Amazon forest, the Meso-American 
and Andean hotspots, and the Atlantic Forest. However, the expansion of agricultural 
production has increasingly come at the cost of environmental degradation. Land-use 
change, nutrient runoff, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and biodiversity loss are 
all accelerating, undermining the ecological resilience of agricultural systems. The 
Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) sector accounts for 43% of the 
region‚Äôs total GHG emissions. Between 1990 and 2020, forest cover in LAC declined 
from 53% to 46%, and South America registered the world‚Äôs second-highest rate of 
net forest loss between 2010 and 2020. Soil degradation is another serious concern, 
with nearly 50% of arable land in Central America and the Caribbean and 18% in South 
America facing high degradation severity, translating into economic losses estimated 
at 3% to 7% of agricultural GDP. 
2.4 These challenges are compounded by structural constraints in the agricultural sector. 
Climate change, manifesting through droughts, flooding, and extreme weather events, 
continues to threaten yields and increase production volatility. At the same time, family 
farmers often face limited access to financing, technology, and markets, which inhibits 
their ability to adapt and compete. High production costs, driven by fertilizer and fuel 
prices, restrict profitability. Compounding these issues is persistent food insecurity: as 
of 2023, 28.2% of the region's population, roughly 187.6 million people, faced 
moderate or severe food insecurity, with 6.2% experiencing hunger.
2.5 In response to these multidimensional challenges, governments in LAC must adopt 
agricultural policies that not only drive productivity but also safeguard natural 
resources and strengthen climate resilience. A comprehensive strategy is required, 
one that addresses both the supply and demand sides of the food system, while 
tackling financial, technological, and institutional barriers. The Inter-American 
Development Bank (IDB) is well positioned to support its member countries in this 
transition, due to its extensive experience with the design and implementation of 
evidence-based policies and investment in sustainable agricultural practices.  
2.6 Central to this effort is the use of agro-environmental indicators to inform policy 
decisions. These indicators provide policymakers with a comprehensive view of 
environmental risks and progress in the sector. They enable monitoring of critical 
variables‚Äîsuch as GHG and ammonia emissions, nutrient balances, and biodiversity 
impacts‚Äîand help identify problem areas that require corrective action. Moreover, 
they support LAC countries in aligning their agricultural strategies with international 
sustainability commitments, and in adopting a regional approach to climate and 
environmental governance. This evidence-based framework empowers governments 
to design balanced policies that protect the environment, promote long-term 
- 3 -
sustainability, and ensure the resilience and competitiveness of the region‚Äôs 
agriculture.
2.7 At the same time, conducting Producer Support Estimate (PSE) policy analysis is 
essential to enhance transparency, efficiency, and accountability in the allocation of 
public resources to agriculture. As part of the IDB‚Äôs Agrimonitor initiative, the PSE 
methodology provides a harmonized and internationally recognized framework to 
quantify the level and structure of support provided to agricultural producers. This 
analysis allows governments to identify whether public spending is effectively 
promoting productivity, sustainability, and inclusion, or reinforcing distortions and 
environmental degradation. By shedding light on who benefits, how much, and through 
which instruments, the PSE serves as a valuable diagnostic tool to inform policy 
reforms, align support with climate and development goals, and foster evidence-based 
dialogue across countries.
2.8 The TC is aligned with the Bank's institutional strategy IDBStrategy+ Transforming for 
Scale and Impact 2024-2030 (CA-631), in the following core objectives: (i) Addressing 
Climate Change, and (ii) Bolstering Sustainable Growth. To realize these aims, the TC 
directs its efforts toward the following focus areas: (i) Productive Development and 
Innovation through the Private Sector: This TC seeks to boost productivity and 
innovation by measuring and assessing the level of government support provided to 
agricultural producers, measuring agri-environmental indicators, supporting key 
programs, and providing robust evidence to foster a more resilient, productive, and 
innovative agricultural sector. These studies are important for LAC countries because 
agriculture plays a significant role in the region's economy, and the PSE and other 
studies related to agricultural policies can provide valuable information on the extent 
and nature of government support to the sector; (ii) Institutional capacity, rule of law, 
and citizen security: The TC will strengthen the dialogue between different national 
and regional institutions. This aims to generate greater technical capacity and 
knowledge on sustainable agriculture and efficient spending allocation. For instance, 
PSE and agri-environmental indicators are used as benchmarks to compare 
agricultural policies across countries and regions, enabling policymakers to learn from 
each other's experiences, identify best practices, and incorporate them to build 
institutional capacity; (iii) Biodiversity, Natural Capital and Climate Action: IDB has set 
a goal of aligning all its operations with the Paris Agreement. This TC seeks to build 
capacity, develop inputs and tools to measure the relationship between commodity-
specific policies and the environmental impact of these commodities, and boost 
ecosystem conservation; (iv) Regional Integration: The TC promotes regional 
integration by generating harmonized agro-environmental indicators, policy evaluation 
methodologies, and support measurement tools (PSE/FSE) that facilitate 
comparability and policy dialogue across countries. It also fosters cross-country 
collaboration through joint studies, peer learning, and dissemination workshops 
involving multiple LAC governments and regional institutions
2.9 The TC also aligns with the three challenges of the IDB Agriculture Sector Framework 
(GN-2709-16): (i) Improve food and nutrition security through agriculture; (ii) Increase 
income and climate resilience; and (iii) Promote agricultural practices that foster 
environmental sustainability. It also aligns with three of four of the cross-cutting lines 
of action: (i) Strengthen agricultural institutions; (ii) Reduce gender and ethnic gaps in 
agriculture; and (iii) Maintain an active and relevant knowledge agenda. Measuring the 
- 4 -
Producer Support Estimate (PSE) and developing robust studies on the effects of 
agricultural policies is important for boosting productivity and improving resource 
allocation in a more efficient and effective way to address the challenges the sector 
faces in a timely manner.
2.10 In addition, it aligns with the IDB Environment and Biodiversity Sector Framework (GN-
2827-8) by focusing on one of the three challenges it addresses: (i) Insufficiency of 
protecting mechanisms and gaps in governance. The TC will contribute to this 
challenge by assessing how different agricultural policies are affecting key biodiversity 
indicators and the mechanisms that exist in these agricultural policies to improve 
biodiversity. 
2.11 The TC also aligns with the GN-2819-14 OC-SDP, specifically with the following 
priority areas: (i) Climate Change and Environmental Sustainability (W2A) as it 
promotes opportunities for the productive sectors of LAC that directly depend on 
healthy and functional ecosystems (especially agriculture, and associated segments) 
to improve the transition towards sustainable production and development techniques; 
and (ii) Competitive Global and Regional Integration (W2D), by strengthening 
countries' capacity to design and implement agricultural and environmental policies 
that meet international standards, improving their ability to compete in global markets. 
By promoting harmonized indicators, transparency in public support, and climate-
smart practices, it enhances regional policy coherence and supports the region‚Äôs 
integration into sustainable and rules-based agri-food value chains. 
2.12 The TC aligns closely with the Country Strategies of Brazil (GN-3243-3, validity period 
2024-2027), Chile (GN-3140-3, validity period 2022-2026), the Dominican Republic 
(GN-3084-2, validity period 2021-2024), Ecuador (GN-3103-1, validity period 2022-
2025), El Salvador (GN-3046-4, validity period 2021-2024), Guatemala (GN-3260-1, 
validity period 2024-2028), Honduras (GN-2944-3, validity period 2019-2024), Mexico 
(GN-2982, validity period 2019-2024), Panama (GN-3289-1, validity period 2025-
2029), Paraguay (GN-3261-3, validity period 2025-2029), and Uruguay (GN-3056, 
validity period 2021-2025). It supports environmental sustainability, climate resilience, 
institutional strengthening, and evidence-based agricultural policymaking across the 
region.  In Brazil (GN-3243-3), the TC supports Pillar 1: Green Transition and Climate 
Resilience by evaluating the ABC+ Plan, advancing low-carbon agriculture, soil 
management, and institutional capacity through impact evaluation and policy learning. 
In Chile (GN-3140-3), the TC aligns with goals for inclusive and sustainable economic 
growth, climate action, and innovation, through its evaluation of the TAS program and 
use of agro-environmental indicators to enhance sustainability among small and 
medium-sized farmers. In Uruguay (GN-3056), the TC contributes to Pillar 1: 
Sustainable Productive Development by evaluating the National Soil Rotation Plan, 
supporting soil conservation and agro-environmental monitoring aligned with the 
strategy‚Äôs cross-cutting environmental objectives. In the Dominican Republic (GN-
3084-2), the TC supports Pillar 2: Sustainable and Inclusive Productive Reactivation, 
promoting transparency in public support through PSE studies and providing tools for 
more sustainable agricultural policy design. In Ecuador (GN-3103-1), the TC 
contributes to Pillar 1: Promote productive development in a sustainable and inclusive 
manner by applying PSE methodology and analyzing GHG emissions from agricultural 
policies, aligned with goals on green growth and institutional efficiency. In El Salvador             
(GN-3046-4), the TC supports the third priority area, revitalizing and restructuring 
- 5 -
production, by modernizing the agricultural sector through policy evaluations and 
sustainability indicators. It also addresses cross-cutting issues such as climate 
change, institutional capacity, and resilience to natural disasters. In Guatemala        
(GN-3260-1), the TC supports Pillar 3: Climate Action and Food Availability, advancing 
sustainable agriculture, GHG mitigation, and capacity building in agro-environmental 
management. In Honduras (GN-2944-3), the TC aligns with Priority Area III: Expansion 
of Sustainable Production Opportunities by offering tools and analysis to support rural 
development, climate adaptation, and agricultural sustainability, despite not 
conducting a direct evaluation. In Mexico (GN-2982), the TC supports goals for 
inclusive and sustainable growth, particularly through its extension of agro-
environmental indicators and support for climate adaptation and transparency in rural 
public expenditure. In Panama (GN-3289-1), the TC contributes to the goals of 
productive diversification and modernized public management, offering PSE/FSE 
analysis, policy studies, and GHG assessments, aligned with cross-cutting themes of 
environmental governance and digital modernization. In Paraguay (GN-3261-3), the 
TC supports Pillar 2: Sustainable and Resilient Productive Transformation and Pillar 
3: Institutional Capacity and State Modernization, advancing low-carbon agriculture 
and transparent evaluation of agricultural and fisheries support systems.

II. Objectives and Justification of the TC 
2.1 The general objective of this Technical Cooperation (TC) is to enhance agricultural 
productivity and innovation, strengthen climate change resilience, and promote food 
security by supporting the governments of the Latin America and Caribbean (LAC) 
region through the following specific objectives: (i) improving the efficiency and 
effectiveness of agricultural policies and identifying innovative opportunities to mitigate 
the environmental impact of agricultural practices; (ii) implementing and monitoring 
- 2 -
agricultural policies and programs; and (iii) designing policies that recognize and 
quantify the value of ecosystem services within agricultural systems.
2.2 The beneficiaries of the TC are the Ministries of Agriculture and the Agricultural 
Innovation Institutes, as well as the private actors of the agricultural sector of the 
countries included in the TC.
2.3 Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) stands at a critical juncture where agricultural 
development and environmental sustainability must be addressed in an integrated 
manner. Agriculture remains a vital economic driver in the region, contributing nearly 
7% of total GDP, above the global average. The region is home to several of the 
world‚Äôs most biodiverse ecosystems, including the Amazon forest, the Meso-American 
and Andean hotspots, and the Atlantic Forest. However, the expansion of agricultural 
production has increasingly come at the cost of environmental degradation. Land-use 
change, nutrient runoff, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and biodiversity loss are 
all accelerating, undermining the ecological resilience of agricultural systems. The 
Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) sector accounts for 43% of the 
region‚Äôs total GHG emissions. Between 1990 and 2020, forest cover in LAC declined 
from 53% to 46%, and South America registered the world‚Äôs second-highest rate of 
net forest loss between 2010 and 2020. Soil degradation is another serious concern, 
with nearly 50% of arable land in Central America and the Caribbean and 18% in South 
America facing high degradation severity, translating into economic losses estimated 
at 3% to 7% of agricultural GDP. 
2.4 These challenges are compounded by structural constraints in the agricultural sector. 
Climate change, manifesting through droughts, flooding, and extreme weather events, 
continues to threaten yields and increase production volatility. At the same time, family 
farmers often face limited access to financing, technology, and markets, which inhibits 
their ability to adapt and compete. High production costs, driven by fertilizer and fuel 
prices, restrict profitability. Compounding these issues is persistent food insecurity: as 
of 2023, 28.2% of the region's population, roughly 187.6 million people, faced 
moderate or severe food insecurity, with 6.2% experiencing hunger.
2.5 In response to these multidimensional challenges, governments in LAC must adopt 
agricultural policies that not only drive productivity but also safeguard natural 
resources and strengthen climate resilience. A comprehensive strategy is required, 
one that addresses both the supply and demand sides of the food system, while 
tackling financial, technological, and institutional barriers. The Inter-American 
Development Bank (IDB) is well positioned to support its member countries in this 
transition, due to its extensive experience with the design and implementation of 
evidence-based policies and investment in sustainable agricultural practices.  
2.6 Central to this effort is the use of agro-environmental indicators to inform policy 
decisions. These indicators provide policymakers with a comprehensive view of 
environmental risks and progress in the sector. They enable monitoring of critical 
variables‚Äîsuch as GHG and ammonia emissions, nutrient balances, and biodiversity 
impacts‚Äîand help identify problem areas that require corrective action. Moreover, 
they support LAC countries in aligning their agricultural strategies with international 
sustainability commitments, and in adopting a regional approach to climate and 
environmental governance. This evidence-based framework empowers governments 
to design balanced policies that protect the environment, promote long-term 
- 3 -
sustainability, and ensure the resilience and competitiveness of the region‚Äôs 
agriculture.
2.7 At the same time, conducting Producer Support Estimate (PSE) policy analysis is 
essential to enhance transparency, efficiency, and accountability in the allocation of 
public resources to agriculture. As part of the IDB‚Äôs Agrimonitor initiative, the PSE 
methodology provides a harmonized and internationally recognized framework to 
quantify the level and structure of support provided to agricultural producers. This 
analysis allows governments to identify whether public spending is effectively 
promoting productivity, sustainability, and inclusion, or reinforcing distortions and 
environmental degradation. By shedding light on who benefits, how much, and through 
which instruments, the PSE serves as a valuable diagnostic tool to inform policy 
reforms, align support with climate and development goals, and foster evidence-based 
dialogue across countries.
2.8 The TC is aligned with the Bank's institutional strategy IDBStrategy+ Transforming for 
Scale and Impact 2024-2030 (CA-631), in the following core objectives: (i) Addressing 
Climate Change, and (ii) Bolstering Sustainable Growth. To realize these aims, the TC 
directs its efforts toward the following focus areas: (i) Productive Development and 
Innovation through the Private Sector: This TC seeks to boost productivity and 
innovation by measuring and assessing the level of government support provided to 
agricultural producers, measuring agri-environmental indicators, supporting key 
programs, and providing robust evidence to foster a more resilient, productive, and 
innovative agricultural sector. These studies are important for LAC countries because 
agriculture plays a significant role in the region's economy, and the PSE and other 
studies related to agricultural policies can provide valuable information on the extent 
and nature of government support to the sector; (ii) Institutional capacity, rule of law, 
and citizen security: The TC will strengthen the dialogue between different national 
and regional institutions. This aims to generate greater technical capacity and 
knowledge on sustainable agriculture and efficient spending allocation. For instance, 
PSE and agri-environmental indicators are used as benchmarks to compare 
agricultural policies across countries and regions, enabling policymakers to learn from 
each other's experiences, identify best practices, and incorporate them to build 
institutional capacity; (iii) Biodiversity, Natural Capital and Climate Action: IDB has set 
a goal of aligning all its operations with the Paris Agreement. This TC seeks to build 
capacity, develop inputs and tools to measure the relationship between commodity-
specific policies and the environmental impact of these commodities, and boost 
ecosystem conservation; (iv) Regional Integration: The TC promotes regional 
integration by generating harmonized agro-environmental indicators, policy evaluation 
methodologies, and support measurement tools (PSE/FSE) that facilitate 
comparability and policy dialogue across countries. It also fosters cross-country 
collaboration through joint studies, peer learning, and dissemination workshops 
involving multiple LAC governments and regional institutions
2.9 The TC also aligns with the three challenges of the IDB Agriculture Sector Framework 
(GN-2709-16): (i) Improve food and nutrition security through agriculture; (ii) Increase 
income and climate resilience; and (iii) Promote agricultural practices that foster 
environmental sustainability. It also aligns with three of four of the cross-cutting lines 
of action: (i) Strengthen agricultural institutions; (ii) Reduce gender and ethnic gaps in 
agriculture; and (iii) Maintain an active and relevant knowledge agenda. Measuring the 
- 4 -
Producer Support Estimate (PSE) and developing robust studies on the effects of

II. Objectives and Justification of the TC 
2.1 The general objective of this Technical Cooperation (TC) is to enhance agricultural 
productivity and innovation, strengthen climate change resilience, and promote food 
security by supporting the governments of the Latin America and Caribbean (LAC) 
region through the following specific objectives: (i) improving the efficiency and 
effectiveness of agricultural policies and identifying innovative opportunities to mitigate 
the environmental impact of agricultural practices; (ii) implementing and monitoring 
- 2 -
agricultural policies and programs; and (iii) designing policies that recognize and 
quantify the value of ecosystem services within agricultural systems.
2.2 The beneficiaries of the TC are the Ministries of Agriculture and the Agricultural 
Innovation Institutes, as well as the private actors of the agricultural sector of the 
countries included in the TC.
2.3 Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) stands at a critical juncture where agricultural 
development and environmental sustainability must be addressed in an integrated 
manner. Agriculture remains a vital economic driver in the region, contributing nearly 
7% of total GDP, above the global average. The region is home to several of the 
world‚Äôs most biodiverse ecosystems, including the Amazon forest, the Meso-American 
and Andean hotspots, and the Atlantic Forest. However, the expansion of agricultural 
production has increasingly come at the cost of environmental degradation. Land-use 
change, nutrient runoff, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and biodiversity loss are 
all accelerating, undermining the ecological resilience of agricultural systems. The 
Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) sector accounts for 43% of the 
region‚Äôs total GHG emissions. Between 1990 and 2020, forest cover in LAC declined 
from 53% to 46%, and South America registered the world‚Äôs second-highest rate of 
net forest loss between 2010 and 2020. Soil degradation is another serious concern, 
with nearly 50% of arable land in Central America and the Caribbean and 18% in South 
America facing high degradation severity, translating into economic losses estimated 
at 3% to 7% of agricultural GDP. 
2.4 These challenges are compounded by structural constraints in the agricultural sector. 
Climate change, manifesting through droughts, flooding, and extreme weather events, 
continues to threaten yields and increase production volatility. At the same time, family 
farmers often face limited access to financing, technology, and markets, which inhibits 
their ability to adapt and compete. High production costs, driven by fertilizer and fuel 
prices, restrict profitability. Compounding these issues is persistent food insecurity: as 
of 2023, 28.2% of the region's population, roughly 187.6 million people, faced 
moderate or severe food insecurity, with 6.2% experiencing hunger.
2.5 In response to these multidimensional challenges, governments in LAC must adopt 
agricultural policies that not only drive productivity but also safeguard natural 
resources and strengthen climate resilience. A comprehensive strategy is required, 
one that addresses both the supply and demand sides of the food system, while 
tackling financial, technological, and institutional barriers. The Inter-American 
Development Bank (IDB) is well positioned to support its member countries in this 
transition, due to its extensive experience with the design and implementation of 
evidence-based policies and investment in sustainable agricultural practices.  
2.6 Central to this effort is the use of agro-environmental indicators to inform policy 
decisions. These indicators provide policymakers with a comprehensive view of 
environmental risks and progress in the sector. They enable monitoring of critical 
variables‚Äîsuch as GHG and ammonia emissions, nutrient balances, and biodiversity 
impacts‚Äîand help identify problem areas that require corrective action. Moreover, 
they support LAC countries in aligning their agricultural strategies with international 
sustainability commitments, and in adopting a regional approach to climate and 
environmental governance. This evidence-based framework empowers governments 
to design balanced policies that protect the environment, promote long-term 
- 3 -
sustainability, and ensure the resilience and competitiveness of the region‚Äôs 
agriculture.
2.7 At the same time, conducting Producer Support Estimate (PSE) policy analysis is 
essential to enhance transparency, efficiency, and accountability in the allocation of 
public resources to agriculture. As part of the IDB‚Äôs Agrimonitor initiative, the PSE 
methodology provides a harmonized and internationally recognized framework to 
quantify the level and structure of support provided to agricultural producers. This 
analysis allows governments to identify whether public spending is effectively 
promoting productivity, sustainability, and inclusion, or reinforcing distortions and 
environmental degradation. By shedding light on who benefits, how much, and through 
which instruments, the PSE serves as a valuable diagnostic tool to inform policy 
reforms, align support with climate and development goals, and foster evidence-based 
dialogue across countries.
2.8 The TC is aligned with the Bank's institutional strategy IDBStrategy+ Transforming for 
Scale and Impact 2024-2030 (CA-631), in the following core objectives: (i) Addressing 
Climate Change, and (ii) Bolstering Sustainable Growth. To realize these aims, the TC 
directs its efforts toward the following focus areas: (i) Productive Development and 
Innovation through the Private Sector: This TC seeks to boost productivity and 
innovation by measuring and assessing the level of government support provided to 
agricultural producers, measuring agri-environmental indicators, supporting key 
programs, and providing robust evidence to foster a more resilient, productive, and 
innovative agricultural sector. These studies are important for LAC countries because 
agriculture plays a significant role in the region's economy, and the PSE and other 
studies related to agricultural policies can provide valuable information on the extent 
and nature of government support to the sector; (ii) Institutional capacity, rule of law, 
and citizen security: The TC will strengthen the dialogue between different national 
and regional institutions. This aims to generate greater technical capacity and 
knowledge on sustainable agriculture and efficient spending allocation. For instance, 
PSE and agri-environmental indicators are used as benchmarks to compare 
agricultural policies across countries and regions, enabling policymakers to learn from 
each other's experiences, identify best practices, and incorporate them to build 
institutional capacity; (iii) Biodiversity, Natural Capital and Climate Action: IDB has set 
a goal of aligning all its operations with the Paris Agreement. This TC seeks to build 
capacity, develop inputs and tools to measure the relationship between commodity-
specific policies and the environmental impact of these commodities, and boost 
ecosystem conservation; (iv) Regional Integration: The TC promotes regional 
integration by generating harmonized agro-environmental indicators, policy evaluation 
methodologies, and support measurement tools (PSE/FSE) that facilitate 
comparability and policy dialogue across countries. It also fosters cross-country 
collaboration through joint studies, peer learning, and dissemination workshops 
involving multiple LAC governments and regional institutions

income and climate resilience; and (iii) Promote agricultural practices that foster 
environmental sustainability. It also aligns with three of four of the cross-cutting lines

II. Objectives and Justification of the TC 
2.1 The general objective of this Technical Cooperation (TC) is to enhance agricultural 
productivity and innovation, strengthen climate change resilience, and promote food 
security by supporting the governments of the Latin America and Caribbean (LAC) 
region through the following specific objectives: (i) improving the efficiency and 
effectiveness of agricultural policies and identifying innovative opportunities to mitigate 
the environmental impact of agricultural practices; (ii) implementing and monitoring 
- 2 -
agricultural policies and programs; and (iii) designing policies that recognize and 
quantify the value of ecosystem services within agricultural systems.
2.2 The beneficiaries of the TC are the Ministries of Agriculture and the Agricultural 
Innovation Institutes, as well as the private actors of the agricultural sector of the 
countries included in the TC.
2.3 Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) stands at a critical juncture where agricultural 
development and environmental sustainability must be addressed in an integrated 
manner. Agriculture remains a vital economic driver in the region, contributing nearly 
7% of total GDP, above the global average. The region is home to several of the 
world‚Äôs most biodiverse ecosystems, including the Amazon forest, the Meso-American 
and Andean hotspots, and the Atlantic Forest. However, the expansion of agricultural 
production has increasingly come at the cost of environmental degradation. Land-use 
change, nutrient runoff, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and biodiversity loss are 
all accelerating, undermining the ecological resilience of agricultural systems. The 
Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) sector accounts for 43% of the 
region‚Äôs total GHG emissions. Between 1990 and 2020, forest cover in LAC declined 
from 53% to 46%, and South America registered the world‚Äôs second-highest rate of 
net forest loss between 2010 and 2020. Soil degradation is another serious concern, 
with nearly 50% of arable land in Central America and the Caribbean and 18% in South 
America facing high degradation severity, translating into economic losses estimated 
at 3% to 7% of agricultural GDP. 
2.4 These challenges are compounded by structural constraints in the agricultural sector. 
Climate change, manifesting through droughts, flooding, and extreme weather events, 
continues to threaten yields and increase production volatility. At the same time, family 
farmers often face limited access to financing, technology, and markets, which inhibits 
their ability to adapt and compete. High production costs, driven by fertilizer and fuel 
prices, restrict profitability. Compounding these issues is persistent food insecurity: as 
of 2023, 28.2% of the region's population, roughly 187.6 million people, faced 
moderate or severe food insecurity, with 6.2% experiencing hunger.
2.5 In response to these multidimensional challenges, governments in LAC must adopt 
agricultural policies that not only drive productivity but also safeguard natural 
resources and strengthen climate resilience. A comprehensive strategy is required, 
one that addresses both the supply and demand sides of the food system, while 
tackling financial, technological, and institutional barriers. The Inter-American 
Development Bank (IDB) is well positioned to support its member countries in this 
transition, due to its extensive experience with the design and implementation of 
evidence-based policies and investment in sustainable agricultural practices.  
2.6 Central to this effort is the use of agro-environmental indicators to inform policy 
decisions. These indicators provide policymakers with a comprehensive view of 
environmental risks and progress in the sector. They enable monitoring of critical 
variables‚Äîsuch as GHG and ammonia emissions, nutrient balances, and biodiversity 
impacts‚Äîand help identify problem areas that require corrective action. Moreover, 
they support LAC countries in aligning their agricultural strategies with international 
sustainability commitments, and in adopting a regional approach to climate and 
environmental governance. This evidence-based framework empowers governments 
to design balanced policies that protect the environment, promote long-term 
- 3 -
sustainability, and ensure the resilience and competitiveness of the region‚Äôs 
agriculture.
2.7 At the same time, conducting Producer Support Estimate (PSE) policy analysis is 
essential to enhance transparency, efficiency, and accountability in the allocation of 
public resources to agriculture. As part of the IDB‚Äôs Agrimonitor initiative, the PSE 
methodology provides a harmonized and internationally recognized framework to 
quantify the level and structure of support provided to agricultural producers. This 
analysis allows governments to identify whether public spending is effectively 
promoting productivity, sustainability, and inclusion, or reinforcing distortions and 
environmental degradation. By shedding light on who benefits, how much, and through 
which instruments, the PSE serves as a valuable diagnostic tool to inform policy 
reforms, align support with climate and development goals, and foster evidence-based 
dialogue across countries.
2.8 The TC is aligned with the Bank's institutional strategy IDBStrategy+ Transforming for 
Scale and Impact 2024-2030 (CA-631), in the following core objectives: (i) Addressing 
Climate Change, and (ii) Bolstering Sustainable Growth. To realize these aims, the TC 
directs its efforts toward the following focus areas: (i) Productive Development and 
Innovation through the Private Sector: This TC seeks to boost productivity and 
innovation by measuring and assessing the level of government support provided to 
agricultural producers, measuring agri-environmental indicators, supporting key 
programs, and providing robust evidence to foster a more resilient, productive, and 
innovative agricultural sector. These studies are important for LAC countries because 
agriculture plays a significant role in the region's economy, and the PSE and other 
studies related to agricultural policies can provide valuable information on the extent 
and nature of government support to the sector; (ii) Institutional capacity, rule of law, 
and citizen security: The TC will strengthen the dialogue between different national 
and regional institutions. This aims to generate greater technical capacity and 
knowledge on sustainable agriculture and efficient spending allocation. For instance, 
PSE and agri-environmental indicators are used as benchmarks to compare 
agricultural policies across countries and regions, enabling policymakers to learn from 
each other's experiences, identify best practices, and incorporate them to build 
institutional capacity; (iii) Biodiversity, Natural Capital and Climate Action: IDB has set 
a goal of aligning all its operations with the Paris Agreement. This TC seeks to build 
capacity, develop inputs and tools to measure the relationship between commodity-
specific policies and the environmental impact of these commodities, and boost 
ecosystem conservation; (iv) Regional Integration: The TC promotes regional 
integration by generating harmonized agro-environmental indicators, policy evaluation 
methodologies, and support measurement tools (PSE/FSE) that facilitate 
comparability and policy dialogue across countries. It also fosters cross-country 
collaboration through joint studies, peer learning, and dissemination workshops 
involving multiple LAC governments and regional institutions
2.9 The TC also aligns with the three challenges of the IDB Agriculture Sector Framework 
(GN-2709-16): (i) Improve food and nutrition security through agriculture; (ii) Increase 
income and climate resilience; and (iii) Promote agricultural practices that foster 
environmental sustainability. It also aligns with three of four of the cross-cutting lines

agriculture; and (iii) Maintain an active and relevant knowledge agenda. Measuring the 
- 4 -
Producer Support Estimate (PSE) and developing robust studies on the effects of

2.7 At the same time, conducting Producer Support Estimate (PSE) policy analysis is 
essential to enhance transparency, efficiency, and accountability in the allocation of 
public resources to agriculture. As part of the IDB‚Äôs Agrimonitor initiative, the PSE 
methodology provides a harmonized and internationally recognized framework to 
quantify the level and structure of support provided to agricultural producers. This 
analysis allows governments to identify whether public spending is effectively 
promoting productivity, sustainability, and inclusion, or reinforcing distortions and 
environmental degradation. By shedding light on who benefits, how much, and through 
which instruments, the PSE serves as a valuable diagnostic tool to inform policy 
reforms, align support with climate and development goals, and foster evidence-based 
dialogue across countries.

Scale and Impact 2024-2030 (CA-631), in the following core objectives: (i) Addressing

directs its efforts toward the following focus areas: (i) Productive Development and 
Innovation through the Private Sector: This TC seeks to boost productivity and 
innovation by measuring and assessing the level of government support provided to 
agricultural producers, measuring agri-environmental indicators, supporting key 
programs, and providing robust evidence to foster a more resilient, productive, and 
innovative agricultural sector. These studies are important for LAC countries because 
agriculture plays a significant role in the region's economy, and the PSE and other 
studies related to agricultural policies can provide valuable information on the extent 
and nature of government support to the sector; (ii) Institutional capacity, rule of law, 
and citizen security: The TC will strengthen the dialogue between different national 
and regional institutions. This aims to generate greater technical capacity and 
knowledge on sustainable agriculture and efficient spending allocation. For instance, 
PSE and agri-environmental indicators are used as benchmarks to compare 
agricultural policies across countries and regions, enabling policymakers to learn from 
each other's experiences, identify best practices, and incorporate them to build 
institutional capacity; (iii) Biodiversity, Natural Capital and Climate Action: IDB has set

capacity, develop inputs and tools to measure the relationship between commodity-

ecosystem conservation; (iv) Regional Integration: The TC promotes regional 
integration by generating harmonized agro-environmental indicators, policy evaluation 
methodologies, and support measurement tools (PSE/FSE) that facilitate 
comparability and policy dialogue across countries. It also fosters cross-country 
collaboration through joint studies, peer learning, and dissemination workshops 
involving multiple LAC governments and regional institutions

III. Description of activities/components and budget 
3.1Component I. Agro-environmental Analysis and Policy Impact Evaluation 
(US$300,000). The agri-environmental indicators developed by the OECD capture key 
aspects of the relationship between agricultural activities and environmental 
performance. This includes: (i) characterization of the agricultural sector; 
(ii) agricultural land-use change; (iii) production and input use; (iv) nutrients; 
(v) greenhouse gas emissions; (vi) ammonia emissions; and (vii) farmland birds‚Äô 
biodiversity (OECD, 2023)1. The indicators highlight the progress and challenges in 
balancing agricultural productivity with environmental sustainability, including the risks 
of nutrient runoff, greenhouse gas emissions, and biodiversity loss. Currently the 
OECD has analyzed four LAC countries: Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica and Mexico.  
This component aims to expand and deepen the analysis in other LAC countries as 
well. The goal is to support evidence-based policy-making that promotes sustainable 
agricultural development in LAC countries, aligning regional performance with global 
environmental goals.  
3.2 This component will produce a set of outputs aimed at strengthening the analytical 
foundations and monitoring tools for agro-environmental policymaking in LAC. First, it 
will deliver a regional review of existing agro-environmental policies, providing a 
comparative analysis of policy frameworks and identifying key gaps and opportunities. 
Second, it will develop and systematize a set of agro-environmental indicators to 
improve the monitoring of sustainability outcomes in agriculture, adapted to the 
specific contexts of at least one participating country. Third, a cross-country analytical 
study will examine the relationship between agricultural policies and greenhouse gas 
(GHG) emissions, identifying key policy drivers and potential mitigation pathways. 
Fourth, three rigorous impact evaluations will assess the environmental effects of 
specific agricultural policy instruments, with a focus on GHG emissions and other  
agro-environmental outcomes. In Chile, the analysis will focus on the environmental 
1 OECD (2025), Environmental Performance of Agriculture in OECD Countries: Key Trends and Insights, 
OECD Publishing, Paris, https://doi.org/10.1787/2679ba38-en.
- 6 -
impacts of the ‚ÄúTransici√≥n a la Agricultura Sostenible‚Äù (TAS) program implemented by 
INDAP. This program supports small and medium-sized farmers in adopting 
sustainable production practices through technical assistance, incentives for 
agroecological transition, and sustainable land use planning. The evaluation will 
examine the program‚Äôs effects on soil quality, input use efficiency, and GHG 
emissions, particularly in regions with significant TAS implementation. In Uruguay, the 
study will conduct an in-depth evaluation of the National Soil Rotation Plan, assessing 
its environmental impacts on soil loss and quality. The plan promotes sustainable soil 
management by requiring farmers to submit planting plans aligned with land use 
capacity and erosion risk criteria. In Brazil, the focus will be on the Plan for Adaptation 
and Low Carbon Emission in Agriculture (ABC+), assessing its environmental impacts 
on soil quality, deforestation and GHG emissions. The plan integrates landscape-level 
approaches, environmental compliance, adoption of low-carbon technologies, 
capacity-building, and improved rural management systems. Finally, the component 
will include three participatory workshops (one in person and two online) to present 
and discuss findings with stakeholders, and a set of communication and dissemination 
products to support knowledge sharing and policy dialogue. 
3.3 The expected outputs of this component include: (i) a regional review of agricultural 
policies; (ii) agro-environmental indicators developed in one country; (iii) a cross-
sectional analysis on the relationship between agricultural policies and GHG 
emissions; (iv) three impact evaluations; and (v) three dissemination workshops. 
3.4 The activities will include contracting local research consultants in each country and 
partnering with specialized regional universities with extensive experience in 
agricultural sector research. Also, a peer review process will be conducted, in which 
the studies will be evaluated by experts in the field.
3.5Component II. Agricultural and Fisheries Policy Analysis (US$320,000). This 
component will enhance transparency and support evidence-based decision-making 
by analyzing both the level and structure of public support to agriculture and the 
effectiveness of agricultural policy implementation. Developed within the framework of 
the IDB‚Äôs Agrimonitor initiative, it builds on the Bank‚Äôs ongoing efforts to promote 
harmonized measurement of agricultural support and informed policy dialogue in the 
region. Key outputs will include four Producer Support Estimate (PSE) studies 
conducted at the national or subnational level, applying internationally recognized 
methodologies to assess the magnitude, composition, and trends of government 
support in Ecuador, Paraguay, Panama, and the Dominican Republic. Additionally, 
two Fisheries Support Estimate (FSE) studies will evaluate public support to the 
fisheries sector, contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of support 
across food production systems. The component will also produce three technical 
studies on the implementation of key agricultural policies or programs, focusing on 
institutional design, coordination mechanisms, operational challenges, and lessons 
learned. These analytical products will be complemented by four workshops (two in 
person and two online) that combine results validation with training sessions for 
government officials and technical staff, and by communication and dissemination 
activities aimed at sharing findings and encouraging regional dialogue on policy reform 
and implementation.
- 7 -
3.6 The expected outputs of this component include: (i) four national PSE studies that 
quantify and analyze public support to agriculture; (ii) two FSE studies assessing 
support to the fisheries sector; (iii) three technical studies on the implementation of 
key agricultural policies or programs; (iv) four workshops that serve both as validation 
and capacity-building events for government officials and technical counterparts; and 
(v) a set of communication and dissemination products, such as policy briefs, 
summaries, and infographics, to promote broader visibility and facilitate the use of 
findings in policy processes.
3.7 The activities will include the contracting of local consultants in each country as well 
as the contracting of specialized regional agencies, such as FAO and/or IFPRI, which 
have extensive experience in the agricultural sector, the PSE and FSE indicators. For 
Component 3, the hiring of IFPRI is planned through a direct contracting, as the 
activities included in the Component are part of the AVANZAR 2030 initiative, that 
IFPRI is leading in the region. Therefore, no other company on the market can provide 
similar services. 
3.8Component III. Evidence Synthesis on Carbon Sequestration Interventions in 
Agriculture (US$80,000). This component will support the implementation of a study 
led by the AVANZAR2030 initiative, in collaboration with IFPRI, IICA, and Juno 
Evidence Alliance, aimed at synthesizing evidence on interventions that promote 
carbon sequestration in agrifood systems as a key strategy to address climate change. 
In line with AVANZAR2030‚Äôs guiding principles of rigor, inclusiveness, transparency, 
and accessibility, the study will generate actionable evidence for policymakers through 
a structured synthesis of available research. It will focus on two countries, considering 
their diverse ecological, climatic, and production contexts, including variations in cattle 
breeds and land use practices. The analysis will identify, prioritize, and assess the 
impact of promising carbon sequestration practices, particularly in the livestock sector. 
Drawing on both scientific and grey literature in Spanish and English, the study will 
involve a systematic screening process using predefined inclusion and exclusion 
criteria, followed by in-depth review, data extraction, and both quantitative and 
qualitative analysis. The final output, a research paper, will provide policy 
recommendations tailored to national contexts and contribute to building a regional 
public good that supports evidence-informed decision-making for climate-smart 
agricultural policies.
3.9 The expected outputs of this component are: (i) one working paper; (ii) one 
participatory workshop (in person) with government officials and key private sector 
actors from the selected countries; and (iii) one dissemination event. The activities will 
include the direct contracting of IFPRI, as the activities included in Component III are 
part of the AVANZAR 2030 initiative, that IFPRI is leading in the region. Therefore, no 
other company on the market can provide similar services. Also, a peer review process 
will be conducted, in which the research paper will be evaluated by experts in the field.
3.10 The financing of the operation is provided by the IDB (W2A and W2D). No local 
financial contribution is expected.

recommendations tailored to national contexts and contribute to building a regional 
public good that supports evidence-informed decision-making for climate-smart 
agricultural policies.

IV. Executing agency and execution structure 
4.1 This operation will be executed by the IDB given the regional coverage of the activities 
to be performed and possible synergies and complementarities with Bank operations 
and research. The execution and disbursement period will be 30 months. Carmine 
Paolo De Salvo (PTI/ARD) and Gonzalo Rondinone (PTI/ARD) will jointly share 
execution responsibilities of the proposed TC. Sectoral specialists in the respective 
countries will also participate in the studies and their supervision. The Climate Change 
Division (CSD/CCS) will also support the implementation of the TC. The technical 
counterparts in the respective governments will be public policy planning offices in the 
Ministries of Agriculture and Fisheries. The TC will be executed by the IDB in 
accordance with the Bank's Policy for Technical Cooperation (GN-2470-2) and the 
corresponding Operational Guidelines (OP-619-4).
4.2 The principal reason for this execution scheme is that the Bank has the expertise, 
capacity and experience identifying and filling knowledge gaps and building 
institutional capacities at the regional scale. A second reason is related to 
dissemination given that the policy implications from the proposed studies will be 
informative and helpful to other countries in the region. The ARD team has a proven 
track record of executing similar TCs with satisfactory results. The team has executed 
similar TCs in the Caribbean Region and Central American Region. In addition to the 
ongoing TC RG-T4292 being implemented for selected countries in the region. Three 
country studies have been completed under TC RG-T4292 so far, and two are 
currently under finalization.  ARD has collaborated with the Climate Change Division 
on similar studies, such as the ongoing Producer Support Estimate (PSE) analyses in 
Belize and El Salvador. These studies include an examination of agricultural policies 
and programs across LAC countries. Another study was conducted at the regional 
level in 2023 and successfully published. It was disseminated at the IDB Agrimonitor 
10-year event in 2024, targeting a wide audience interested in agricultural policies. 
This report, the third in its series, systematically analyzed agricultural support policies 
in 25 LAC countries, using the OECD‚Äôs PSE methodology. In addition, other ongoing 
studies include analyses of the maize tortilla value chain in Mexico and the rice value 
chain in Colombia.
- 9 -
4.3 These studies have significantly contributed to improving policy dialogue in the 
countries that are the focus of this TC. The forthcoming studies funded by this TC will 
provide a closer examination of domestic agricultural, fisheries, and environmental 
policies. They will generate the necessary information to update the studies mentioned 
earlier and will be of great help in addressing the challenges faced by the LAC region 
in the areas of agricultural productivity and innovation, food security, and enhancing 
climate change resilience. Prior to the initiation of activities in the beneficiary countries 
the corresponding letter of non-objection will be sought from the Bank's liaison entity 
in the country. 
4.1 The supervision of the TC will be led by the PTI/ARD team, in coordination with 
PTI/ARD sector specialists in the respective countries who will also act as focal points. 
The data collection and research activities will be carried out by local contractuals, 
who will be hired and remunerated through the TC. The work of the contractuals will 
be closely monitored bi-monthly, and as often as required by the TC team. Given that 
this supervision will be conducted remotely and by sectoral specialists in the countries, 
there will be no additional cost associated with monitoring and data revision. The three 
components can be worked on in parallel during the TC period, as they are 
independent and do not rely on one another. This approach allows for efficient 
progress across all of them simultaneously. Most of the workshops will be conducted 
remotely in order to save time and resources. 
4.2Procurement. All procurement to be executed under this Technical Cooperation have 
been included in the Procurement Plan (Annex IV) and will be hired in compliance with 
the applicable Bank policies and regulations as follows: (a) Hiring of individual 
consultants, as established in the regulation on Complementary Workforce (AM-650) 
and (b) Contracting of services provided by consulting firms in accordance with the 
Corporate procurement Policy (GN-2303-33) and its Guidelines

V. Major issues 
5.1 The main risk during the execution of the TC is the availability of information to carry 
out the analysis. Limited access to reliable and up-to-date data could make it 
challenging to analyze the effectiveness of agricultural policies and develop evidence-
based recommendations. To mitigate this risk, governments will express their interest 
and commitment in each specific initiative and will assign technical counterparts for 
supporting the gathering and analysis of information. Another risk is the change of 
policy priorities in countries that will change their administration during the execution 
of this TC and, therefore, the sustainability of the efforts made. This risk is mitigated 
by the permanent dialogue of the IDB, including a strong continuous coordination effort 
with the Country Representative and Chief of Operations, in the different countries and 
the neutral, evidence-based nature of the proposed studies.
5.2 The knowledge products generated from Bank-executed activities within this TC will 
be the property of the Bank and may be made available to the public under a creative 
commons license. However, at the request of the beneficiaries, in accordance with the 
provisions of AM-331, the intellectual property of said products may also be licensed 
through specific contractual commitments that shall be prepared with the advice of the 
Legal Department.

II. Description of the Associated Loan
2.1 Since 2017, the city of Salvador has been implementing a program aimed at increasing 
employment and income generated by tourism in the municipality, Prodetur Salvador 
(BR-L1412). The general objective of the program is to promote tourism development 
to increase income and formal employment generated for the population of Salvador, 
with an emphasis on local culture and Afro-descendants. The specific objectives are 
to increase the spending by tourists in Salvador, as well as the portion of that spending 
that benefits the community, particularly the Afro-descendant population, through the 
promotion of cultural and beach tourism, infrastructure improvement, and institutional 
support for tourism management.
2.2 With a range of varied actions, the program included specific activities aimed at 
qualifying workers and entrepreneurs for the tourism sector labor market. These 
specific projects aimed to qualify vulnerable workers for the tourism sector, as well as 
qualify entrepreneurs for Afro-ethnic tourism related activities (including a wide array 
of activities, such as gastronomy, culture, guiding services, etc.). Prodetur had its last 
disbursement in June 2024, and its PCR is under preparation.
- 2 -
2.3 The IDB will also finance a second loan operation with the city, Salvador Capital Afro 
(BR-L1636), in design stage. The new Program aims to improve the quality of the 
experience of tourists visiting the municipality, as well as contribute to reducing the 
socioeconomic inequalities affecting the Afro-descendant population within the local 
tourism sector's value chain. The loan will include a component focused on Afro-
tourism and is expected to be approved in 2025.
