section_text:
III. Objectives and Justification of the TC
3.1Objective. The objective of this TC is to develop and implement an impact evaluation 
of the Afroestima Training Program (AFE), financed by operation BR-L1412 (Prodetur 
Salvador), and provide inputs for the design of optimal interventions under the scope 
of the new loan in preparation, BR-L1636 (Salvador Capital Afro).
3.2Main questions to be focused. The evaluation aims to compare what happened to 
individuals who were trained by the AFE with what would have happened to those 
same individuals that had not taken the training course. Using technical resources, we 
will evaluate five training cycles carried out in the AFE, financed between 2021 and 
2024, with the aim of answering some key questions: Was the AFE successful in 
increasing the average income and employability of those trained? Are there 
heterogeneous effects - men vs women, spec. age groups, different levels of 
education? Was the AFE capable of increasing formalization and accreditation of 
participants?
3.3Justification and theory of change. Public training policies for owners of small and 
medium-sized businesses have become common around the world, especially in 
developing countries. Such initiatives are mostly aimed at increasing productivity, 
income, and the skills of more vulnerable workers. According to the literature, there 
are several reasons to believe that minorities benefit even more from these types of 
programs than non-minority populations. First, networks are generally an important 
asset for the success of businesses, and there is evidence that minorities have 
experienced smaller and less connected networks (Ibarra, 1993; Aldrich and 
Waldinger, 1990; Seidel, Polzer, and Stewart, 2000)1. Moreover, training programs for 
small and medium-sized businesses can provide access to knowledge that would 
otherwise be difficult for minorities to obtain (Card and Giuliano, 2016)2. Another 
important factor is that minorities are disproportionately exposed to self-employment 
and have less access to capital to start their businesses, thus potentially benefiting 
more from training (Dunn and Holtz-Eakin, 2000; Fairlie and Robb, 2007; Fairlie, 
2006)3. Lastly, minorities may face discrimination from investors and consumers 
1 IBARRA, HERMINIA (1993). ‚ÄúPersonal Networks of Women and Minorities in Management: A Conceptual 
Framework.‚Äù Academy of Management Review 18 (1): 56‚Äì87. ALDRICH, HOWARD E., & ROGER 
WALDINGER (1990). ‚ÄúEthnicity and Entrepreneurship.‚Äù Annual Review of Sociology 16 (1): 111‚Äì35. 
SEIDEL, MARC-DAVID L., JEFFREY T. POLZER, & KATHERINE J. STEWART (2000). ‚ÄúFriends in High 
Places: The Effects of Social Networks on Discrimination in Salary Negotiations.‚Äù Administrative Science 
Quarterly 45 (1): 1‚Äì24.
2 CARD, DAVID, & LAURA GIULIANO (2016). ‚ÄúCan Tracking Raise the Test Scores of High-Ability Minority 
Students?‚Äù American Economic Review 106 (10): 2783‚Äì816.
3 DUNN, THOMAS, & DOUGLAS HOLTZ-EAKIN (2000). ‚ÄúFinancial Capital, Human Capital, and the 
Transition to Self-Employment: Evidence from Intergenerational Links.‚Äù Journal of Labor Economics 18 
(2): 282‚Äì305 FAIRLIE, ROBERT W (2006). ‚ÄúEntrepreneurship among Disadvantaged Groups: Women, 
Minorities and the Less Educated.‚Äù In International Handbook Series on Entrepreneurship, Vol. 3. New 
York: Springer. FAIRLIE, ROBERT W., & ALICIA M. ROBB. 2007. ‚ÄúWhy Are Black-Owned Businesses 
- 3 -
(Blanchflower, Levine, and Zimmerman, 2003; Brooks et al., 2014)4. Other studies 
have also shown that, in the short term, non-minorities benefit more from 
entrepreneurial training programs, but in the long term, the effect is much greater for 
women and non-whites. Although these findings are related to the program to be 
studied in this evaluation, AFE has slightly different aspects, such as part of the 
training program's curriculum focusing on the appreciation of Afro-Ethnic culture and 
tourism. In this regard, based on the positive results that programs focusing on socio-
emotional aspects have achieved (Camargo et al, 2021; Barrera-Osorio et al, 2021), 
an even better outcome is expected from AFE compared to the above-mentioned 
evaluation articles.
3.4 The costs and benefits of these policies vary greatly from case to case, and it is difficult 
to predict their effect ex-ante. Nevertheless, they continue to be implemented in

section_text:
III. Objectives and Justification of the TC
3.1Objective. The objective of this TC is to develop and implement an impact evaluation 
of the Afroestima Training Program (AFE), financed by operation BR-L1412 (Prodetur 
Salvador), and provide inputs for the design of optimal interventions under the scope 
of the new loan in preparation, BR-L1636 (Salvador Capital Afro).
3.2Main questions to be focused. The evaluation aims to compare what happened to 
individuals who were trained by the AFE with what would have happened to those 
same individuals that had not taken the training course. Using technical resources, we 
will evaluate five training cycles carried out in the AFE, financed between 2021 and 
2024, with the aim of answering some key questions: Was the AFE successful in 
increasing the average income and employability of those trained? Are there 
heterogeneous effects - men vs women, spec. age groups, different levels of 
education? Was the AFE capable of increasing formalization and accreditation of 
participants?
3.3Justification and theory of change. Public training policies for owners of small and 
medium-sized businesses have become common around the world, especially in 
developing countries. Such initiatives are mostly aimed at increasing productivity, 
income, and the skills of more vulnerable workers. According to the literature, there 
are several reasons to believe that minorities benefit even more from these types of 
programs than non-minority populations. First, networks are generally an important 
asset for the success of businesses, and there is evidence that minorities have 
experienced smaller and less connected networks (Ibarra, 1993; Aldrich and 
Waldinger, 1990; Seidel, Polzer, and Stewart, 2000)1. Moreover, training programs for 
small and medium-sized businesses can provide access to knowledge that would 
otherwise be difficult for minorities to obtain (Card and Giuliano, 2016)2. Another 
important factor is that minorities are disproportionately exposed to self-employment 
and have less access to capital to start their businesses, thus potentially benefiting 
more from training (Dunn and Holtz-Eakin, 2000; Fairlie and Robb, 2007; Fairlie, 
2006)3. Lastly, minorities may face discrimination from investors and consumers

Framework.‚Äù Academy of Management Review 18 (1): 56‚Äì87. ALDRICH, HOWARD E., & ROGER 
WALDINGER (1990). ‚ÄúEthnicity and Entrepreneurship.‚Äù Annual Review of Sociology 16 (1): 111‚Äì35. 
SEIDEL, MARC-DAVID L., JEFFREY T. POLZER, & KATHERINE J. STEWART (2000). ‚ÄúFriends in High 
Places: The Effects of Social Networks on Discrimination in Salary Negotiations.‚Äù Administrative Science 
Quarterly 45 (1): 1‚Äì24.
2 CARD, DAVID, & LAURA GIULIANO (2016). ‚ÄúCan Tracking Raise the Test Scores of High-Ability Minority 
Students?‚Äù American Economic Review 106 (10): 2783‚Äì816.
3 DUNN, THOMAS, & DOUGLAS HOLTZ-EAKIN (2000). ‚ÄúFinancial Capital, Human Capital, and the 
Transition to Self-Employment: Evidence from Intergenerational Links.‚Äù Journal of Labor Economics 18 
(2): 282‚Äì305 FAIRLIE, ROBERT W (2006). ‚ÄúEntrepreneurship among Disadvantaged Groups: Women, 
Minorities and the Less Educated.‚Äù In International Handbook Series on Entrepreneurship, Vol. 3. New 
York: Springer. FAIRLIE, ROBERT W., & ALICIA M. ROBB. 2007. ‚ÄúWhy Are Black-Owned Businesses

(Blanchflower, Levine, and Zimmerman, 2003; Brooks et al., 2014)4. Other studies 
have also shown that, in the short term, non-minorities benefit more from 
entrepreneurial training programs, but in the long term, the effect is much greater for 
women and non-whites. Although these findings are related to the program to be 
studied in this evaluation, AFE has slightly different aspects, such as part of the 
training program's curriculum focusing on the appreciation of Afro-Ethnic culture and 
tourism. In this regard, based on the positive results that programs focusing on socio-
emotional aspects have achieved (Camargo et al, 2021; Barrera-Osorio et al, 2021), 
an even better outcome is expected from AFE compared to the above-mentioned 
evaluation articles.
3.4 The costs and benefits of these policies vary greatly from case to case, and it is difficult 
to predict their effect ex-ante. Nevertheless, they continue to be implemented in 
different countries and in different sectors, such as tourism and creative economies. 
Therefore, it is necessary to evaluate these policies for a better understanding of their 
effects and to identify areas for improvement.
3.5The context of Salvador, Bahia. A study conducted by the IDB under the preparation 
of Prodetur Salvador5 shows that the leisure tourism chain in Salvador heavily relies 
on the Afro community for its existence and competitiveness in two ways: (i) as 
producers and owners of the unique cultural tourism content that distinguishes 
Salvador from other tourist destinations; and (ii) as the workforce, accounting for up to 
77% of formal employees in the sector. However, the study also demonstrates that the 
Afro-descendant community faces racial inequality within the tourism industry: (i) they 
are the least benefited racial group (receiving 67% of tourist spending despite being 
77% of formal employees, while other races, comprising 23% of formal employees, 
receive 33% of spending) and earn less (1.8 times less than other groups); (ii) they 
have less career progression and occupy fewer high positions than other races, even 
when they have similar educational levels; few access managerial positions, even in 
cultural activities (between 0.5 and 4% depending on the chain link); and (iii) they face 
high informality: for every formal Afro tourism employee, there are 0.8 informal ones, 
who suffer greater social vulnerability. The study also reveals that all these indicators 
of racial inequality worsen if the Afro-descendant is a woman.

qualify Afro descendant individuals involved in businesses related to the tourism value 
chain in the capital of Bahia. Through the training of these individuals, the project aims 
to improve their income, enhance the recognition of the value of Afro culture to the 
tourism sector in Salvador, and to improve boost the self-esteem of those working in 
this sector, with a special focus on Afro-descendant women. Its conception was based 
on the Salvador Afro Tourism Plan, which identified gaps related to both the technical 
and business training of this population and low self-esteem. A total of 1,066 students

methodologies: (i) Synthetic Differences-in-Differences + Matching; (ii) Stepped

III. Objectives and Justification of the TC
3.1Objective. The objective of this TC is to develop and implement an impact evaluation 
of the Afroestima Training Program (AFE), financed by operation BR-L1412 (Prodetur 
Salvador), and provide inputs for the design of optimal interventions under the scope 
of the new loan in preparation, BR-L1636 (Salvador Capital Afro).
3.2Main questions to be focused. The evaluation aims to compare what happened to 
individuals who were trained by the AFE with what would have happened to those 
same individuals that had not taken the training course. Using technical resources, we 
will evaluate five training cycles carried out in the AFE, financed between 2021 and 
2024, with the aim of answering some key questions: Was the AFE successful in 
increasing the average income and employability of those trained? Are there 
heterogeneous effects - men vs women, spec. age groups, different levels of 
education? Was the AFE capable of increasing formalization and accreditation of 
participants?
3.3Justification and theory of change. Public training policies for owners of small and 
medium-sized businesses have become common around the world, especially in 
developing countries. Such initiatives are mostly aimed at increasing productivity, 
income, and the skills of more vulnerable workers. According to the literature, there 
are several reasons to believe that minorities benefit even more from these types of 
programs than non-minority populations. First, networks are generally an important 
asset for the success of businesses, and there is evidence that minorities have 
experienced smaller and less connected networks (Ibarra, 1993; Aldrich and 
Waldinger, 1990; Seidel, Polzer, and Stewart, 2000)1. Moreover, training programs for 
small and medium-sized businesses can provide access to knowledge that would 
otherwise be difficult for minorities to obtain (Card and Giuliano, 2016)2. Another 
important factor is that minorities are disproportionately exposed to self-employment 
and have less access to capital to start their businesses, thus potentially benefiting 
more from training (Dunn and Holtz-Eakin, 2000; Fairlie and Robb, 2007; Fairlie, 
2006)3. Lastly, minorities may face discrimination from investors and consumers

Framework.‚Äù Academy of Management Review 18 (1): 56‚Äì87. ALDRICH, HOWARD E., & ROGER 
WALDINGER (1990). ‚ÄúEthnicity and Entrepreneurship.‚Äù Annual Review of Sociology 16 (1): 111‚Äì35. 
SEIDEL, MARC-DAVID L., JEFFREY T. POLZER, & KATHERINE J. STEWART (2000). ‚ÄúFriends in High 
Places: The Effects of Social Networks on Discrimination in Salary Negotiations.‚Äù Administrative Science 
Quarterly 45 (1): 1‚Äì24.
2 CARD, DAVID, & LAURA GIULIANO (2016). ‚ÄúCan Tracking Raise the Test Scores of High-Ability Minority 
Students?‚Äù American Economic Review 106 (10): 2783‚Äì816.

York: Springer. FAIRLIE, ROBERT W., & ALICIA M. ROBB. 2007. ‚ÄúWhy Are Black-Owned Businesses

(Blanchflower, Levine, and Zimmerman, 2003; Brooks et al., 2014)4. Other studies 
have also shown that, in the short term, non-minorities benefit more from 
entrepreneurial training programs, but in the long term, the effect is much greater for 
women and non-whites. Although these findings are related to the program to be 
studied in this evaluation, AFE has slightly different aspects, such as part of the 
training program's curriculum focusing on the appreciation of Afro-Ethnic culture and 
tourism. In this regard, based on the positive results that programs focusing on socio-
emotional aspects have achieved (Camargo et al, 2021; Barrera-Osorio et al, 2021), 
an even better outcome is expected from AFE compared to the above-mentioned 
evaluation articles.
3.4 The costs and benefits of these policies vary greatly from case to case, and it is difficult 
to predict their effect ex-ante. Nevertheless, they continue to be implemented in 
different countries and in different sectors, such as tourism and creative economies. 
Therefore, it is necessary to evaluate these policies for a better understanding of their 
effects and to identify areas for improvement.
3.5The context of Salvador, Bahia. A study conducted by the IDB under the preparation 
of Prodetur Salvador5 shows that the leisure tourism chain in Salvador heavily relies 
on the Afro community for its existence and competitiveness in two ways: (i) as 
producers and owners of the unique cultural tourism content that distinguishes 
Salvador from other tourist destinations; and (ii) as the workforce, accounting for up to 
77% of formal employees in the sector. However, the study also demonstrates that the

are the least benefited racial group (receiving 67% of tourist spending despite being 
77% of formal employees, while other races, comprising 23% of formal employees, 
receive 33% of spending) and earn less (1.8 times less than other groups); (ii) they 
have less career progression and occupy fewer high positions than other races, even 
when they have similar educational levels; few access managerial positions, even in 
cultural activities (between 0.5 and 4% depending on the chain link); and (iii) they face 
high informality: for every formal Afro tourism employee, there are 0.8 informal ones, 
who suffer greater social vulnerability. The study also reveals that all these indicators 
of racial inequality worsen if the Afro-descendant is a woman.

qualify Afro descendant individuals involved in businesses related to the tourism value 
chain in the capital of Bahia. Through the training of these individuals, the project aims 
to improve their income, enhance the recognition of the value of Afro culture to the 
tourism sector in Salvador, and to improve boost the self-esteem of those working in 
this sector, with a special focus on Afro-descendant women. Its conception was based 
on the Salvador Afro Tourism Plan, which identified gaps related to both the technical 
and business training of this population and low self-esteem. A total of 1,066 students

organized into learning paths, each containing a set of modules and topics. 
3.7Methodology. To conduct this evaluation, this TC intends to employ two separate 
methodologies: (i) Synthetic Differences-in-Differences + Matching; (ii) Stepped 
Synthetic Differences-in-Differences.
3.8 In the first method, we plan to use enrollment data of past participants as the treatment 
group (T). Due to the low representativeness of the waitlist (small sample), missing 
information will be corrected using synthetic control, creating a control group (C) with 
characteristics similar to the treated population. Historical data from the RAIS

population, ensuring the creation of a control group with characteristics closer to those 
of the treated population.

subnational levels. The proposed evaluation fills a crucial knowledge gap by

3.4 The costs and benefits of these policies vary greatly from case to case, and it is difficult 
to predict their effect ex-ante. Nevertheless, they continue to be implemented in 
different countries and in different sectors, such as tourism and creative economies. 
Therefore, it is necessary to evaluate these policies for a better understanding of their 
effects and to identify areas for improvement.
3.5The context of Salvador, Bahia. A study conducted by the IDB under the preparation 
of Prodetur Salvador5 shows that the leisure tourism chain in Salvador heavily relies 
on the Afro community for its existence and competitiveness in two ways: (i) as 
producers and owners of the unique cultural tourism content that distinguishes 
Salvador from other tourist destinations; and (ii) as the workforce, accounting for up to 
77% of formal employees in the sector. However, the study also demonstrates that the 
Afro-descendant community faces racial inequality within the tourism industry: (i) they 
are the least benefited racial group (receiving 67% of tourist spending despite being 
77% of formal employees, while other races, comprising 23% of formal employees, 
receive 33% of spending) and earn less (1.8 times less than other groups); (ii) they 
have less career progression and occupy fewer high positions than other races, even 
when they have similar educational levels; few access managerial positions, even in 
cultural activities (between 0.5 and 4% depending on the chain link); and (iii) they face 
high informality: for every formal Afro tourism employee, there are 0.8 informal ones, 
who suffer greater social vulnerability. The study also reveals that all these indicators 
of racial inequality worsen if the Afro-descendant is a woman.

qualify Afro descendant individuals involved in businesses related to the tourism value

to improve their income, enhance the recognition of the value of Afro culture to the 
tourism sector in Salvador, and to improve boost the self-esteem of those working in 
this sector, with a special focus on Afro-descendant women. Its conception was based 
on the Salvador Afro Tourism Plan, which identified gaps related to both the technical 
and business training of this population and low self-esteem. A total of 1,066 students

3.7Methodology. To conduct this evaluation, this TC intends to employ two separate 
methodologies: (i) Synthetic Differences-in-Differences + Matching; (ii) Stepped 
Synthetic Differences-in-Differences.
3.8 In the first method, we plan to use enrollment data of past participants as the treatment 
group (T). Due to the low representativeness of the waitlist (small sample), missing 
information will be corrected using synthetic control, creating a control group (C) with 
characteristics similar to the treated population. Historical data from the RAIS 
(Brazilian Registry of Employed and Unemployed Persons) and databases from the 
Salvador Economic Development Secretariat will be utilized for this modeling.
3.9 For the second method, the treatment group (T) remains the same, but the control 
group (C) will consist of yet untreated groups to be drawn from newly registered 
participants for the upcoming training cycle starting in August 2024 (approximately 350 
participants). Historical information from existing databases will be sought for this 
population, ensuring the creation of a control group with characteristics closer to those 
of the treated population.
3.10 It‚Äôs worth mentioning that, although there is an established methodology for evaluating 
the effectiveness of similar tourism programs to generate employment and income 
(Castillo et al., 2015; Blackman et al., 2012; UNESCO, 2014), there is no specific 
assessment of the effects of training and development of Afro-entrepreneurship in the 
tourism sector, such as AFE, on income and labor supply of individuals.
3.11Strategic relevance. The IDB has as one of its strategic priorities to work to address 
the exclusion of Afro-descendants due to origin, racial or ethnic status. Projects like 
Afroestima include economic empowerment, identification of racial gaps through data 
collection and harmonization, and promotion of policy development at national and 
subnational levels. The proposed evaluation fills a crucial knowledge gap by 
investigating the impact of tourism projects with a racial focus, as there is a shortage 
of comprehensive studies that have systematically and empirically evaluated the effect 
of these training programs on the Afro descendant community, particularly in terms of 
increased income, employability, and possible heterogeneous effects. A specific 
evaluation of AFE is of utmost relevance for guiding better resource allocation in future 
Bank-financed operations, both in tourism sector or others related.6
3.12Data and main variables. The data to be used will be sourced from: RAIS (Registry 
of Employed and Unemployed Persons), information on formalization of micro-
entrepreneurs provided by SEBRAE (Brazilian Support Service for Micro and Small 
Enterprises), Cad√önico (Unified Registry for Social Programs), Federal Revenue 
Service, as well as data from the Salvador Economic Development Secretariat related 
to beneficiaries of training programs conducted by the Municipality such as name, 
locality, race, gender, income, type of business . The Municipality has already shared 
with the IDB team data on the profile of the AFE beneficiaries in each cycle (1.066 
people). This data set includes contact information and national registry identification

numbers, that will make possible the connection with other datasets previously

information about the population that can be utilized as context. Additionally, the 
registry of micro and small entrepreneurs in the city provides inputs such as profit data,

3.13Strategic alignment. The TC is aligned with the IDB Group's Country Strategy with 
Brazil 2024-2027 (GN-3243-1), specifically with the specific objectives of 
strengthening policies for the protection and welfare of women and diverse population 
and empowering sustainable investments. Furthermore, the TC is consistent with the 
IDB Group's Institutional Strategy: Transformation for Scale and Impact (CA 631) and 
aligns with the objectives of: (i) reducing poverty and inequality; and (iii) fostering 
sustainable regional growth. The TC is also aligned with the following operational focus 
areas: gender equality and inclusion of diverse population groups; institutional 
capacity, rule of law and citizen security; social protection and human capital 
development. The TC is also aligned with the Ordinary Capital Strategic Development 
Program (OC SDP), Window 2, Priority Area 1: Climate Change and Environmental 
Sustainability (W2A) (GN-2819-14), especially with the priority area of inclusive social 
development and inclusive economic growth, considering it will generate knowledge 
products, data and relevant operational inputs to guide future interventions in those 
areas. Finally, the CT is aligned with the Tourism Sector Framework (GN-2779-12), 
especially in its area focused on expanding the economic benefits of tourism and its 
distribution to the most vulnerable groups.
3.14Synergies. Inputs provided by the studies conducted within the scope of this TC will 
also be valuable inputs for future programs developed by IDB Invest related to training 
and entrepreneurial assistance in the tourism sector, providing evidence-based data 
for future investment opportunities.  
3.15Beneficiaries. The main beneficiary of the TC is the Municipality of Salvador, that will 
benefit from the results of studies conducted in order to better design future training 
interventions. The IDB and other financial institutions will also benefit from the results, 
considering the ample dissemination strategy to be conducted, and that results 
achieved might be widely adapted to other training programs contexts.

4.1 The activities to be financed by the TC have been grouped into two components as 
described below:
4.2Component 1: Impact assessment of the Afroestima program (US$200,000). This 
component focuses on the design and execution of the impact evaluation of the 
Afroestima program. The component will finance consultancy services aimed at 
(i) collecting the data needed to carry out the evaluation from both public databases 
(RAIS, Cad√∫nico, Receita Federal, etc.) and the information provided by Salvador 
Municipality; (ii) designing and implementing the selected methodologies. The 
expected result for this component is to establish the basis for an adequate impact 
assessment of AFE and to have methodologies selected and validated.
4.3Component 2: Analysis and dissemination of Impact Evaluation Results 
(US$70,000). This component aims to analyze and disseminate the results obtained 
through the impact evaluation of the Afroestima program. The component will finance 
- 6 -
consultancy services to (i) carry out a detailed interpretation of the results, highlighting 
the main economic and social impacts achieved by the participants; (ii) prepare 
comprehensive reports that will include robust statistical analysis and explanatory 
graphs, as well as recommendations for improving public policies and future strategies 
focused on the tourism value-chain, specifically producing inputs for further 
incorporation under the BR-L1636. The main inputs generated through the analysis 
will be disseminated to internal audiences in the IDB Group so they can be 
incorporated in future program designs ‚Äì not only in BR-L1636. The expected result 
for this component is to analyze and disseminate information on the impact 
assessment for both internal and external audiences, contributing for better planning 
of future interventions financed by the IDB and the Municipality of Salvador.

or sensitive information due to the activities that will be financed, those will be 
conducted ensuring compliance with the Bank's Personal Data Privacy Policy (GN-
3030), as well as coordinating with the VPF/ADS team.

Capital Strategic Development Program (OC SDP), Window 2, Priority Area 1: Climate

the average income and employability of the participants, demonstrating the program's 
effectiveness in improving their economic conditions. It is expected to identify 
heterogeneous effects, with results varying between men and women, different age 
groups, and educational levels, revealing how different subgroups benefited from the 
training. Additionally, the AFE is anticipated to have contributed to the formalization 
and accreditation of participants, increasing their inclusion in formal and recognized 
employment, thus highlighting the program's positive impact on professionalization

Basic Information for TC
Objectives and Justification of the TC 
The objective of this TC is to strengthen institutional capacity within the quality infrastructure system to promote Micro, Small, Medium Enterprises (MSME) competitiveness under a sustainable development framework. 
Context: Quality Infrastructure systems facilitate competitiveness and growth. In the context of chronic low growth (GDP growth in Jamaica averaged 0.73% per year between 2001-2024 compared to a global average of 3.4% and a Caribbean regional average of 1.3%) and steadily declining total factor productivity (TFP), understanding the factors that influence MSME innovation and competitiveness are important for long term growth. Quality Infrastructure Systems (QIS), which consist of standards development, accreditation, metrology, and conformity assessment, are one such enabling factors vital for economic growth. Promoting regulations and standards have been evidenced to increase GDP between 1% and 2.4% in the short term (Maskus and Tsunehiro 2001). Several studies also evidence the effect of certifications on competitiveness. Certifications like ISO 9001 are associated with larger reductions in product costs (Corbett et al 2005); better financial performance (Sharma, 2005); and higher rates of corporate survival as well as increasing sales, employment, and wages (Levine and Toffel 2010). Moreover, literature has shown that certification increases revenues because quality certification allows firms to access new markets and customers (Singh et al 2010), has positive impacts on innovative behavior (Manders et al 2016) or improves the capabilities of human capital (Lo et al 2013).  
Low levels of quality certification among firms, especially women-led firms. According to the 2020 Innovation, Firm Performance and Gender (IFPG), the percentage of Jamaican firms that had obtained an internationally recognized quality certification was 21.88% compared to 29.16% in Guyana and 33.34% in Suriname (the OECS countries have the lowest percentage, averaging around 14%). Only 17.63% women owned firms compared to 24.18% male owned firms have an internationally recognized quality certification in Jamaica. Several factors may be at play such as cost of quality certification, access to quality certification, information asymmetry regarding certifications required for operating and exporting, etc. yet there is limited data to fully understand the level of awareness and types of constraints MSMEs face in accessing quality infrastructure services and in obtaining quality certification.  
Institutional capacity gaps of the National Quality Infrastructure. Jamaica‚Äôs National Quality Infrastructure (NQI) includes institutions such as the Bureau of Standards, Jamaica (BSJ), the National Certification Body of Jamaica (NCBJ), and the Jamaica National Agency for Accreditation (JANAAC) Global Accreditation that provide quality infrastructure services to MSMEs, laboratories, conformity assessment bodies, and others. The 2024 Quality Infrastructure Index for Sustainable Development (QI4SD) ranked Jamaica 126th globally, and 16th within the Latin America and Caribbean region, placing it behind Barbados (109th globally and 13th regionally) and Trinidad and Tobago (110th globally and 14th regionally). Significant weaknesses persisted in metrology (score of 8.8/100), standardization (23.2/100) and conformity assessment (7.1/100), highlighting areas that require improvement to enhance Jamaica‚Äôs overall quality infrastructure (UNIDO, 2024). These findings align to the WB‚Äôs recent study on Jamaica‚Äôs ‚ÄúNational Coordinated Laboratory Strategy Framework and Implementation Plan for Jamaica‚Äù which emphasized the need for modernization and improved service delivery to various industries and private enterprises including the need for upgrading ‚Äúmodern equipment and digital systems to improve turnaround times, enhance test accuracy, and streamline laboratory information management systems‚Äù.
Expected Results and Beneficiaries. To address these constraints, it is critical to enhance the national quality infrastructure, especially physical facilities and service offerings, in alignment with MSME needs. This TC will provide the Government of Jamaica with a detailed roadmap to guide future investments to improve quality infrastructure services for Jamaica and the region. As such, the project ultimately aims to benefit MSMEs, especially women-led firms, as well as other entities that may have demand for QI services (such as laboratories, conformity assessment bodies, etc.). Indirect beneficiaries include the wider public that consume MSME products and services. The TC also seeks to strengthen the public‚Äôs sector‚Äôs capabilities in private sector development (PSD) public investment program design, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation with the value-added focus of building advanced econometric and data analytics expertise amongst public sector officials responsible for private sector and innovation policy and instrument design.
Complementarities. This TC is complementary to national development priorities contained in Vision 2030 which seeks to create a prosperous economy through the development of internationally competitive industry structures, namely: maintaining economic stability; enabling business environment, strong economic infrastructure; and entrepreneurship. Specifically, (GOAL -3, National Outcome -8) states that Jamaica will develop the capabilities of the MSME sector and ‚Äúimprove the channels in which they participate in economic activity.‚Äù The project is firmly anchored in the priority programs and objectives of Ministry of Industry, Investment, and Commerce (MIIC‚Äôs) Strategic Business Plan 2023-2027 such as identifying and engaging MSMEs to participate in targeted activities aimed at supporting their growth and development. Policies such as the National Quality Policy (NQP) of Jamaica 2019 and 2018 MSME and Entrepreneurship Policy in Jamaica aim to improve Jamaica‚Äôs quality infrastructure and MSME access to business support services, standards and certification. Finally, at the regional level, the TC will complement capacity building efforts at CARICOM Regional Organization for Standards and Quality (CROSQ).
The TC draws lessons from operations such as 3824/BL-GY ‚ÄúEnhancing the National Quality Infrastructure for Economic Diversification and Trade Promotion‚Äù and 5594/OC-GY ‚ÄúEnhancing the National Quality Infrastructure for Competitiveness"; Reformulation and Additional Financing‚Äù is the importance of firm level data for monitoring and evaluation of large national quality infrastructure programs. Another key lesson learnt is the importance of stakeholder coordination to address bottlenecks that may arise during execution. It builds on previous work completed under ATN/OC-20171-JA ‚ÄúSupport for National MSME Innovation, Competitiveness and Productive Growth‚Äù where a roadmap was developed to identify business support programs/services from over 20 government agencies, commercial banks, and universities in Jamaica that participated in roadshows across the country where MSMEs were able to directly access business support services in one location. The TC will complement ATN/OC-21285-JA ‚ÄúStrengthening the National Quality Infrastructure for Competitiveness and Green Growth in Jamaica‚Äù which intends to provide training in accreditation and to develop a pilot to promote the adoption of green standards and certifications which can be incorporated into Component 1 of this TC.
Strategic Alignment. This TC is consistent with the IDB Group Institutional Strategy 2024-2030: Transforming for Scale and Impact (CA-631) and is aligned with the objectives of Bolster Sustainable Growth by building the capacity of institutions within the quality infrastructure system to encourage competitiveness and quality service offerings for MSMEs. It is also aligned with the operational focus areas of: (i) Institutional Capacity, Rule of Law, and Citizen Security as it relates to institutional strengthening of the MIIC and BSJ in Monitoring, evaluation and learning, specific to private sector development programs; and (ii) Productive Development and Innovation through encouraging demand for quality services to promote competitiveness of MSMEs. This TC also aligns with the objectives of the IDB Group‚Äôs Country Strategy with Jamaica 2022-2026 (GN-3138) and the specific strategic objective 1.1 ‚Äúto create and expand channels for sustainable businesses‚Äù as it aims to support private sector productivity and sustainable growth. This TC is aligned with the objectives and activities of The Ordinary Capital Strategic Development Program (OC SDP) Window 2, Priority Area 3: Effective, Efficient, and Transparent Institutions (W2C) (GN-2819-14), given that the TC activities aim to strengthen the institutional capacity of actors in the NQI ecosystem. This TC is aligned with the priorities defined in the Innovation, Science and Technology Sector Framework Document (GN-2791-13) as it relates to line action 2 ‚ÄúBoost investment in key public goods for innovation‚Äù, where specific mention is made to support countries in the region in implementing quality certification standards. This TC hopes to strengthen collaboration between partners and the IDB Group (IDB Lab, IDB Invest, and other sectors) which have conducted studies and projects related to promoting quality certification amongst firms.
Alignment with One Caribbean Framework. The TC aligns with the IDB One Caribbean Framework (GN-3201-5) and its priority area of private sector engagement, as it will be providing technical inputs to the design of a regional center of excellence in quality infrastructure. Thus, it will provide services across the region, which has potential for replication across the Caribbean countries. It also aligns with One Caribbean‚Äôs cross-cutting area of strengthening technical capabilities and institutional capacity given that Component 2 of the TC, which focuses on building the capacity of selected public sector officials in data analytics and the design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of private sector development programs, will develop training materials that can be disseminated across the region.  
Description of activities
Component 1: Roadmap for Improving Quality Infrastructure Services (US$130,000.00). This component will finance technical studies that will provide a roadmap for modernizing and expanding QI service offerings primarily targeted to MSMEs in Jamaica and across the Caribbean region. The following outputs are expected: (i) design and implementation of a survey to collect data to map current and future demands for quality infrastructure services amongst MSMEs, particularly to understand constraints of exporting MSMEs and women-led firms; (ii) a detailed demand analysis utilizing survey results and other data to provide insight on sector specific and gender sensitized quality infrastructure service needs, as well as recommendations for streamlining and digitalization of services; (iii) an institutional gap analysis to identify the equipment, technologies, facility upgrades, accreditation processes, and training/capacity development required for modernizing the quality infrastructure and improving/expanding services tailored to MSMEs, especially women-led firms; and (iv) a feasibility study for establishing a Centre of Excellence (COE) in Jamaica for quality under a sustainable development framework. The study will assess similar models, incentives, and strategies for long-term sustainability. It will include recommendations for key services to be offered, detailed architectural design, financial requirements analysis, legal and regulatory analysis, risk assessment, and an operating model.
Component 2: Strengthening Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning Capacity. (US$20,000.00). This component will finance activities intended to strengthen the institutional capacity of the MIIC, particularly the BSJ, to monitor and evaluate private sector development public investment programs. Specifically, the TC will finance the design and implementation of a training workshop that will develop the capabilities of at least ten competitively selected public sector professionals to design, implement, monitor and evaluate private sector development programs. The training workshop will utilize existing IDB courses(such as Development Effectiveness and Project Management for Results) and will include additional modules focused on data analytics for monitoring and reporting and advanced quantitative methods for conducting economic analyses and robust impact evaluations of PSD programs. Outputs include (i) the development and dissemination of training materials; and (ii) the implementation of one in-person training workshop for at least 10 public sector officials.
The total cost of the TC will be US$150,000.00, and it will be executed and disbursed for 24 months. The funding source of this TC is the OC SDP Window 2 ‚Äì Institutions (W2C). There will be no local counterpart funding. The funds will be used as follows:

Indicative Budget
Executing agency and execution structure
In adherence to the Bank‚Äôs Technical Cooperation Policy (GN-2470-2) and the Procedures for the Processing of Technical Cooperation Operations and Related Matters (OP-619-4), the beneficiary has requested the TC to be executed by the Bank. This TC will thus be executed through the Bank‚Äôs Competitiveness, Technology and Innovation Division of the Productivity, Trade and Innovation Sector (PTI/CTI) in coordination with the Country Office of Jamaica (CCB/CJA) which will be the Unit of Disbursement Responsibility. This is justified by the limited institutional capacity of the BSJ to design, implement, monitor and evaluate projects and to procure qualified expertise. CTI will support the identification and supervision of consultancies to ensure the quality and timeliness of the products, according to section 4.5 of the Bank‚Äôs Technical Cooperation Guidelines (GN-2629-1). The project intends to build capacity within the beneficiary to design, execute, and monitor future PSD projects and investment loan programs. The project team will closely coordinate implementation of the TC with the MIIC and BSJ and other institutions and/or entities identified as key stakeholders in the project.
All procurement to be executed under this TC has been included in the Procurement Plan (Annex IV) and will be hired in compliance with the applicable Bank‚Äôs established procurement methods, namely: (i) contracting of individual consultants, as set forth in Section AM-650 of the Administrative Manual "Complementary Workforce" for individual consultants; and (ii) contracting of consulting firms for services of an intellectual nature, in accordance with the IDB‚Äôs Corporate Procurement Policy (GN-2303-33) and its associated guidelines.
Monitoring. Project output indicators will be monitored by the Project Team in accordance with the proposed results matrix.
Intellectual Property. The knowledge products generated within the framework of this TC will be the property of the Bank and may be made available to the public under a creative commons license.
Major issues 
One major risk is a low response rate to the proposed demand survey. This will be mitigated through targeted campaigns that clearly communicate the benefits of participating and highlight any available incentives for MSMEs to complete the survey. Another key risk is potential delays in receiving timely inputs from various participating agencies, which could impact the project timeline. To address this, dedicated project management will be implemented to monitor timelines, facilitate effective communication, and promote coordination across agencies.
Exceptions to Bank policy
There are not exceptions to the Bank‚Äôs policy. 
Environmental and Social Aspects
This TC is intended to finance pre-feasibility or feasibility studies of specific investment projects and the environmental and social studies associated with them; therefore, the terms of reference and products of this TC will be consistent with the applicable requirements of the Bank‚Äôs Environmental and Social Policy Framework (ESPF).

Objectives and Justification of the TC 
The objective of this TC is to strengthen institutional capacity within the quality infrastructure system to promote Micro, Small, Medium Enterprises (MSME) competitiveness under a sustainable development framework. 
Context: Quality Infrastructure systems facilitate competitiveness and growth. In the context of chronic low growth (GDP growth in Jamaica averaged 0.73% per year between 2001-2024 compared to a global average of 3.4% and a Caribbean regional average of 1.3%) and steadily declining total factor productivity (TFP), understanding the factors that influence MSME innovation and competitiveness are important for long term growth. Quality Infrastructure Systems (QIS), which consist of standards development, accreditation, metrology, and conformity assessment, are one such enabling factors vital for economic growth. Promoting regulations and standards have been evidenced to increase GDP between 1% and 2.4% in the short term (Maskus and Tsunehiro 2001). Several studies also evidence the effect of certifications on competitiveness. Certifications like ISO 9001 are associated with larger reductions in product costs (Corbett et al 2005); better financial performance (Sharma, 2005); and higher rates of corporate survival as well as increasing sales, employment, and wages (Levine and Toffel 2010). Moreover, literature has shown that certification increases revenues because quality certification allows firms to access new markets and customers (Singh et al 2010), has positive impacts on innovative behavior (Manders et al 2016) or improves the capabilities of human capital (Lo et al 2013).  
Low levels of quality certification among firms, especially women-led firms. According to the 2020 Innovation, Firm Performance and Gender (IFPG), the percentage of Jamaican firms that had obtained an internationally recognized quality certification was 21.88% compared to 29.16% in Guyana and 33.34% in Suriname (the OECS countries have the lowest percentage, averaging around 14%). Only 17.63% women owned firms compared to 24.18% male owned firms have an internationally recognized quality certification in Jamaica. Several factors may be at play such as cost of quality certification, access to quality certification, information asymmetry regarding certifications required for operating and exporting, etc. yet there is limited data to fully understand the level of awareness and types of constraints MSMEs face in accessing quality infrastructure services and in obtaining quality certification.  
Institutional capacity gaps of the National Quality Infrastructure. Jamaica‚Äôs National Quality Infrastructure (NQI) includes institutions such as the Bureau of Standards, Jamaica (BSJ), the National Certification Body of Jamaica (NCBJ), and the Jamaica National Agency for Accreditation (JANAAC) Global Accreditation that provide quality infrastructure services to MSMEs, laboratories, conformity assessment bodies, and others. The 2024 Quality Infrastructure Index for Sustainable Development (QI4SD) ranked Jamaica 126th globally, and 16th within the Latin America and Caribbean region, placing it behind Barbados (109th globally and 13th regionally) and Trinidad and Tobago (110th globally and 14th regionally). Significant weaknesses persisted in metrology (score of 8.8/100), standardization (23.2/100) and conformity assessment (7.1/100), highlighting areas that require improvement to enhance Jamaica‚Äôs overall quality infrastructure (UNIDO, 2024). These findings align to the WB‚Äôs recent study on Jamaica‚Äôs ‚ÄúNational Coordinated Laboratory Strategy Framework and Implementation Plan for Jamaica‚Äù which emphasized the need for modernization and improved service delivery to various industries and private enterprises including the need for upgrading ‚Äúmodern equipment and digital systems to improve turnaround times, enhance test accuracy, and streamline laboratory information management systems‚Äù.

To address these constraints, it is critical to enhance the national quality infrastructure, especially physical facilities and service offerings, in alignment with MSME needs. This TC will provide the Government of Jamaica with a detailed roadmap to guide future investments to improve quality infrastructure services for Jamaica and the region. As such, the project ultimately aims to benefit MSMEs, especially women-led firms, as well as other entities that may have demand for QI services (such as laboratories, conformity assessment bodies, etc.). Indirect beneficiaries include the wider public that consume MSME products and services. The TC also seeks to strengthen the public‚Äôs sector‚Äôs capabilities in private sector development (PSD) public investment program design, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation with the value-added focus of building advanced econometric and data analytics expertise amongst public sector officials responsible for private sector and innovation policy and instrument design.
Complementarities. This TC is complementary to national development priorities contained in Vision 2030 which seeks to create a prosperous economy through the development of internationally competitive industry structures, namely: maintaining economic stability; enabling business environment, strong economic infrastructure; and entrepreneurship. Specifically, (GOAL -3, National Outcome -8) states that Jamaica will develop the capabilities of the MSME sector and ‚Äúimprove the channels in which they participate in economic activity.‚Äù The project is firmly anchored in the priority programs and objectives of Ministry of Industry, Investment, and Commerce (MIIC‚Äôs) Strategic Business Plan 2023-2027 such as identifying and engaging MSMEs to participate in targeted activities aimed at supporting their growth and development. Policies such as the National Quality Policy (NQP) of Jamaica 2019 and 2018 MSME and Entrepreneurship Policy in Jamaica aim to improve Jamaica‚Äôs quality infrastructure and MSME access to business support services, standards and certification. Finally, at the regional level, the TC will complement capacity building efforts at CARICOM Regional Organization for Standards and Quality (CROSQ).
The TC draws lessons from operations such as 3824/BL-GY ‚ÄúEnhancing the National Quality Infrastructure for Economic Diversification and Trade Promotion‚Äù and 5594/OC-GY ‚ÄúEnhancing the National Quality Infrastructure for Competitiveness"; Reformulation and Additional Financing‚Äù is the importance of firm level data for monitoring and evaluation of large national quality infrastructure programs. Another key lesson learnt is the importance of stakeholder coordination to address bottlenecks that may arise during execution. It builds on previous work completed under ATN/OC-20171-JA ‚ÄúSupport for National MSME Innovation, Competitiveness and Productive Growth‚Äù where a roadmap was developed to identify business support programs/services from over 20 government agencies, commercial banks, and universities in Jamaica that participated in roadshows across the country where MSMEs were able to directly access business support services in one location. The TC will complement ATN/OC-21285-JA ‚ÄúStrengthening the National Quality Infrastructure for Competitiveness and Green Growth in Jamaica‚Äù which intends to provide training in accreditation and to develop a pilot to promote the adoption of green standards and certifications which can be incorporated into Component 1 of this TC.

Basic Information for TC
Objectives and Justification of the TC 
The objective of this TC is to strengthen institutional capacity within the quality infrastructure system to promote Micro, Small, Medium Enterprises (MSME) competitiveness under a sustainable development framework. 
Context: Quality Infrastructure systems facilitate competitiveness and growth. In the context of chronic low growth (GDP growth in Jamaica averaged 0.73% per year between 2001-2024 compared to a global average of 3.4% and a Caribbean regional average of 1.3%) and steadily declining total factor productivity (TFP), understanding the factors that influence MSME innovation and competitiveness are important for long term growth. Quality Infrastructure Systems (QIS), which consist of standards development, accreditation, metrology, and conformity assessment, are one such enabling factors vital for economic growth. Promoting regulations and standards have been evidenced to increase GDP between 1% and 2.4% in the short term (Maskus and Tsunehiro 2001). Several studies also evidence the effect of certifications on competitiveness. Certifications like ISO 9001 are associated with larger reductions in product costs (Corbett et al 2005); better financial performance (Sharma, 2005); and higher rates of corporate survival as well as increasing sales, employment, and wages (Levine and Toffel 2010). Moreover, literature has shown that certification increases revenues because quality certification allows firms to access new markets and customers (Singh et al 2010), has positive impacts on innovative behavior (Manders et al 2016) or improves the capabilities of human capital (Lo et al 2013).  
Low levels of quality certification among firms, especially women-led firms. According to the 2020 Innovation, Firm Performance and Gender (IFPG), the percentage of Jamaican firms that had obtained an internationally recognized quality certification was 21.88% compared to 29.16% in Guyana and 33.34% in Suriname (the OECS countries have the lowest percentage, averaging around 14%). Only 17.63% women owned firms compared to 24.18% male owned firms have an internationally recognized quality certification in Jamaica. Several factors may be at play such as cost of quality certification, access to quality certification, information asymmetry regarding certifications required for operating and exporting, etc. yet there is limited data to fully understand the level of awareness and types of constraints MSMEs face in accessing quality infrastructure services and in obtaining quality certification.  
Institutional capacity gaps of the National Quality Infrastructure. Jamaica‚Äôs National Quality Infrastructure (NQI) includes institutions such as the Bureau of Standards, Jamaica (BSJ), the National Certification Body of Jamaica (NCBJ), and the Jamaica National Agency for Accreditation (JANAAC) Global Accreditation that provide quality infrastructure services to MSMEs, laboratories, conformity assessment bodies, and others. The 2024 Quality Infrastructure Index for Sustainable Development (QI4SD) ranked Jamaica 126th globally, and 16th within the Latin America and Caribbean region, placing it behind Barbados (109th globally and 13th regionally) and Trinidad and Tobago (110th globally and 14th regionally). Significant weaknesses persisted in metrology (score of 8.8/100), standardization (23.2/100) and conformity assessment (7.1/100), highlighting areas that require improvement to enhance Jamaica‚Äôs overall quality infrastructure (UNIDO, 2024). These findings align to the WB‚Äôs recent study on Jamaica‚Äôs ‚ÄúNational Coordinated Laboratory Strategy Framework and Implementation Plan for Jamaica‚Äù which emphasized the need for modernization and improved service delivery to various industries and private enterprises including the need for upgrading ‚Äúmodern equipment and digital systems to improve turnaround times, enhance test accuracy, and streamline laboratory information management systems‚Äù.
Expected Results and Beneficiaries. To address these constraints, it is critical to enhance the national quality infrastructure, especially physical facilities and service offerings, in alignment with MSME needs. This TC will provide the Government of Jamaica with a detailed roadmap to guide future investments to improve quality infrastructure services for Jamaica and the region. As such, the project ultimately aims to benefit MSMEs, especially women-led firms, as well as other entities that may have demand for QI services (such as laboratories, conformity assessment bodies, etc.). Indirect beneficiaries include the wider public that consume MSME products and services. The TC also seeks to strengthen the public‚Äôs sector‚Äôs capabilities in private sector development (PSD) public investment program design, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation with the value-added focus of building advanced econometric and data analytics expertise amongst public sector officials responsible for private sector and innovation policy and instrument design.
Complementarities. This TC is complementary to national development priorities contained in Vision 2030 which seeks to create a prosperous economy through the development of internationally competitive industry structures, namely: maintaining economic stability; enabling business environment, strong economic infrastructure; and entrepreneurship. Specifically, (GOAL -3, National Outcome -8) states that Jamaica will develop the capabilities of the MSME sector and ‚Äúimprove the channels in which they participate in economic activity.‚Äù The project is firmly anchored in the priority programs and objectives of Ministry of Industry, Investment, and Commerce (MIIC‚Äôs) Strategic Business Plan 2023-2027 such as identifying and engaging MSMEs to participate in targeted activities aimed at supporting their growth and development. Policies such as the National Quality Policy (NQP) of Jamaica 2019 and 2018 MSME and Entrepreneurship Policy in Jamaica aim to improve Jamaica‚Äôs quality infrastructure and MSME access to business support services, standards and certification. Finally, at the regional level, the TC will complement capacity building efforts at CARICOM Regional Organization for Standards and Quality (CROSQ).
The TC draws lessons from operations such as 3824/BL-GY ‚ÄúEnhancing the National Quality Infrastructure for Economic Diversification and Trade Promotion‚Äù and 5594/OC-GY ‚ÄúEnhancing the National Quality Infrastructure for Competitiveness"; Reformulation and Additional Financing‚Äù is the importance of firm level data for monitoring and evaluation of large national quality infrastructure programs. Another key lesson learnt is the importance of stakeholder coordination to address bottlenecks that may arise during execution. It builds on previous work completed under ATN/OC-20171-JA ‚ÄúSupport for National MSME Innovation, Competitiveness and Productive Growth‚Äù where a roadmap was developed to identify business support programs/services from over 20 government agencies, commercial banks, and universities in Jamaica that participated in roadshows across the country where MSMEs were able to directly access business support services in one location. The TC will complement ATN/OC-21285-JA ‚ÄúStrengthening the National Quality Infrastructure for Competitiveness and Green Growth in Jamaica‚Äù which intends to provide training in accreditation and to develop a pilot to promote the adoption of green standards and certifications which can be incorporated into Component 1 of this TC.
Strategic Alignment. This TC is consistent with the IDB Group Institutional Strategy 2024-2030: Transforming for Scale and Impact (CA-631) and is aligned with the objectives of Bolster Sustainable Growth by building the capacity of institutions within the quality infrastructure system to encourage competitiveness and quality service offerings for MSMEs. It is also aligned with the operational focus areas of: (i) Institutional Capacity, Rule of Law, and Citizen Security as it relates to institutional strengthening of the MIIC and BSJ in Monitoring, evaluation and learning, specific to private sector development programs; and (ii) Productive Development and Innovation through encouraging demand for quality services to promote competitiveness of MSMEs. This TC also aligns with the objectives of the IDB Group‚Äôs Country Strategy with Jamaica 2022-2026 (GN-3138) and the specific strategic objective 1.1 ‚Äúto create and expand channels for sustainable businesses‚Äù as it aims to support private sector productivity and sustainable growth. This TC is aligned with the objectives and activities of The Ordinary Capital Strategic Development Program (OC SDP) Window 2, Priority Area 3: Effective, Efficient, and Transparent Institutions (W2C) (GN-2819-14), given that the TC activities aim to strengthen the institutional capacity of actors in the NQI ecosystem. This TC is aligned with the priorities defined in the Innovation, Science and Technology Sector Framework Document (GN-2791-13) as it relates to line action 2 ‚ÄúBoost investment in key public goods for innovation‚Äù, where specific mention is made to support countries in the region in implementing quality certification standards. This TC hopes to strengthen collaboration between partners and the IDB Group (IDB Lab, IDB Invest, and other sectors) which have conducted studies and projects related to promoting quality certification amongst firms.

The TC aligns with the IDB One Caribbean Framework (GN-3201-5) and its priority area of private sector engagement, as it will be providing technical inputs to the design of a regional center of excellence in quality infrastructure. Thus, it will provide services across the region, which has potential for replication across the Caribbean countries. Component 1: Roadmap for Improving Quality Infrastructure Services (US$130,000.00). This component will finance technical studies that will provide a roadmap for modernizing and expanding QI service offerings primarily targeted to MSMEs in Jamaica and across the Caribbean region. The following outputs are expected: (i) design and implementation of a survey to collect data to map current and future demands for quality infrastructure services amongst MSMEs, particularly to understand constraints of exporting MSMEs and women-led firms; (ii) a detailed demand analysis utilizing survey results and other data to provide insight on sector specific and gender sensitized quality infrastructure service needs, as well as recommendations for streamlining and digitalization of services; (iii) an institutional gap analysis to identify the equipment, technologies, facility upgrades, accreditation processes, and training/capacity development required for modernizing the quality infrastructure and improving/expanding services tailored to MSMEs, especially women-led firms; and (iv) a feasibility study for establishing a Centre of Excellence (COE) in Jamaica for quality under a sustainable development framework. The study will assess similar models, incentives, and strategies for long-term sustainability. It will include recommendations for key services to be offered, detailed architectural design, financial requirements analysis, legal and regulatory analysis, risk assessment, and an operating model.

This component will finance activities intended to strengthen the institutional capacity of the MIIC, particularly the BSJ, to monitor and evaluate private sector development public investment programs. Specifically, the TC will finance the design and implementation of a training workshop that will develop the capabilities of at least ten competitively selected public sector professionals to design, implement, monitor and evaluate private sector development programs. The training workshop will utilize existing IDB courses(such as Development Effectiveness and Project Management for Results) and will include additional modules focused on data analytics for monitoring and reporting and advanced quantitative methods for conducting economic analyses and robust impact evaluations of PSD programs. Outputs include (i) the development and dissemination of training materials; and (ii) the implementation of one in-person training workshop for at least 10 public sector officials.
The total cost of the TC will be US$150,000.00, and it will be executed and disbursed for 24 months. The funding source of this TC is the OC SDP Window 2 ‚Äì Institutions (W2C). There will be no local counterpart funding. The funds will be used as follows:

This TC will thus be executed through the Bank‚Äôs Competitiveness, Technology and Innovation Division of the Productivity, Trade and Innovation Sector (PTI/CTI) in coordination with the Country Office of Jamaica (CCB/CJA) which will be the Unit of Disbursement Responsibility. To address this, dedicated project management will be implemented to monitor timelines, facilitate effective communication, and promote coordination across agencies.

There are not exceptions to the Bank‚Äôs policy.

This TC is intended to finance pre-feasibility or feasibility studies of specific investment projects and the environmental and social studies associated with them; therefore, the terms of reference and products of this TC will be consistent with the applicable requirements of the Bank‚Äôs Environmental and Social Policy Framework (ESPF).

Certifications like ISO 9001 are associated with larger reductions in product costs (Corbett et al 2005); better financial performance (Sharma, 2005); and higher rates of corporate survival as well as increasing sales, employment, and wages (Levine and Toffel 2010). Moreover, literature has shown that certification increases revenues because quality certification allows firms to access new markets and customers (Singh et al 2010), has positive impacts on innovative behavior (Manders et al 2016) or improves the capabilities of human capital (Lo et al 2013).

Promoting regulations and standards have been evidenced to increase GDP between 1% and 2.4% in the short term (Maskus and Tsunehiro 2001). Several studies also evidence the effect of certifications on competitiveness. Certifications like ISO 9001 are associated with larger reductions in product costs (Corbett et al 2005); better financial performance (Sharma, 2005); and higher rates of corporate survival as well as increasing sales, employment, and wages (Levine and Toffel 2010). Moreover, literature has shown that certification increases revenues because quality certification allows firms to access new markets and customers (Singh et al 2010), has positive impacts on innovative behavior (Manders et al 2016) or improves the capabilities of human capital (Lo et al 2013).  
Low levels of quality certification among firms, especially women-led firms. According to the 2020 Innovation, Firm Performance and Gender (IFPG), the percentage of Jamaican firms that had obtained an internationally recognized quality certification was 21.88% compared to 29.16% in Guyana and 33.34% in Suriname (the OECS countries have the lowest percentage, averaging around 14%). Only 17.63% women owned firms compared to 24.18% male owned firms have an internationally recognized quality certification in Jamaica. Several factors may be at play such as cost of quality certification, access to quality certification, information asymmetry regarding certifications required for operating and exporting, etc. yet there is limited data to fully understand the level of awareness and types of constraints MSMEs face in accessing quality infrastructure services and in obtaining quality certification.

Moreover, literature has shown that certification increases revenues because quality certification allows firms to access new markets and customers (Singh et al 2010), has positive impacts on innovative behavior (Manders et al 2016) or improves the capabilities of human capital (Lo et al 2013).
