section_title: Objectives and Justification of the TC
section_text:
II. Objectives and Justification of the TC
2.1 Empowering Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) is essential for a successful green 
transition in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC). The emergence of the green 
growth paradigm has highlighted the critical link between economic and environmental 
performance in business. Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in LAC 
represent 99.5% of all businesses in the region and account for 61.1% of employment, 
yet they contribute only 24.6% of total productivity1. While each MSME generates 
relatively low greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions individually, their collective 
environmental impact is significant accounting for over 13% of global energy 
consumption. The objective of this TC is to enhance the capacities of policymakers in 
1 International Energy Agency (2015). Policy Pathway ‚Äì Accelerating Energy Efficiency in Small 
and Medium-sized Enterprises. IEA, Paris.
- 2 -
Brazil and Colombia to design and implement strategies that promote the green 
transition and climate resilience of SMEs, through the assessment of current practices, 
international benchmarking, and targeted policy recommendations in areas such as 
green innovation, skills, technologies, energy efficiency, and entrepreneurship.
2.2 According to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), 
SMEs contributed between 60% and 70% of industrial sector GHG emissions. 
Similarly, recent UK studies indicate that SMEs are responsible for 43% to 53% of the 
country‚Äôs industrial emissions2. Despite 60% of SMEs being familiar with key net-zero 
concepts, 53% are not yet prepared to prioritize decarbonization in their operations, 
and 56% have taken no action at all. Only 3% of surveyed SMEs have measured their 
carbon footprint and developed emission reduction strategies3.
2.3 At the same time, SMEs in LAC face high vulnerability to climate change. Their limited 
adaptive capacity, resource constraints, and exposure to extreme weather events 
pose serious challenges. Many operate in climate-sensitive sectors such as 
agriculture, tourism, and manufacturing, making them especially susceptible to 
droughts, floods, and hurricanes. Unlike larger firms, SMEs often lack financial buffers, 
technical know-how, and institutional support to invest in resilience measures or adopt 
more sustainable business models. In addition, supply chain disruptions, infrastructure 
damage, and volatile energy costs further jeopardize their stability‚Äîoften resulting in 
reduced productivity, higher operating costs, or even permanent closure.
2.4 In the case of Colombia, the country has made ambitious commitments, including 
reducing its GHG emissions by 51% by 2030, and achieving carbon neutrality by 
20504.  Although the country accounted for only 0.32% of global energy consumption 
in 2020 and reported a per capita energy use of 36 GJ and emissions of 1.85 tons of 
CO‚ÇÇ per inhabitant in 2021, it faces major challenges. The industrial sector, 
responsible for 22% of final energy consumption, uses energy efficiently in only 31% 
of its processes. The 2021 Climate Action Law established a legal framework with 237 
goals at national, subnational, and business levels, including achieving net-zero 
deforestation and reducing black carbon emissions by 40% by 20305. However, GHG 
emissions have increased since 2000, mainly from land use and energy consumption. 
Without adequate investment in adaptation, the national GDP could fall by 1.5% to 
2.5% by 2050. Moreover, over 50% of Colombia's exports depend on fossil fuels‚Äî
mainly oil and coal‚Äîputting up to 10% of export revenues and 8% of GDP at risk in a 
global low-carbon transition6.
2.5 Considering this, SMEs, which make up 99.7% of the country‚Äôs business fabric, are 
key to the green transition, yet they face significant gaps. Fewer than 3% have 
measured their carbon footprint, and over 50% are not prepared to prioritize 
decarbonization. The green finance market remains small: in 2023, only 10 green 
bonds and 5 sustainability bonds were issued, and green loans made up just 5% of 
2 OECD (2021). No Net Zero Without SMEs: Exploring the Key Issues for Greening SMEs and 
Green Entrepreneurship. OECD SME and Entrepreneurship Papers No. 30, OECD Publishing, 
Paris
3 British Business Bank et al. (2023). Policy Recommendations to Enhance Small-to-Medium Sized 
Enterprise Support for Achieving the UK‚Äôs Net Zero Targets. Sustainability, 16(22), 10116
4 IEA (2023). Colombia 2023 ‚Äì Executive Summary. IEA, Paris.
5 UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre (2023). Boosting Energy Efficiency at the Industrial level in 
Colombia, in support of NDC implementation. UNEP.
6 World Bank Group (2023). Colombia Country Climate and Development Report. World Bank, 
Washington, DC.
- 3 -
the total banking portfolio7. While progress has been made, such as Colombia‚Äôs first 
local green bond in 2021, and the adoption of a national green taxonomy in 2022, 
green businesses still face limited domestic demand, export barriers, and restricted 
access to finance. This is compounded by the local financial sector‚Äôs low risk appetite, 
especially toward small firms that often operate with survival rather than growth 
models8.  
2.6 In the case of Brazil, the country holds a strategic position to lead in the global green 
economy, leveraging its abundant natural resources, renewable energy capacity, and 
emerging low-carbon industries. The industrial sector plays a central role in this 
transition, particularly SMEs, which represent most of firms and employment in the 
country. A coordinated green transition could add up to USD 100 billion to GDP and 
generate 6.4 million new jobs by 2030 through the expansion of sustainable exports, 
such as green pig iron, bioproducts, and low-carbon technologies. At the same time, 
Brazil‚Äôs bioeconomy could reach an annual value of USD 284 billion by 2050 if the 
country strengthens the integration of its SMEs into global green value chains9.
2.7 From this standpoint, energy efficiency emerges as one of the most cost-effective and 
impactful levers for greening the industrial sector, especially among SMEs, which often 
operate with aging infrastructure and limited access to technical assistance or 
financing. The industrial sector consumes 32.3% of Brazil‚Äôs final energy and 37.3% of 
electricity, with thermal energy accounting for 80% of industrial energy use. Despite 
these high levels of consumption, most companies have not yet adopted available 
efficient solutions such as cogeneration systems, high-temperature heat pumps, waste 
heat recovery technologies, and insulation improvements. Increasing awareness and 
supporting the adoption of these technologies can significantly reduce energy costs, 
improve productivity, and contribute to a more competitive and sustainable industrial 
base10.
2.8 In this context, public policies play a critical role in enabling the green transition of 
SMEs, particularly by addressing barriers these firms face in adopting sustainable 
practices. Across OECD countries, governments are actively supporting this process 
by designing environmental regulations tailored to the realities of smaller enterprises, 
and by promoting measures that help them improve energy efficiency, adopt circular 
economy models, acquire new green skills, and access sustainable finance. 
Considering this, a comprehensive assessment of the main challenges and 
opportunities for SMEs is essential not only to strengthen technical capabilities, 
enhance access to sustainable markets, and increase green resilience, but also as a 
key input for designing public policies and instruments that can more effectively 
promote the green transition of SMEs. These efforts are critical to ensuring that SMEs 
can contribute meaningfully to green goals while improving their productivity and long-
term competitiveness.
2.9Results. As a result of this TC, the project will contribute to strengthening the 
institutional capacities of the governments of Brazil and Colombia by generating 
additional evidence to inform decision-making processes related to the green 
7 Climate Bonds Initiative (2023). Colombia Sustainable Finance State of the Market 2022. Climate 
Bonds Initiative.
8 IFC & SFC Colombia (2022). Colombia Green Taxonomy Guidelines. IFC, Bogot√°.
9 Statista (2023). Brazil industrial electricity consumption 2022. Statista.
10 McKinsey (2024). Greener shores: Brazil‚Äôs $100 billion decarbonization opportunity. McKinsey & 
Company, S√£o‚ÄØPaulo.
- 4 -
transition of SMEs. The assessments and policy recommendations produced will 
serve as key inputs to design more effective instruments and strategies to support 
climate resilience, and sustainable competitiveness. The effectiveness of this project 
will be measured through outcome indicators such as the number of downloads of the 
SME green transition assessments and the number of citations of the project‚Äôs findings 
in official policy documents in both countries.
2.10Beneficiaries. This TC will directly benefit policy-making institutions in LAC, 
particularly in Colombia and Brazil that are responsible for industrial development, 
innovation, and SME support. In Colombia, key institutions include the Ministry of 
Commerce, Industry and Tourism, The National Planning Department, The Ministry of 
Science, Technology and Innovation, and iNNpulsa Colombia. In Brazil, relevant 
actors include The Ministry of Entrepreneurship, Microenterprise and Small Business, 
The Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services, The Ministry of Science, 
Technology and Innovation, The Brazilian Agency for Industrial Development, among 
others. In addition to public institutions, the TC will also generate indirect benefits for 
a broad range of private sector actors, including micro, small, and medium-sized 
enterprises, business associations, chambers of commerce, industry federations, 
among others.
2.11Strategic Alignment. The TC aligns with the IDB Group‚Äôs Institutional Strategy (CA-
631) 2024-2030: Transforming for Scale and Impact; specifically, its objective of 
Bolstering Sustainable Regional Growth by generating knowledge and policy 
recommendations for stimulating SMEs green transition as a channel to foster firm 
investment, innovation and competitiveness. Also, aligns with the operational focus 
areas of: (i) Productive Development and Innovation through the private sector; (ii) 
Institutional capacity, Rule of Law and Citizen Security; and (iii) Biodiversity, Natural 
Capital and Climate Action. Furthermore, the TC contributes to the strategic priorities: 
(i) IDB CLIMA, as it aims at strengthening knowledge and stimulating SME green 
transition, contributing to demonstrate climate action toward national commitments; 
and (ii) COP-30, by developing policy recommendations to promote SME 
decarbonization and climate-resilient actions, aligned with the NDCs that beneficiary 
countries will present at COP-30. Also aligns with the Innovation, Science, and 
Technology Sector Framework (GN-2791-13), particularly Action Lines 5 of 
strengthening key institutions to drive innovation, and 6 of knowledge agenda, by 
enhancing institutional capacity to design and implement policies that support SME 
decarbonization and climate resilience through the generation and use of novel data. 
Therefore, this TC supports the Climate Change Sector Framework (GN-2835-13), 
contributing to Action Line 1 of adaptation and climate resilience, and Action Line 2 of 
rapid decarbonization, by fostering an enabling environment tailored to SMEs that 
promotes their green transition and improve competitiveness through targeted 
adaptation and mitigation measures. Also, this TC is aligned with the objectives of 
Window 2, Priority Area 1 ‚ÄúClimate Change and Environmental Sustainability‚Äù, and 3 
‚ÄúEffective, Efficient and Transparent Institutions‚Äù (W2C) of the Ordinary Capital 
Strategic Development Program (GN-2819-14), which has as expected results: (i) the 
provision of adequate knowledge and innovation ecosystems by contributing to 
policies that facilitate the use of technology to sustainably seize the region‚Äôs natural 
resource endowment; and (ii) to strengthen institutional and policy quality and service 
delivery and policy implementation to improve public sector management and promote 
private sector development, as well as leverage digital transformation to promote more 
effective, efficient, and transparent governments, better and more equal opportunities 
for citizens, and more productive and innovative firms.
- 5 -
2.12Country Strategy with the IDB Group. The TC is aligned with key strategic pillars of 
the Country Strategy of Brazil with the IDB Group (GN-3243-3) 2024-2027; by the 
support of green transition and climate resilience of SMEs, and by identifying key 
barriers and best practices, fostering sustainable business models, and enabling 
policy instruments that promote productive investments and long-term 
competitiveness. Also, aligns with the Country Strategy of Colombia with the IDB 
Group (GN-3238-3) 2024-2027; by the contribution to higher productivity and growth, 
supporting climate action and biodiversity protection, enhancing financial inclusion and 
business innovation, and advancing in the integration into global value chains and 
decarbonization of energy and transport sectors. Overall, it strengthens institutional 
frameworks and policy action toward a low-carbon economy, improving resource 
allocation, economic competitiveness, and climate resilience.

II. Objectives and Justification of the TC
2.1 Empowering Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) is essential for a successful green 
transition in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC). The emergence of the green 
growth paradigm has highlighted the critical link between economic and environmental 
performance in business. Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in LAC 
represent 99.5% of all businesses in the region and account for 61.1% of employment, 
yet they contribute only 24.6% of total productivity1. While each MSME generates 
relatively low greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions individually, their collective 
environmental impact is significant accounting for over 13% of global energy 
consumption. The objective of this TC is to enhance the capacities of policymakers in 
1 International Energy Agency (2015). Policy Pathway ‚Äì Accelerating Energy Efficiency in Small 
and Medium-sized Enterprises. IEA, Paris.
- 2 -
Brazil and Colombia to design and implement strategies that promote the green 
transition and climate resilience of SMEs, through the assessment of current practices, 
international benchmarking, and targeted policy recommendations in areas such as 
green innovation, skills, technologies, energy efficiency, and entrepreneurship.
2.2 According to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), 
SMEs contributed between 60% and 70% of industrial sector GHG emissions. 
Similarly, recent UK studies indicate that SMEs are responsible for 43% to 53% of the 
country‚Äôs industrial emissions2. Despite 60% of SMEs being familiar with key net-zero 
concepts, 53% are not yet prepared to prioritize decarbonization in their operations, 
and 56% have taken no action at all. Only 3% of surveyed SMEs have measured their 
carbon footprint and developed emission reduction strategies3.
2.3 At the same time, SMEs in LAC face high vulnerability to climate change. Their limited 
adaptive capacity, resource constraints, and exposure to extreme weather events 
pose serious challenges. Many operate in climate-sensitive sectors such as 
agriculture, tourism, and manufacturing, making them especially susceptible to 
droughts, floods, and hurricanes. Unlike larger firms, SMEs often lack financial buffers, 
technical know-how, and institutional support to invest in resilience measures or adopt 
more sustainable business models. In addition, supply chain disruptions, infrastructure 
damage, and volatile energy costs further jeopardize their stability‚Äîoften resulting in 
reduced productivity, higher operating costs, or even permanent closure.
2.4 In the case of Colombia, the country has made ambitious commitments, including 
reducing its GHG emissions by 51% by 2030, and achieving carbon neutrality by 
20504.  Although the country accounted for only 0.32% of global energy consumption 
in 2020 and reported a per capita energy use of 36 GJ and emissions of 1.85 tons of 
CO‚ÇÇ per inhabitant in 2021, it faces major challenges. The industrial sector, 
responsible for 22% of final energy consumption, uses energy efficiently in only 31% 
of its processes. The 2021 Climate Action Law established a legal framework with 237 
goals at national, subnational, and business levels, including achieving net-zero 
deforestation and reducing black carbon emissions by 40% by 20305. However, GHG 
emissions have increased since 2000, mainly from land use and energy consumption. 
Without adequate investment in adaptation, the national GDP could fall by 1.5% to 
2.5% by 2050. Moreover, over 50% of Colombia's exports depend on fossil fuels‚Äî
mainly oil and coal‚Äîputting up to 10% of export revenues and 8% of GDP at risk in a 
global low-carbon transition6.
2.5 Considering this, SMEs, which make up 99.7% of the country‚Äôs business fabric, are 
key to the green transition, yet they face significant gaps. Fewer than 3% have 
measured their carbon footprint, and over 50% are not prepared to prioritize 
decarbonization. The green finance market remains small: in 2023, only 10 green 
bonds and 5 sustainability bonds were issued, and green loans made up just 5% of

5 UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre (2023). Boosting Energy Efficiency at the Industrial level in 
Colombia, in support of NDC implementation. UNEP.
6 World Bank Group (2023). Colombia Country Climate and Development Report. World Bank, 
Washington, DC.
- 3 -
the total banking portfolio7. While progress has been made, such as Colombia‚Äôs first 
local green bond in 2021, and the adoption of a national green taxonomy in 2022, 
green businesses still face limited domestic demand, export barriers, and restricted 
access to finance. This is compounded by the local financial sector‚Äôs low risk appetite, 
especially toward small firms that often operate with survival rather than growth 
models8.  
2.6 In the case of Brazil, the country holds a strategic position to lead in the global green 
economy, leveraging its abundant natural resources, renewable energy capacity, and 
emerging low-carbon industries. The industrial sector plays a central role in this 
transition, particularly SMEs, which represent most of firms and employment in the 
country. A coordinated green transition could add up to USD 100 billion to GDP and 
generate 6.4 million new jobs by 2030 through the expansion of sustainable exports, 
such as green pig iron, bioproducts, and low-carbon technologies. At the same time, 
Brazil‚Äôs bioeconomy could reach an annual value of USD 284 billion by 2050 if the 
country strengthens the integration of its SMEs into global green value chains9.

impactful levers for greening the industrial sector, especially among SMEs, which often 
operate with aging infrastructure and limited access to technical assistance or 
financing. The industrial sector consumes 32.3% of Brazil‚Äôs final energy and 37.3% of

heat recovery technologies, and insulation improvements. Increasing awareness and 
supporting the adoption of these technologies can significantly reduce energy costs, 
improve productivity, and contribute to a more competitive and sustainable industrial 
base10.
2.8 In this context, public policies play a critical role in enabling the green transition of 
SMEs, particularly by addressing barriers these firms face in adopting sustainable 
practices. Across OECD countries, governments are actively supporting this process 
by designing environmental regulations tailored to the realities of smaller enterprises, 
and by promoting measures that help them improve energy efficiency, adopt circular 
economy models, acquire new green skills, and access sustainable finance. 
Considering this, a comprehensive assessment of the main challenges and 
opportunities for SMEs is essential not only to strengthen technical capabilities, 
enhance access to sustainable markets, and increase green resilience, but also as a 
key input for designing public policies and instruments that can more effectively 
promote the green transition of SMEs. These efforts are critical to ensuring that SMEs 
can contribute meaningfully to green goals while improving their productivity and long-
term competitiveness.

institutional capacities of the governments of Brazil and Colombia by generating 
additional evidence to inform decision-making processes related to the green

transition of SMEs. The assessments and policy recommendations produced will 
serve as key inputs to design more effective instruments and strategies to support 
climate resilience, and sustainable competitiveness. The effectiveness of this project 
will be measured through outcome indicators such as the number of downloads of the 
SME green transition assessments and the number of citations of the project‚Äôs findings 
in official policy documents in both countries.
2.10Beneficiaries. This TC will directly benefit policy-making institutions in LAC, 
particularly in Colombia and Brazil that are responsible for industrial development, 
innovation, and SME support. In Colombia, key institutions include the Ministry of 
Commerce, Industry and Tourism, The National Planning Department, The Ministry of 
Science, Technology and Innovation, and iNNpulsa Colombia. In Brazil, relevant 
actors include The Ministry of Entrepreneurship, Microenterprise and Small Business, 
The Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services, The Ministry of Science, 
Technology and Innovation, The Brazilian Agency for Industrial Development, among 
others. In addition to public institutions, the TC will also generate indirect benefits for 
a broad range of private sector actors, including micro, small, and medium-sized 
enterprises, business associations, chambers of commerce, industry federations, 
among others.
2.11Strategic Alignment. The TC aligns with the IDB Group‚Äôs Institutional Strategy (CA-
631) 2024-2030: Transforming for Scale and Impact; specifically, its objective of 
Bolstering Sustainable Regional Growth by generating knowledge and policy 
recommendations for stimulating SMEs green transition as a channel to foster firm 
investment, innovation and competitiveness. Also, aligns with the operational focus 
areas of: (i) Productive Development and Innovation through the private sector; (ii) 
Institutional capacity, Rule of Law and Citizen Security; and (iii) Biodiversity, Natural 
Capital and Climate Action. Furthermore, the TC contributes to the strategic priorities: 
(i) IDB CLIMA, as it aims at strengthening knowledge and stimulating SME green 
transition, contributing to demonstrate climate action toward national commitments; 
and (ii) COP-30, by developing policy recommendations to promote SME 
decarbonization and climate-resilient actions, aligned with the NDCs that beneficiary 
countries will present at COP-30. Also aligns with the Innovation, Science, and 
Technology Sector Framework (GN-2791-13), particularly Action Lines 5 of 
strengthening key institutions to drive innovation, and 6 of knowledge agenda, by 
enhancing institutional capacity to design and implement policies that support SME 
decarbonization and climate resilience through the generation and use of novel data. 
Therefore, this TC supports the Climate Change Sector Framework (GN-2835-13), 
contributing to Action Line 1 of adaptation and climate resilience, and Action Line 2 of 
rapid decarbonization, by fostering an enabling environment tailored to SMEs that 
promotes their green transition and improve competitiveness through targeted 
adaptation and mitigation measures. Also, this TC is aligned with the objectives of 
Window 2, Priority Area 1 ‚ÄúClimate Change and Environmental Sustainability‚Äù, and 3 
‚ÄúEffective, Efficient and Transparent Institutions‚Äù (W2C) of the Ordinary Capital 
Strategic Development Program (GN-2819-14), which has as expected results: (i) the 
provision of adequate knowledge and innovation ecosystems by contributing to 
policies that facilitate the use of technology to sustainably seize the region‚Äôs natural 
resource endowment; and (ii) to strengthen institutional and policy quality and service 
delivery and policy implementation to improve public sector management and promote 
private sector development, as well as leverage digital transformation to promote more 
effective, efficient, and transparent governments, better and more equal opportunities 
for citizens, and more productive and innovative firms.

2.12Country Strategy with the IDB Group. The TC is aligned with key strategic pillars of 
the Country Strategy of Brazil with the IDB Group (GN-3243-3) 2024-2027; by the 
support of green transition and climate resilience of SMEs, and by identifying key 
barriers and best practices, fostering sustainable business models, and enabling 
policy instruments that promote productive investments and long-term 
competitiveness. Also, aligns with the Country Strategy of Colombia with the IDB 
Group (GN-3238-3) 2024-2027; by the contribution to higher productivity and growth, 
supporting climate action and biodiversity protection, enhancing financial inclusion and 
business innovation, and advancing in the integration into global value chains and 
decarbonization of energy and transport sectors. Overall, it strengthens institutional 
frameworks and policy action toward a low-carbon economy, improving resource 
allocation, economic competitiveness, and climate resilience.

2.1 Empowering Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) is essential for a successful green 
transition in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC). The emergence of the green 
growth paradigm has highlighted the critical link between economic and environmental 
performance in business. Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in LAC 
represent 99.5% of all businesses in the region and account for 61.1% of employment, 
yet they contribute only 24.6% of total productivity1. While each MSME generates 
relatively low greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions individually, their collective 
environmental impact is significant accounting for over 13% of global energy 
consumption. The objective of this TC is to enhance the capacities of policymakers in 
1 International Energy Agency (2015). Policy Pathway ‚Äì Accelerating Energy Efficiency in Small 
and Medium-sized Enterprises. IEA, Paris.

Brazil and Colombia to design and implement strategies that promote the green 
transition and climate resilience of SMEs, through the assessment of current practices, 
international benchmarking, and targeted policy recommendations in areas such as 
green innovation, skills, technologies, energy efficiency, and entrepreneurship.
2.2 According to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), 
SMEs contributed between 60% and 70% of industrial sector GHG emissions. 
Similarly, recent UK studies indicate that SMEs are responsible for 43% to 53% of the 
country‚Äôs industrial emissions2. Despite 60% of SMEs being familiar with key net-zero 
concepts, 53% are not yet prepared to prioritize decarbonization in their operations, 
and 56% have taken no action at all. Only 3% of surveyed SMEs have measured their 
carbon footprint and developed emission reduction strategies3.
2.3 At the same time, SMEs in LAC face high vulnerability to climate change. Their limited 
adaptive capacity, resource constraints, and exposure to extreme weather events 
pose serious challenges. Many operate in climate-sensitive sectors such as 
agriculture, tourism, and manufacturing, making them especially susceptible to 
droughts, floods, and hurricanes. Unlike larger firms, SMEs often lack financial buffers, 
technical know-how, and institutional support to invest in resilience measures or adopt 
more sustainable business models. In addition, supply chain disruptions, infrastructure 
damage, and volatile energy costs further jeopardize their stability‚Äîoften resulting in 
reduced productivity, higher operating costs, or even permanent closure.
2.4 In the case of Colombia, the country has made ambitious commitments, including 
reducing its GHG emissions by 51% by 2030, and achieving carbon neutrality by 
20504.  Although the country accounted for only 0.32% of global energy consumption 
in 2020 and reported a per capita energy use of 36 GJ and emissions of 1.85 tons of 
CO‚ÇÇ per inhabitant in 2021, it faces major challenges. The industrial sector, 
responsible for 22% of final energy consumption, uses energy efficiently in only 31% 
of its processes. The 2021 Climate Action Law established a legal framework with 237 
goals at national, subnational, and business levels, including achieving net-zero 
deforestation and reducing black carbon emissions by 40% by 20305. However, GHG 
emissions have increased since 2000, mainly from land use and energy consumption. 
Without adequate investment in adaptation, the national GDP could fall by 1.5% to 
2.5% by 2050. Moreover, over 50% of Colombia's exports depend on fossil fuels‚Äî
mainly oil and coal‚Äîputting up to 10% of export revenues and 8% of GDP at risk in a 
global low-carbon transition6.

key to the green transition, yet they face significant gaps. Fewer than 3% have 
measured their carbon footprint, and over 50% are not prepared to prioritize 
decarbonization. The green finance market remains small: in 2023, only 10 green 
bonds and 5 sustainability bonds were issued, and green loans made up just 5% of

the total banking portfolio7. While progress has been made, such as Colombia‚Äôs first

access to finance. This is compounded by the local financial sector‚Äôs low risk appetite, 
especially toward small firms that often operate with survival rather than growth 
models8.  
2.6 In the case of Brazil, the country holds a strategic position to lead in the global green

emerging low-carbon industries. The industrial sector plays a central role in this 
transition, particularly SMEs, which represent most of firms and employment in the 
country. A coordinated green transition could add up to USD 100 billion to GDP and 
generate 6.4 million new jobs by 2030 through the expansion of sustainable exports, 
such as green pig iron, bioproducts, and low-carbon technologies. At the same time,

country strengthens the integration of its SMEs into global green value chains9.

impactful levers for greening the industrial sector, especially among SMEs, which often 
operate with aging infrastructure and limited access to technical assistance or

improve productivity, and contribute to a more competitive and sustainable industrial 
base10.

SMEs, particularly by addressing barriers these firms face in adopting sustainable 
practices. Across OECD countries, governments are actively supporting this process 
by designing environmental regulations tailored to the realities of smaller enterprises, 
and by promoting measures that help them improve energy efficiency, adopt circular 
economy models, acquire new green skills, and access sustainable finance.

opportunities for SMEs is essential not only to strengthen technical capabilities, 
enhance access to sustainable markets, and increase green resilience, but also as a 
key input for designing public policies and instruments that can more effectively 
promote the green transition of SMEs. These efforts are critical to ensuring that SMEs 
can contribute meaningfully to green goals while improving their productivity and long-
term competitiveness.

2.1 Empowering Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) is essential for a successful green 
transition in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC). The emergence of the green 
growth paradigm has highlighted the critical link between economic and environmental 
performance in business. Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in LAC 
represent 99.5% of all businesses in the region and account for 61.1% of employment, 
yet they contribute only 24.6% of total productivity1. While each MSME generates 
relatively low greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions individually, their collective 
environmental impact is significant accounting for over 13% of global energy 
consumption. The objective of this TC is to enhance the capacities of policymakers in 
1 International Energy Agency (2015). Policy Pathway ‚Äì Accelerating Energy Efficiency in Small 
and Medium-sized Enterprises. IEA, Paris.

Brazil and Colombia to design and implement strategies that promote the green 
transition and climate resilience of SMEs, through the assessment of current practices, 
international benchmarking, and targeted policy recommendations in areas such as 
green innovation, skills, technologies, energy efficiency, and entrepreneurship.
2.2 According to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), 
SMEs contributed between 60% and 70% of industrial sector GHG emissions. 
Similarly, recent UK studies indicate that SMEs are responsible for 43% to 53% of the 
country‚Äôs industrial emissions2. Despite 60% of SMEs being familiar with key net-zero 
concepts, 53% are not yet prepared to prioritize decarbonization in their operations, 
and 56% have taken no action at all. Only 3% of surveyed SMEs have measured their 
carbon footprint and developed emission reduction strategies3.
2.3 At the same time, SMEs in LAC face high vulnerability to climate change. Their limited 
adaptive capacity, resource constraints, and exposure to extreme weather events 
pose serious challenges. Many operate in climate-sensitive sectors such as 
agriculture, tourism, and manufacturing, making them especially susceptible to 
droughts, floods, and hurricanes. Unlike larger firms, SMEs often lack financial buffers, 
technical know-how, and institutional support to invest in resilience measures or adopt 
more sustainable business models. In addition, supply chain disruptions, infrastructure 
damage, and volatile energy costs further jeopardize their stability‚Äîoften resulting in 
reduced productivity, higher operating costs, or even permanent closure.
2.4 In the case of Colombia, the country has made ambitious commitments, including 
reducing its GHG emissions by 51% by 2030, and achieving carbon neutrality by 
20504.  Although the country accounted for only 0.32% of global energy consumption 
in 2020 and reported a per capita energy use of 36 GJ and emissions of 1.85 tons of 
CO‚ÇÇ per inhabitant in 2021, it faces major challenges. The industrial sector, 
responsible for 22% of final energy consumption, uses energy efficiently in only 31% 
of its processes. The 2021 Climate Action Law established a legal framework with 237 
goals at national, subnational, and business levels, including achieving net-zero 
deforestation and reducing black carbon emissions by 40% by 20305. However, GHG 
emissions have increased since 2000, mainly from land use and energy consumption. 
Without adequate investment in adaptation, the national GDP could fall by 1.5% to 
2.5% by 2050. Moreover, over 50% of Colombia's exports depend on fossil fuels‚Äî
mainly oil and coal‚Äîputting up to 10% of export revenues and 8% of GDP at risk in a 
global low-carbon transition6.

key to the green transition, yet they face significant gaps. Fewer than 3% have 
measured their carbon footprint, and over 50% are not prepared to prioritize 
decarbonization. The green finance market remains small: in 2023, only 10 green 
bonds and 5 sustainability bonds were issued, and green loans made up just 5% of

green businesses still face limited domestic demand, export barriers, and restricted 
access to finance. This is compounded by the local financial sector‚Äôs low risk appetite, 
especially toward small firms that often operate with survival rather than growth 
models8.  
2.6 In the case of Brazil, the country holds a strategic position to lead in the global green 
economy, leveraging its abundant natural resources, renewable energy capacity, and 
emerging low-carbon industries. The industrial sector plays a central role in this 
transition, particularly SMEs, which represent most of firms and employment in the 
country. A coordinated green transition could add up to USD 100 billion to GDP and

base10.

SMEs, particularly by addressing barriers these firms face in adopting sustainable 
practices. Across OECD countries, governments are actively supporting this process

economy models, acquire new green skills, and access sustainable finance.

opportunities for SMEs is essential not only to strengthen technical capabilities, 
enhance access to sustainable markets, and increase green resilience, but also as a 
key input for designing public policies and instruments that can more effectively 
promote the green transition of SMEs. These efforts are critical to ensuring that SMEs

V. Executing agency and execution structure 
5.1 The Bank will execute this TC through the Competitiveness, Technology and 
Innovation Division (PTI/CTI). CTI‚Äôs experience in green innovation, green 
technologies, SME policy, and green entrepreneurship in the region will play a 
catalyzing role in the success of this TC, and as a request from the beneficiaries. 
Considering that this is Regional TC, as per the OP-619-4, Annex II, C 2.2, the Bank 
is the proposed EA. Execution by the Bank will ensure effective coordination between 
the activities in the two countries, stakeholders involved, and centralization of efforts 
and knowledge. Therefore, PTI/CTI will guarantee the quality and timeliness of the 
financed products, according to section 4.5 of the Bank‚Äôs Technical Cooperation 
Guidelines (GN-2470-2). This section requires that for Bank executed technical 
cooperation: (a) the beneficiary country agrees and (b) the proposed activities are 
aligned with the strategies and programs of the Bank in the Country.
5.2 The activities to be carried out under this operation have been included in the 
Procurement Plan and will be executed in accordance with the Bank‚Äôs established 
procurement methods, namely: (i) Corporate procurement of individual consultants, as 
set forth in Section AM-650 of the Administrative Manual "Complementary Workforce" 
for individual consultants; and (ii) contracting of consulting firms for services of an 
intellectual nature, as well as logistical and other non-consulting services, in 
accordance with the IDB‚Äôs Corporate  Procurement Policy (GN-2303-33) and its 
associated guidelines. In accordance with these regulations, the unique combination 
of technical expertise, innovative policy tools, and active engagement with 
policymakers positions the OECD as a uniquely qualified partner for the assessments. 
5.3 The CTI Division (PTI/CTI) will be responsible for the supervision, monitoring, and 
evaluation of this TC, in close coordination with the Bank‚Äôs Country Offices in Brazil 
and Colombia. Monitoring activities will include regular follow-up meetings with 
executing entities and stakeholders, review of interim deliverables, and the use of 
output and outcome indicators defined in the Results Matrix. The final evaluation will 
synthesize lessons learned and inform future operations, in alignment with the Bank‚Äôs 
results-oriented approach and TC guidelines.

of the Bank and may be made available to the public under a creative commons 
license. However, those outputs jointly produced with the OECD will be co-published 
by the IDB and the OECD. Both institutions will be acknowledged as co-authors and 
may use, publish, and reproduce these outputs, provided that appropriate credit is 
given to the other institution‚Äôs contribution.

section_text:
VI. Major issues 
6.1 The first risk identified is the limited access to information in both countries, as the 
quality of the diagnostics will largely depend on the availability and reliability of existing 
data. To mitigate this risk, it is proposed to complement secondary data with primary 
inputs such as surveys and interviews. Additionally, with the support of local 
consultants, it will be essential to engage key local actors, such as think tanks and 
business associations, that can contribute additional data and facilitate access to 
relevant information.
6.2 The second risk is related to the level of engagement of public and private 
stakeholders, which could affect both the sense of ownership over the diagnostics and 
the action plans. To address this, the TC aims to foster early and sustained 
involvement of key actors from both sectors, starting from the planning phase through 
implementation. This includes identifying focal points within relevant institutions and 
establishing follow-up mechanisms. It is important that stakeholders are not only 
recipients of the deliverables but are actively engaged as partners throughout the 
process.
6.3 The third risk is the potential impact of the 2026 electoral cycle in Colombia and Brazil, 
which could lead to shifts in institutional priorities and leadership. These dynamics, 
along with varying levels of institutional capacity, may influence the continuity of 
stakeholder engagement. To help mitigate these risks, the TC will prioritize early and 
sustained engagement with key counterparts, support institutional capacity-building, 
and ensure that outputs are closely aligned with national long-term strategies, thus 
contributing to the sustainability of results.

 PROJECT SUMMARY  
(TT-T1172 ) 
 
Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) significantly contribute to GDP and 
employment in Trinidad and Tobago, yet face barriers such as limited mentorship, networking 
opportunities, and targeted skills development. These challenges hinder founders' a bility to 
scale their businesses and contribute to regional economic growth and innovation.  
The Ignite the World project aims to reduce barriers related to mentorship, networking, and 
skills development for founders in Trinidad and Tobago. The project will engage participants 
annually, focusing on innovative business models in sectors such as Fin Tech, HealthTech, 
AgriTech, and ClimateTech. Activities include mentorship, networking events, mini -MBA 
courses, startup weekends, and workshops for high school and university students from 
marginalized backgrounds.  
Ignite the World is innovative due to its deep stakeholder engagement through ethnographic 
interviews and community co -creation sessions, ensuring relevance to the Caribbean context. 
It prioritizes foundational business skills and business model developmen t for highly innovative 
start-ups and fosters regional collaboration.  
The primary expected results include engaging 500 unique founders, 40% of whom are 
women, accelerating 50 founders/startups, and launching a mini -MBA program with 150 
enrolled participants.  
The project has a total cost of US$ 600,300 , of which US$ 300,000  (49.98 %) will be a non -
reimbursable technical cooperation grant provided by IDB Lab with resources from the  
European Commission and Restarted Framework Agreement (ECR) , and US$ 300,300  
(50.02 %) in counterpart by the Executing Agency . The project aligns with the IDB Group‚Äôs 
institutional strategy, supporting private sector innovation and gender equality. It also 
contributes to several Sustainable Development Goals, such as Quality Education, Decent 
Work and Economic Growth, Reduced Ineq ualities, and Gender Equality .

I. The Problem  
A. Problem Description  
1.1. The contribution of micro and small businesses to GDP and employment in Latin America 
and the Caribbean is well documented. According  to the Caribbean Development Bank  
(CDB) , in 2021 micro, small and medium  enterprises (MSME) in the Caribbean region 
account for 70-85% of firms, contribute between 60 -70% of Gross Domestic Product  
(GDP)  and account for an estimated 50% of employment . The CDB estimated that 40% 
of these businesses are owned by women .1 2In Trinidad and Tobago, the International 
Labor  Organization  (ILO)  published a 2023 study which cited Central Bank of Trinidad and 
Tobago data that there are approximately 20,000 -25,000 small and medium enterprises 
(SME)  representing about 85% of formal businesses and contributing an estimated 30% 
to GDP .3 
1.2. In terms of contribution to poverty reduction, the United Nations Department of Economic 
and Social Affairs (UNDESA )‚Äôs publication ‚ÄúMSMEs and their role in achieving the 
Sustainable Development Goals ‚Äù4 examines the role of MSMEs to each of the SDGs. The 
report unpacks the role of MSMEs in economic activity, in creating employment and 
incomes, particularly for the poor and marginalized groups, as service providers (for 
example in education, health, water  and sanitation) and examines the private sector led 
contributions of MSMEs globally to achievement of SDGs including contributing 
significantly to poverty reduction via employment.  
1.3. A growing MSME sector is critical to the growth and development of Tri nidad and Tobago 
and the wider region, however founders encounter significant barriers that hinder their 
ability to establish and scale their businesses, including limited mentorship and networking 
opportunities, and the need for targeted skills development .5 These challenges can 
impede founders‚Äô  ability  to grow  their business and to contribute to economic growth and 
innovation in the region .  
1.4. Whereas Caribbean economies have historically relied on traditional industries like 
agriculture, tourism, and natural resources, there has been a significant shift towards 
diversified economic activities in recent years, with a growing emphasis on digital 
technologies and innovative business models. Digital technology has been a game -
changer for Caribbean entrepreneurs. With the proliferation of mobile devices and internet

 connectivity, even remote islands now have access to global markets. This connectivity 
has enabled the rise of startups in various sectors, including fintech, agritech, healthtech, 
and edtech. These startups address local problems and create solutions with  global 
applicability6. 
1.5. With the acceleration of technology driven b usinesses, there are now greater opportunities  
and activities for tech led businesses  to develop models and value propositions to solve 
problems that disproportionately affect lower income populations, specifically in areas 
such as financial inclusion, heath technologies, climate adaptation, climate smart 
agriculture and citizen security. These types of businesses typically find access to finance 
and support more difficult, in part as they are not based on a typical  asset basis. In this 
regard these types  of inclusive business models struggle to secure support for growth.7  
1.6. Supporting a new generation of founders and fostering the growth of the MSME sector 
involves developing and deploying founder -centric, cost -effective, practical, and 
sustainable solutions to overcome key barriers that hinder their ability to establish and 
scale businesses. This is a critical component of the business ecosystem.  Caribbean 
Dragons, through ongoing engagement with ecosystem actors and start -ups identifies the 
most pressing problems / needs as defined by founders as follows:  
‚Ä¢ Challenges with starting up  and scaling a new business : It can be difficult for 
aspiring entrepreneurs  to successfully navigate  the administration and legal 
requirements of registering their business.  Respondents8 cited a l ack of 
experience and knowledge in how to establish and scale businesses that are not 
based on typical asset bases : Start Ups , particularly  those that are tech -focused,  
express a need for increased knowledge support  in specialized areas such as 
early -stage  financing, product development, market growth strategies, and  
management of  intellectual properly . 
‚Ä¢ Limited Networking Opportunities : Founders need and value community, 
especially start -ups. There is a clear demand for more events, seminars, and 
introductions to key players within specific ecosystems to help entrepreneurs grow 
their personal networks and connect with potential partners.  Respondents 
indicated a need for entrepreneurial support and exposure. Entrepreneurs are 
looking for more visibility for their ventures, including the development of a 
directory of skills and resources to present their work to a broader audience.   
‚Ä¢ Mentorship for Innovation and Market Understanding : Entrepreneurs seek 
mentorship to better understand market needs and implement innovative ideas, 
favoring collaborative learning environments for exchanging insights.

 ‚Ä¢ Professional Development and Coaching:  There is a significant need for 
guidance and one -on-one coaching  in various  startup specific skills such as: non -
traditional/alternate forms of early -stage financing (e.g. crowdfunding, angel 
investing, and venture capital), customer need identification, market segmentation 
for emerging technologies, technical knowledge (e.g. cod ing and U/X design), 
growth hacking, regulatory compliance (e.g. intellectual property and evolving 
technology legislation) . 
 
1.7. Project Beneficiaries:  The project aims to engage 500 participants during the execution 
term in its core service delivery . These will be Founders , primarily in Trinidad and Tobago  
(TT), that are seeking to accel erate growth of an innovative business. In the context of this 
project, innovation  will be represented by a business which is disrupting its industry 
vertically  by either (a) offering a new product or service , (b) using  new technologies , (c) 
leveraging a new  /novel business operational model , or (d) entering a new market ; and 
that has an identifiable path to scalability.  Companies focused on fossil fuel exploration 
and production  will be excluded . Within this group , 10% of beneficiary  founders will be 
leading disruptive  technology - driven business  models that can impact / provide viable 
solutions to low income, poor / vulnerable segments of the population(s) they aim to serve. 
These firm s will be selected based on fintech and health tech providers and /or other 
businesses , that are primarily focused on delivering value for low-income  population 
segments of the market . In addition to building capacity of 500 businesses in Trinidad and 
Tobago, with 40% of these (200) being women and 10% or 50 leading b usinesses that 
primarily target  low income/vulnerable market segments, in order to encourage innovation 
in the next generation, Caribbean Drago ns will deliver training to the project intervention 
will offer a series of interactive workshops on innovation for 200 high sc hool students . 
1.8. Gender  Equity : Although women in in Latin America and Caribbean make up 43.1% of 
entrepreneurs operating in export -oriented businesses9, the global participation average 
for women in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) spaces is 
13.2% as of 202310. Based on Caribbean Dragons experience in the ecosystem and its 
2024 study, the rate of participation/leadership of women in STEM enterprises in TT is 
even lower than the global average with  less than 10% of technology founders interviewed 
being women (out of 123 technology founders participating in the study ). As such , the 
project is seeking to deliver support to female technology business founders as a specific 
and under -represented segment and has set a target of least 40% of benefic iaries being   
(a) women who have founded technology -led or technology -assisted businesses, (b) 
women who are working for technology -led or technology -assisted businesses as 
managers, (c) women who are working in traditional businesses but in technology 
disciplines (e.g. Information Technology teams) or (d) female leaders and managers of 
traditional busine sses/sectors .

 1.9. To achieve this, the project will take a two -fold approach of recruiting and content  
development. For recruiting efforts, the team will source participants by working with 
existing IDB Lab ecosystem  programs, such as Sh aping the Future of Innovation, as well 
as several Trinidad -based organizations that focus on female professional engagement, 
including  but not limited to : The Women in Tech Network of Trinidad and Tobago, Women 
Techmakers Trinidad and Tobago, Caribbean Tech Women, The SheTrades Hub run out 
of the Ministry of Trade and Industry, The Association of Female Executives of Trinidad 
and Tobago, The Women in Busin ess Association of Trinidad and Tobago, The 
International Women‚Äôs Forum of Trinidad and Tobago, and Th e Caribbean Women‚Äôs

and recommended channels  to actively encourage these women to participate, by clearly 
defining the importance placed on women business leadership and the value proposition

1.10.  With respect to content development , the team will engage with expert organizations that 
have extensive experience in understanding and address ing female challenges within

II. The Innovation Proposal  
A. Project Description  
2.1 Ignite the World seeks to catalyze the support that is needed for accelerated growth and 
viability of start -ups in the Caribbean, piloting  its approach in Trinidad and Tobago which 
has the Caribbean Region‚Äôs largest industrial base and an urgent mandate for 
diversification . The project‚Äôs main objective is to reduce the barriers related to mentorship , 
networking opportunities, and skills development that founders in Trinidad and Tobago 
face when trying to establish and scale their businesses.  
2.2 The targeted beneficiaries of this project will be engaged as follows : 
‚Ä¢ Founders : These founders will commit  to creating meaningful changes  through the 
application of new technologies, driving innovation in their respective industries.  They 
will be  exposed to networking, learning opportunities and have the option to be 
matched  with experienced international founders within their verticals, to access 
specialized knowledge not available within T T. To maximize benefits, these

 innovators should ideally have developed an initial version of a business plan prior to 
engagement. This plan should include the definition of their value proposition, market 
hypothesis, and commercialization strategy.  
‚Ä¢ Ten percent  of founders  engaged and accelerated via  the program will be focused on 
innovation  from key sectors  that serve specific need s of low 
income/vulnerable /marginalized  population . These will be identified following a three -
folded criteria: (1) Self-reported  data provided by the entrepreneur declaring the 
solution is aimed at the poor/vulnerable/low -income ; (2) The proposed solution will 
provide products/services for lower prices whilst maintaining quality standards as of 
what is available in the market ; (3) Eligible segments include but are not limited to 
fintechs (addresses the unbanked, or improves financial literacy/ planning ) and 
healthtechs (supports more active disease prevention and management) . 
‚Ä¢ Female founders and managers will be actively recruited to ensure that they make up 
40% of participants.  These will include women who are currently running or  are 
building businesses . This group will  benefit from  additional gender -focused 
programming including female to female mentorship, confidence and leadership 
building . 50 startups  / founders  are expected to be incubated / accelerated via the 
program . This involves having completed all three main programs offering  mini-MBA 
courses, a startup weekend and one -on-one mentorship.  
‚Ä¢ 200 h igh school  students from  financially marginalized  groups  (lower -tiered schools , 
who are vulnerable to cycles of poverty , will be exposed to financial literacy and 
entrepreneurship programming . In this regard List of schools that are financially and 
socially vulnerable (and from which CD will actively engage student participation ):

2.3 Two aspects of the Ignite the World project make it an innovative initiativ e. Firstly, the 
program was designed on deep stakeholder engagement through a series of quali tative  
research methods including deep ethnographic interviews, and community co -creation 
sessions. This was done to ensure that proposed activities are re levant and fit -for-
purpose, as compared to adopting North American and Eu ropean Startup Community 
frameworks and imposing it to a Caribbean audience.  
2.4 Additionally, within the region, there are very few non -profit accelerators that focus on 
innovation and technology -driven pre -seed companies in the Caribbean. There is a 
disproportionate emphasis on supporting more established and traditional companies. 
7 
 
 Consequently, this project will prioritize foundational business skills and business model 
development, which are critical for disruptive and highly innovative start -ups. Further , 
startup programs  that exis t in the Caribbean tend to be  limited to their country of origin 
and do not typically collaborate across the wider region.  At the core , Caribbean Dragons 
are ecosystem builders seek ing to connect the region in the hopes of leveraging relational 
capital to bring cross -geography resources for their founding community in T T. 
2.5 The project is structured to include three technical components as follows : 
2.6 Component I:  CONNECT  ‚Äì The objective of this component is to c urate and activate  a 
network of individuals engaged as founders or ecosystem players in  startup development 
and growth.  The project aims to connect 275 founders within 2 years . Early -stage founders 
will benefit from guidance provided by seasoned innovators, as well as peer support and 
access to local talent. By establishing a platform for engagement, Caribbean Dragons will 
facilitate critical connections through:  
‚Ä¢ IGNITE Innovation Summit: This annual event will  convene  the key actors in the 
Regional Innovation Ecosystem and allow stakeholders to overcome geographic and 
social boundaries, integrate and foster conditions for greater innovation output.  
‚Ä¢ Quarterly Community Series: These small pop -up events will facilitate spontaneous 
connection making and reinforce existing relationships among  founders and other 
ecosystem  actors through in -person interactions.  
‚Ä¢ Online Engagement: Caribbean Dragons will create  an online community which 
enables self -directed engagement among members and facilitates data collection 
and sharing.  
‚Ä¢ Monthly Newsletter: Caribbean Dragons will use this mechanism  to share success 
stories of Innovators and Investors which inspire and educate the community.  
‚Ä¢ Mentorship : This element of the program will match 50 founders with mentors for a 
total of 8 hours. To be accepted into the mentorship program, founders must complete 
at least four of the mini-MBA  modules , participate in a startup  weekend (as defined 
in Component 2 Learn) , and participate in a Mentorship Onboarding Workshop. 
Mentees will define and agree priority areas for the interactions and both mentors and 
mentees will operate within guidelines developed by Caribbean Dragons.  Mentors  will 
be sourced from the Caribbean Dragons community and will include  experienced  
founders, funders/investors, entrepreneurial hubs, service providers (e.g., coders, 
marketers, accountants), as well as multilateral agencies a nd organizations.  Matching 
will be done on a skills -needs basis.  
2.7 By the end of the project, the expected results  are: 10 networking events for founders and 
ecosystem actors, 40 founders benefiting  from startup weekends  and 275 active users 
within the online community . 
2.8 Component II:  LEARN - The objective of this component is to deliver  comprehensive  
training and experiential learning tailored to accelerate startups . The key activities are as 
follows ; 
‚Ä¢ Mini-MBA:  Caribbean Dragons will develop a n online  mini-MBA program that will 
offer specialized and target ed micro -learning s that can be applied directly into 
participants‚Äô startups . Initially the mini-MBA  will offer 8 foundational modules  specially 
curated to the needs of Caribbean founders. The proposed modules are universal 
topics which are industry/sector agnostic and are therefore applicable to all Founders. 
8 
 
 These will initially be run as virtually assisted s essions to guide the first groups of 
participants with the intent to adapt and improve. By the end of the project, the 
modules will be digitally delivered. Once the content has been digitized, it will be self-
paced and available to the community through paid membership subscriptions. The 
digital delivery model will help facilitate scaling.  Proposed modules includ e: Beyond 
the Pitch: Non -Traditional Funding Strategies, Problem -Solution Fit: Mastering 
Customer Discovery & Validation, Disruptive Markets: Navigating Emerging Tech & 
Segmentation, Startup Tech Toolkit: No -Code, Low -Code & Essential Dev Skills, 
Growth Ha cking & Traction: Scaling Without Breaking the Bank, Startup Law & 
Compliance: Protecting Your Business & IP, Behavioral Econom ics & Pricing 
Psychology, and Founder Resilience & Mental Toughness . As stated above, the 
program address es the general knowledge needs around: early -stage financing, 
product development, market growth strategies, and management of intellectual 
properly . 
‚Ä¢ Startup weekends:  These smaller events will allow 10 founders  at each event to 
apply the relevant learnings of the mini-MBA  and refine their business plans and value 
propositions , leveraging peer -to-peer and specialist advisory and support drawn from 
the Caribbean Dragons communit y. 
‚Ä¢ Quarterly Webinars:  To develop general business building and investment 
knowledge these webinars offer founders a  ‚Äúdeep dive‚Äù learning sessions delivered 
by expert practitioners.  
‚Ä¢ Monthly Podcast:  These podcasts will explore  innovation and technology  trends that 
can assist founders to develop a regional and global business perspective  
‚Ä¢ Igniting the next generation of startups : Caribbean Dragons will facilitate the 
delivery of seminars and workshops to explore the startup  journey and innovation 
methodologies . The targeted participants will be students from high schools  in more 
vulnerable or marginalized communities as well as tertiary students studying 
entrepreneurship and innovation.  
2.9 By the end of the project, the expected results include  launch ing the mini -MBA program 
with 8  modules tailored to acceleration of startups/founders; 150 founders enrolled in  the 
mini-MBA , and 5 workshops on the startup  journey delivered for high school and tertiary 
students . 
2.10 Component III:  SCALE  ‚Äì The objective of this component is to create a model for the 
sustainability and scaling of the IGNITE program . Key activities include:  
‚Ä¢ Development of a f inancial sustainability model : Caribbean Dragons will define and 
adopt a business plan to facilitate ongoing delivery and scale up /evolution of the 
IGNITE program beyond the CARIBEquity  financing . This will include the introduction 
of reve nue generation models that can offset operating costs  such as community  
subscriptions, fees for learning  modules , consultancies  engagement , sponsorships  
and delivery of a for -profit annual conference . 
‚Ä¢ Scaling Up : To scale up the IGNITE program regionally, Caribbean Dragons will seek 
to establish and mentor  Country Champions in at least 2 jurisdictions outside of 
Trinidad and Tobago who  will nurture their local ecosystem and act as a conduit and 
enabler to scale through the Caribbean  via the establishment of Caribbean Drago ns 
Country Chapters.  
9 
 
 2.11 The expected results are to develop a business plan for sustainability a nd to establish 2

students .

sustainability and scaling of the IGNITE program . Key activities include:  
‚Ä¢ Development of a f inancial sustainability model : Caribbean Dragons will define and 
adopt a business plan to facilitate ongoing delivery and scale up /evolution of the 
IGNITE program beyond the CARIBEquity  financing . This will include the introduction 
of reve nue generation models that can offset operating costs  such as community  
subscriptions, fees for learning  modules , consultancies  engagement , sponsorships

Trinidad and Tobago who  will nurture their local ecosystem and act as a conduit and 
enabler to scale through the Caribbean  via the establishment of Caribbean Drago ns 
Country Chapters.

2.2 The targeted beneficiaries of this project will be engaged as follows : 
‚Ä¢ Founders : These founders will commit  to creating meaningful changes  through the 
application of new technologies, driving innovation in their respective industries.  They 
will be  exposed to networking, learning opportunities and have the option to be 
matched  with experienced international founders within their verticals, to access 
specialized knowledge not available within T T. To maximize benefits, these

 innovators should ideally have developed an initial version of a business plan prior to 
engagement. This plan should include the definition of their value proposition, market 
hypothesis, and commercialization strategy.  
‚Ä¢ Ten percent  of founders  engaged and accelerated via  the program will be focused on 
innovation  from key sectors  that serve specific need s of low 
income/vulnerable /marginalized  population . These will be identified following a three -
folded criteria: (1) Self-reported  data provided by the entrepreneur declaring the 
solution is aimed at the poor/vulnerable/low -income ; (2) The proposed solution will 
provide products/services for lower prices whilst maintaining quality standards as of 
what is available in the market ; (3) Eligible segments include but are not limited to 
fintechs (addresses the unbanked, or improves financial literacy/ planning ) and 
healthtechs (supports more active disease prevention and management) . 
‚Ä¢ Female founders and managers will be actively recruited to ensure that they make up 
40% of participants.  These will include women who are currently running or  are 
building businesses . This group will  benefit from  additional gender -focused 
programming including female to female mentorship, confidence and leadership 
building . 50 startups  / founders  are expected to be incubated / accelerated via the 
program . This involves having completed all three main programs offering  mini-MBA 
courses, a startup weekend and one -on-one mentorship.  
‚Ä¢ 200 h igh school  students from  financially marginalized  groups  (lower -tiered schools , 
who are vulnerable to cycles of poverty , will be exposed to financial literacy and 
entrepreneurship programming . In this regard List of schools that are financially and 
socially vulnerable (and from which CD will actively engage student participation ): 
1. Arima Central Secondary School  
2. Bishop Anstey High School East  
3. Five Rivers Secondary School  
4. Trinity College East
