2.3 Two aspects of the Ignite the World project make it an innovative initiativ e. Firstly, the 
program was designed on deep stakeholder engagement through a series of quali tative  
research methods including deep ethnographic interviews, and community co -creation 
sessions. This was done to ensure that proposed activities are re levant and fit -for-
purpose, as compared to adopting North American and Eu ropean Startup Community 
frameworks and imposing it to a Caribbean audience.  
2.4 Additionally, within the region, there are very few non -profit accelerators that focus on 
innovation and technology -driven pre -seed companies in the Caribbean. There is a 
disproportionate emphasis on supporting more established and traditional companies. 
7 
 
 Consequently, this project will prioritize foundational business skills and business model 
development, which are critical for disruptive and highly innovative start -ups. Further , 
startup programs  that exis t in the Caribbean tend to be  limited to their country of origin 
and do not typically collaborate across the wider region.  At the core , Caribbean Dragons 
are ecosystem builders seek ing to connect the region in the hopes of leveraging relational 
capital to bring cross -geography resources for their founding community in T T. 
2.5 The project is structured to include three technical components as follows : 
2.6 Component I:  CONNECT  ‚Äì The objective of this component is to c urate and activate  a 
network of individuals engaged as founders or ecosystem players in  startup development 
and growth.  The project aims to connect 275 founders within 2 years . Early -stage founders 
will benefit from guidance provided by seasoned innovators, as well as peer support and 
access to local talent. By establishing a platform for engagement, Caribbean Dragons will 
facilitate critical connections through:  
‚Ä¢ IGNITE Innovation Summit: This annual event will  convene  the key actors in the 
Regional Innovation Ecosystem and allow stakeholders to overcome geographic and 
social boundaries, integrate and foster conditions for greater innovation output.  
‚Ä¢ Quarterly Community Series: These small pop -up events will facilitate spontaneous 
connection making and reinforce existing relationships among  founders and other 
ecosystem  actors through in -person interactions.  
‚Ä¢ Online Engagement: Caribbean Dragons will create  an online community which 
enables self -directed engagement among members and facilitates data collection 
and sharing.  
‚Ä¢ Monthly Newsletter: Caribbean Dragons will use this mechanism  to share success 
stories of Innovators and Investors which inspire and educate the community.  
‚Ä¢ Mentorship : This element of the program will match 50 founders with mentors for a 
total of 8 hours. To be accepted into the mentorship program, founders must complete 
at least four of the mini-MBA  modules , participate in a startup  weekend (as defined 
in Component 2 Learn) , and participate in a Mentorship Onboarding Workshop. 
Mentees will define and agree priority areas for the interactions and both mentors and 
mentees will operate within guidelines developed by Caribbean Dragons.  Mentors  will 
be sourced from the Caribbean Dragons community and will include  experienced  
founders, funders/investors, entrepreneurial hubs, service providers (e.g., coders, 
marketers, accountants), as well as multilateral agencies a nd organizations.  Matching 
will be done on a skills -needs basis.  
2.7 By the end of the project, the expected results  are: 10 networking events for founders and 
ecosystem actors, 40 founders benefiting  from startup weekends  and 275 active users 
within the online community . 
2.8 Component II:  LEARN - The objective of this component is to deliver  comprehensive  
training and experiential learning tailored to accelerate startups . The key activities are as 
follows ; 
‚Ä¢ Mini-MBA:  Caribbean Dragons will develop a n online  mini-MBA program that will 
offer specialized and target ed micro -learning s that can be applied directly into 
participants‚Äô startups . Initially the mini-MBA  will offer 8 foundational modules  specially 
curated to the needs of Caribbean founders. The proposed modules are universal 
topics which are industry/sector agnostic and are therefore applicable to all Founders. 
8 
 
 These will initially be run as virtually assisted s essions to guide the first groups of 
participants with the intent to adapt and improve. By the end of the project, the 
modules will be digitally delivered. Once the content has been digitized, it will be self-
paced and available to the community through paid membership subscriptions. The 
digital delivery model will help facilitate scaling.  Proposed modules includ e: Beyond 
the Pitch: Non -Traditional Funding Strategies, Problem -Solution Fit: Mastering 
Customer Discovery & Validation, Disruptive Markets: Navigating Emerging Tech & 
Segmentation, Startup Tech Toolkit: No -Code, Low -Code & Essential Dev Skills, 
Growth Ha cking & Traction: Scaling Without Breaking the Bank, Startup Law & 
Compliance: Protecting Your Business & IP, Behavioral Econom ics & Pricing 
Psychology, and Founder Resilience & Mental Toughness . As stated above, the 
program address es the general knowledge needs around: early -stage financing, 
product development, market growth strategies, and management of intellectual 
properly . 
‚Ä¢ Startup weekends:  These smaller events will allow 10 founders  at each event to 
apply the relevant learnings of the mini-MBA  and refine their business plans and value 
propositions , leveraging peer -to-peer and specialist advisory and support drawn from 
the Caribbean Dragons communit y. 
‚Ä¢ Quarterly Webinars:  To develop general business building and investment 
knowledge these webinars offer founders a  ‚Äúdeep dive‚Äù learning sessions delivered 
by expert practitioners.  
‚Ä¢ Monthly Podcast:  These podcasts will explore  innovation and technology  trends that 
can assist founders to develop a regional and global business perspective  
‚Ä¢ Igniting the next generation of startups : Caribbean Dragons will facilitate the 
delivery of seminars and workshops to explore the startup  journey and innovation 
methodologies . The targeted participants will be students from high schools  in more 
vulnerable or marginalized communities as well as tertiary students studying 
entrepreneurship and innovation.  
2.9 By the end of the project, the expected results include  launch ing the mini -MBA program 
with 8  modules tailored to acceleration of startups/founders; 150 founders enrolled in  the 
mini-MBA , and 5 workshops on the startup  journey delivered for high school and tertiary 
students . 
2.10 Component III:  SCALE  ‚Äì The objective of this component is to create a model for the 
sustainability and scaling of the IGNITE program . Key activities include:  
‚Ä¢ Development of a f inancial sustainability model : Caribbean Dragons will define and 
adopt a business plan to facilitate ongoing delivery and scale up /evolution of the 
IGNITE program beyond the CARIBEquity  financing . This will include the introduction 
of reve nue generation models that can offset operating costs  such as community  
subscriptions, fees for learning  modules , consultancies  engagement , sponsorships  
and delivery of a for -profit annual conference . 
‚Ä¢ Scaling Up : To scale up the IGNITE program regionally, Caribbean Dragons will seek 
to establish and mentor  Country Champions in at least 2 jurisdictions outside of 
Trinidad and Tobago who  will nurture their local ecosystem and act as a conduit and 
enabler to scale through the Caribbean  via the establishment of Caribbean Drago ns 
Country Chapters.  
9 
 
 2.11 The expected results are to develop a business plan for sustainability a nd to establish 2  
country chapters at the end of two years.   
B. Project Results , Measurement , Monitoring and Evaluation  
2.12 The Executing Agency (EA)  will be responsible for collecting the data and reporting on 
results and achievements as per the results matrix of the project. The EA will develop a 
monitoring plan at the start of the project  to ensure tracking and measuring of indicators. 
Additionally, the EA will report to the Bank every year through a Project Status Report 
(PSR) and submit a Final PSR  on the project‚Äôs outcomes  after the project is completed . 
2.13 The targeted results  are: 500 unique founders engaged through IGNITE , of which 40% 
are women  working or leading STEM based businesses , and 10% will be founders driving 
business models that have a specific development impact/value proposition for low impact 
communities  with a total of 50 founders / startups accelerated through the IGNITE 
Program . In addition,  200 students from lower tier high schools will benefit from works hops 
in entrepreneurship and innovation.  
2.14 Evaluation:  This project will be evaluated as part of the mid -term and final evaluations to 
be conducted under the overall CARIBEquity Facility. A consulting firm will be hired to 
carry out the evaluation. To facilitate execution of the evaluation, the Executing Agenc y 
will be required to provide project data beyond that which would have been submitted with 
the PSR, within appropriate timelines. Other information collected by the Executing 
Agency, that may be relevant for the purposes of the evaluation, but not part of  the PSR 
reporting, should also be appropriately cataloged and shared during the evaluations ; 
specifically,  data to assess the proposed model‚Äôs success in increasing entrepreneurship 
among the P&V population . 
2.15 Audit:  The CARIBEquity Facility will hire and conduct an independent final audit of this, 
and other projects funded under the CARIBEquity Innovation Ecosystem Challenge Fund. 
The Executing Agency will be required to provide the auditor with access to financial 
reports, f inancial  records and other information as required.    
2.16 Knowledge Exchange & Participation in Events:  The Executing Agency will be required 
to share lessons learned, experiences and participate in events, panels and other 
knowledge exchange activities organized by the CARIBEquity Facility, IDB Lab, the EU 
and/or their partners.  
2.17 EU Funding - Special Requirements: In accordance with the 2020 EU -IDB Financial 
Framework Partnership Agreement (FFPA) which establishes exceptions to Bank‚Äôs 
policies (approved by the Bank under the ‚ÄúProposal for the FFPA between the European 
Commission and the Inter -American Development Ba nk‚Äù [GN -2605 -5, paragraphs 4.14 
and 4.15]) in order to:  
‚Ä¢ allow goods, works or services originating from or rendered by nationals from IDB 
non-member countries be eligible for procurement activities under this operation, 
provided that the country of origin of the goods and the nationality of the suppliers, 
contr actors and service providers is recognized as eligible by the EU under its 
applicable regulations. The EU publishes the list of eligible countries (or any 
10 
 
 updates thereto) as an annex to the ‚ÄúPractical Guide to Contract Procedures for EU 
External Actions‚Äù (PRAG), which is available on its Internet website;  
‚Ä¢ extend the retention period of project documentation required for executing 
agencies and the Bank, from three years to five or more years; and  
‚Ä¢ prevent awarding contracts to entities, individuals or groups of individuals subject 
to EU restrictive measures.  
2.18 EU Funding - Visibility and Communications Requirements: Recipients of EU funding 
have a general obligation to acknowledge the origin and ensure the visibility  of the EU 
funding received. These instructions are defined in the Comm unicating and raising EU 
visibility: Guidance for external actions . It is the responsibility of the Executing Agency to 
review these guidelines and observe all applicable measures required. The EU emblem 
is the single most important visual brand used to acknowledge the origin  and ensure the 
visibility  of EU funding. This project is being implemented the Global Gateway  and 
therefore should also include the Global Gateway logo in addition to the EU emblem. 
Additionally, the project is being implemented in partnership with the Organization of 
African, Caribbean and Pacific S tates (OACPS) . All three logos should be used 
concurrently when promoting activities funded by the EU under this project.  The EU 
emblem and accompanying logos, should be accompanied by a funding statement  
(‚ÄúFunded by the European Union ‚Äù) mentioning the EU‚Äôs support. Both the EU emblem and 
the funding statement are essential to acknowledge EU support. As a rule, they always go 
hand in hand and must not be separated. To assist, IDB Lab will provide guidance to the 
EA including instructions  on the use and positioning of the EU, Global Gateway and 
OACPs logos, and other visibility  and communications requirements.

maintaining adequate accounts of its finances, internal controls and project files 
according to the requirements established above (Article 2.1.4) and in line with the 
financial management policy of IDB Lab.  
‚Ä¢ Procurement: For the procurement of goods and contracting of consulting

‚Ä¢ Annual External Audits ‚Äì the Executing Agency‚Äôs prepare annual financial

section_text:
III. Alignment with IDB Group , Scalability, and Risks  
A. Alignment with IDB Group   
3.1. The project is aligned with the IDB Group‚Äôs new institutional strategy IDBStrategy + and 
specifically under the Productive Development and Innovation through the Private Sector 
operational focus area specifically the objective to deploy interventions leveraging private 
sector capabilities and incentives in partnership with private execut ors such as incubators. 
Additionally, the project will specifically include female founders and startups in its 
programming which supports the Gender Equality and Inclusion of Diverse Population 
Groups operational focus area.  
3.2. The project is aligned to the current IDB Group strategy with Trinidad and Tobago 2021 -
2025 , which focuses on digital transformation and, specifically, digitization to support 
economic transformation. The strategy includes three key development pillars: (i) 
improving the business environment to enable digital transformation; (ii) expanding the 
use of digital to ols to improve educational outcomes and digital capabilities; and (iii) 
improving digital services. This operation directly supports and contributes to the 
implementation of the National Strategy, particularly in areas (i i) and (iii).  
3.3. The project is strategically aligned to the Private Sector Development priority area of the 
ONE Caribbean framework GN -3201 -5. ONE Caribbean is the Bank‚Äôs comprehensive 
strategic framework to promote sustainable development in the Caribbean by targeting 
regional soluti ons to common challenges and scaling ambitious and transformational 
initiatives.  
3.4. The project aligns with the Sector Framework Document on Innovation, Science, and 
Technology, contributing to the action lines of fostering an environment conducive to 
private investment in innovation and connectivity and promoting actions to address marke t 
failures that limit business innovation. The project also aligns with the Sector Framework 
Document on Skills Development, contributing to the challenges of ensuring that all 
students graduate from secondary school with an intermediate level of cognitive , technical, 
and socio -emotional skills that enable them to continue learning throughout their lives, 
access high -quality jobs, and be good citizens, as well as equipping all young adults with 
advanced cognitive, technical, and socio -emotional skills that allow them to continue 
learning throughout their lives and thrive in the labor market.  
3.5. The project will be implemented concurrently with the other nine (9) ecosystem building  
projects selected through the CARIBEquity Facility Innovation Ecosystem Challenge Fund 
Call for Proposals . This project will endeavor  to enhance the Caribbean‚Äôs entrepreneurial 
ecosystem by supporting the development and scaling of startups  in inclusive 
entrepreneurshi p. 
3.6. The project will also build upon the achievements of the IDB/CTI regional project RG -
T3517: Strengthening the Entrepreneurship and Innovation Ecosystems in the OECS 
which closed in 2023.  
3.7. The project aligns with the following Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):  
‚Ä¢ SDG 4: Quality Education, contributing to Target 4.4: "By 2030, substantially 
increase the number of youth and adults who have relevant skills, including 
12 
 
 technical and vocational skills, for employment, decent jobs, and 
entrepreneurship."  
‚Ä¢ SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth, contributing to Target 8.3: "Promote 
development -oriented policies that support productive activities, decent job 
creation, entrepreneurship, creativity, and innovation, and encourage the 
formalization and growth of micro, small, and medium -sized enterprises, including 
through access to financial services."  
‚Ä¢ SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities, contributing to Target 10.2: "By 2030, empower 
and promote the social, economic, and political inclusion of all, irrespective of age, 
sex, disability, race, ethnicity, origin, religion, or economic or other status."  
‚Ä¢ SDG 5: Gender Equality, contributing to Target 5.A: "Undertake reforms to give 
women equal rights to economic resources, as well as access to ownership and 
control over land and other forms of property, financial services, inheritance, and 
natural resource s, in accordance with national laws."  
 
3.8. Connection with RevUp  (JA-1200)  ‚Äì the project is  in active discussions with RevUP , an 
IDB Lab financed initiative, to leverage lessons learned and build synergies from their 
mentorship program.  Relationship s have also been established  with the World Business 
Angels Investment Forum.  
3.9. Connection with Shaping the Future of Innovation TT -T1094 and TT -G1002: Caribbean 
Dragons and CARIRI are expected to collaborate on innovation forums and building out 
the national innovation ecosystem in Trinidad and Tobago.  
 
B. Additionality and Scalability   
3.10.  With the support of IDB Lab and its extensive network, t his project will build on early 
implementation successes, and boost the creation of a hyper -connected ecosystem for 
founders, by seeking to build partnerships with key stakeholders including:  
‚Ä¢ Entrepreneurial Hubs: Collaborating to share data, deal flow, and opportunities, 
across the Caribbean including: Trinidad and Tobago: CARIRI, UWI Ventures, Draper 
Startup House Caricom; Jamaica: Revup Caribbean, Branson Centre of 
Entrepreneurship; Barbados : 10 Habitat; Nassau: Arrowlynk and Guadeloupe: 
Entrepreneurs of Greatness.  
‚Ä¢ Investors: Building trust and credibility within the ecosystem, and including investor 
network partners such as Mscale, First Angels (Jamaica) and other networks and 
family offices.  
‚Ä¢ Educational and Research Partners: Providing academically rigorous instruction and 
analyzing data to support growth, including engagements with Columbia Business 
School and University of Toronto.  
3.11.  These partnerships will collectively strengthen our ecosystem, fostering collaboration and 
innovation among all constituents , and help scale the initiative across the Caribbean 
13 
 
 countries. The goal is to create 8 Caribbean Dragons chapters across the Caribbean 
within the next 5 -10 years, each of which would deliver a similar degree of programming.   
3.12.  Further, the IGNITE Innovation Summit will strategically be moved every 2 -3 years to a 
different Caribbean country to ensure better local engagement and onboarding . 
 
C. Project and Institutional Risks  
3.13.  Several  risks have been identified for this project in terms of achieving results and 
implementation , including:  
3.14.  Execution risks:  The EA has limited experience in running a multi -year project of this 
nature  which can lead to ineffective or sub -standard execution and/or implementation of 
the various program components . This could impact the project with the n on-achievement 
of the program goals and main KPIs . To mitigate this, the project will embed human capital 
and form partnerships that provide access to the necessary skill sets and experience . 
3.15.  Lack of funds to scale and sustain  the program:  If the EA is unable  to attract further 
funding / revenue streams  to continue and expand activities beyond the period of 
CARIBEquity investment, the program will not be sustained. To mitigate  this risk,  the 
founders of Caribbean Dragon will focus on the creation and diversification of sustainable 
revenue streams (e.g. corporate innovation consultancy, deal flow curation for investors 
and business coaching fees)  to finance continuity and expansion of the Ignite program . 
3.16.  Resistance to collaboration from the other ecosystem builders : A lack of willingness 
and/or culture to collaborate  among TT ecosystem builders  might result  in slow progress 
to create a connected ecosystem . This in turn  could  negatively impact achievement of 
project targets.  To mitigate  this risk, the project  team will continuously be engaging  with 
existing ecosystem builders  with a focus in building a stronger value -added offering to 
founders avoid ing duplication and focus ing instead  on collectively enhancing and 
amplifying the current landscape.  
3.17.  Complexity of programming in multiple territories:  The geographic and cultural 
fragmentation of the region  can cause a low pace of program execution and misalign 
localized goals . This will impact the project by l ower ing standard of execution (quality and 
breadth) in countries outside of Trinidad & Tobago . To overcome this, the project will use 
a decentralized  model (Caribbean Chapters and Champions)  in the various islands so that 
each center  has its own customized  work plan and is creating its own deal flow and data 
that will drive decision making.  
3.18.  The DICI Risk Matrix can be found in the project's technical files and the IDB Lab Risk 
Analysis tool has also been applied, which is also included in the technical documents of 
this project .

initiatives.

Technology, contributing to the action lines of fostering an environment conducive to 
private investment in innovation and connectivity and promoting actions to address marke t 
failures that limit business innovation. The project also aligns with the Sector Framework 
Document on Skills Development, contributing to the challenges of ensuring that all 
students graduate from secondary school with an intermediate level of cognitive , technical, 
and socio -emotional skills that enable them to continue learning throughout their lives, 
access high -quality jobs, and be good citizens, as well as equipping all young adults with 
advanced cognitive, technical, and socio -emotional skills that allow them to continue

 technical and vocational skills, for employment, decent jobs, and

creation, entrepreneurship, creativity, and innovation, and encourage the 
formalization and growth of micro, small, and medium -sized enterprises, including 
through access to financial services."  
‚Ä¢ SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities, contributing to Target 10.2: "By 2030, empower

sex, disability, race, ethnicity, origin, religion, or economic or other status."  
‚Ä¢ SDG 5: Gender Equality, contributing to Target 5.A: "Undertake reforms to give

control over land and other forms of property, financial services, inheritance, and 
natural resource s, in accordance with national laws."

the national innovation ecosystem in Trinidad and Tobago.

V. Executing Agency (EA)  and Implementation Structure  
A. Executing Agency(s)  
5.1. Caribbean Dragons  will be the executive  agency of this project and will sign the agreement 
with the Bank. Based in Trinidad & Tobago, Caribbean Dragons seeks to enable 
Caribbean founders accelerate sustainable (economic, ecological, social), global impact 
by building capacity and enabling conne ctions among Caribbean founders, to empower 
the advancement of their innovative ideas.  
5.2. Caribbean Dragons has a program manager  responsible for overseeing  all operations  on 
the ground in T T but all decisions will be made through the ongoing monthly Board of 
Directors ( BOD ) meetings, with consultation from the Advisory Board.  
B. Description  
5.3. Caribbean Dragons officially launched in November 2023 with a strategy based on three 
pillars: (i) Building Connections  (ii) Fostering Knowledge , and (iii) Scaling Impact.  Since 
the official launch , it has already made significant strides in delivering on this strategy 
through:  
5.3.1.  Mentorship and Coaching: providing one -on-one guidance to over twenty 
(20) founders, providing them with valuable advice for both immediate and 
long-term operation.  
5.3.2.  Community Series: In collaboration with the Trinidad and Tobago 
International Financial Centre, Caribbean Dragons has hosted a three -part 
15 
 
 series of networking events. The first was a Startup Pitch Competition and 
Networking event, the second was a Community Co -Build  in defining key 
elements for strengthening the startup  ecosystem , and the third was a 
moderated panel on fundraising. These events  engaged over 150 startup 
founders, investors, multi -lateral agencies and fellow hub . 
5.3.3.  IGNITE Startup Summit: Caribbean Dragons inaugurated the region's  first 
summit focused on startup  acceleration in 2024. This event was focused on 
enabling connections via a three -day summit, convening active and 
aspirational Investors and founders, as well as multilaterals, from across the 
region, Canada, England, and the USA to co -design a collaborative path 
forward.  
5.3.4.  Specialized Workshops: In collaboration with the I DB office in T T, Caribbean 
Dragons hosted a co -creation session with stakeholders in the Creative 
Sector to draft initiatives for strengthening of the island‚Äôs Orange Economy. 
In conjunction with the College of Science, Technology and Applied Arts of 
Trinidad and Tobago (COSTATT), Caribbean Dragons hosted an I nnovation 
workshop with 30 students focused on need identification and idea 
development.  
 
5.4. To date , Caribbean Dragons has been financially sustainable  with low operational 
overheads which are covered by the advisory services provide d, corporate funding 
support (e.g. PWC Trinidad and Tobago) and other donors who underwrite its activities. 
The funding provided through this mechanism enables the incremental activities as 
outlined in the memo . 
5.5. Integrity Review.   The project team, with the support of OII, conducted the integrity due 
diligence (IDD) on the Project in accordance with the Integrity Due Diligence Guidelines 
(OP-474-1) and found no indicators of integrity or related reputational risks for IDB Lab 
that m erit disclosure . 
C. Implementation Structure and  Mechanism  
5.6. Caribbean Dragons  will establish an execution unit and the necessary structure to execute 
project activities and manage project resources effectively and efficiently  including the 
contracting of a dedicated project coordinator  who will report directly to the organization‚Äôs 
directors . Caribbean Dragons  will also be responsible for submitting progress reports on 
project implementation.  
5.7. The intent is to create a hyper -connected ecosystem for all of its constituents, creating 
long-term and successful partnerships. Caribbean Dragons will put in place an advisory 
committee including key actors to provide support for implementation , academically 
rigorous instruction and collect/analyze data to support forward growth .

II. COMPONENTS
2.1Component 1. Governance of the National Statistical System (NSS) 
(US$30,000). The objective of the component is to strengthen governance and 
coordination within the NSS by supporting the establishment and 
operationalization of the National Statistics Committee (NSC) and updating and 
aligning the National Strategy for the Development of Statistics (NSDS) with the 
National Development Plan.
2.1.1 The main activities include organizing and facilitating two workshops, 
structuring and operationalizing the NSC, and providing technical 
assistance for the update, validation, and approval of the NSDS. These 
actions will be implemented by the IDB, as executing agency, in 
coordination with the Bahamas National Statistical Institute (BNSI) and the 
Ministry of Finance.
2.1.2 Procurement will include the hiring of one individual consultant to organize 
and facilitate the workshops and one individual to update and align the 
NSDS, consistent with the Procurement Plan.
2.1.3 The expected outputs of the component are: (i) two workshops organized 
to strengthen the NSC‚Äôs coordination capacity; and (ii) one updated and 
approved NSDS aligned with the National Development Plan, as reflected 
- 6 -in the Results Matrix. The organization of workshops will be subject to prior 
non-objection from the KPR Fund Coordinator.
2.2Component 2. Capacity Development (US$40,000). The objective of the 
component is to strengthen the institutional and human-resource capacities of the 
BNSI through the design and delivery of a structured training program for senior 
management and technical staff, focusing on leadership, change management, 
communication, advocacy, and statistical-quality standards.
2.2.1 The main activity involves designing and implementing two training 
sessions, both to be delivered during 2027 by specialized trainers in 
coordination with the BNSI and the Ministry of Finance. Implementation will 
take place over approximately eight months, as reflected in the 
Procurement Plan.
2.2.2 Procurement will include contracting an individual training provider to 
design and deliver the sessions, in accordance with the Procurement Plan.
2.2.3 The expected output of the component is two training sessions delivered to 
enhance BNSI‚Äôs managerial and technical competencies, consistent with 
the Results Matrix. The organization of training activities will be subject to 
prior non-objection from the KPR Fund Coordinator.
2.3Component 3. Data integration and monitoring and evaluation (US$80,000). 
The objective of the component is to enhance data integration, coordination, and 
modernization of IT systems across the NSS.
2.3.1 The main activities comprise preparing a diagnostic report on current IT and 
datamanagement systems within the NSS, conducting two technical 
workshops with data-producing agencies to validate findings and 
strengthen coordination, and developing a proposal for an integrated IT 
system to improve interoperability and data exchange among institutions. 
The IDB, as the executing agency, will coordinate these actions in 
collaboration with the BNSI.
2.3.2 Procurement will include an individual consultant for the diagnostic report, 
an individual consultant to facilitate the workshops, and an individual 
consultant to design the integrated IT system proposal, consistent with the 
Procurement Plan.
2.3.3 The expected outputs are: (i) one diagnostic report produced; (ii) two 
workshops organized; and (iii) one IT system proposal designed, aligned 
with the Results Matrix. The organization of workshops will be subject to 
prior non-objection from the KPR Fund Coordinator.
2.4Expected Results. This TC will strengthen the capacity of the Bahamas National 
Statistics Institute (BNSI) to design and implement the National Strategy for the 
Development of Statistics (NSDS), providing a coordinating mechanism for the 
National Statistical System (NSS) that ensures the production and dissemination 
of quality and timely official statistics. It is expected that the National Statistics 
Committee will be established, the NSDS will be updated and approved in 
- 7 -alignment with the National Development Plan, the BNSI‚Äôs institutional capacity 
will be reinforced through training and academic partnerships, and a proposal for 
an integrated IT system will be developed to improve coordination and data 
integration. As a result, the Government of The Bahamas will have access to better 
data to design and monitor programs, and the IDB will be able to measure the 
impact of its operations in the country. In addition, the TC is expected to strengthen 
BNSI‚Äôs institutional leadership within the NSS, enhance stakeholder confidence in 
the quality and reliability of official data, and increase coordination among 
government entities producing and using statistics, thereby improving the 
Government‚Äôs capacity to design, monitor, and evaluate public policies and 
development programs based on evidence.
2.5Beneficiaries. The direct beneficiaries of this TC are the Government of The 
Bahamas through the Bahamas National Statistics Institute (BNSI), which will be 
strengthened in its institutional capacity and technical resources, and the National 
Statistics Committee (NSC), including the public entities represented in it such as 
the Ministry of Finance, the Central Bank, the Ministry of Education, and the 
Ministry of Health.  The final beneficiaries are government agencies, the private 
sector, academia, civil society, and the citizens of The Bahamas, who will benefit 
from more timely, accessible, and high-quality official statistics to support 
evidence-based policymaking and improved public policies.

V. POTENTIAL RISKS
5.1 The main potential risks that could affect the successful implementation of this 
Technical Cooperation are related to institutional capacity, governance, and 
inter-agency coordination within the National Statistical System (NSS). A key risk 
is the limited human and institutional capacity of the Bahamas National Statistics 
Institute (BNSI), which could delay the implementation of activities and the timely 
- 9 -delivery of outputs. This risk stems from the still-recent establishment of the BNSI 
as an autonomous entity under the Statistics Act of 2021, and from the ongoing 
process of staff renewal and capacity strengthening. To mitigate this, the project 
will be executed directly by the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), as 
requested by the Government of The Bahamas, and will include targeted training 
and technical assistance activities to strengthen BNSI‚Äôs capacity.
5.2 Another potential risk concerns coordination challenges among data-producing 
agencies, given that the National Statistics Committee (NSC) is not yet fully 
operational. Weak coordination could affect the approval and implementation of 
the National Strategy for the Development of Statistics (NSDS) and limit data 
sharing and integration. This risk will be mitigated through stakeholder 
engagement and workshops designed to strengthen governance and promote the 
NSC‚Äôs effective functioning.
5.3 Finally, delays in the approval of the NSDS or in the validation of the IT system 
proposal could affect project timing. To mitigate this, the TC will maintain close 
coordination with the Ministry of Finance and other key institutions and ensure 
early involvement of relevant stakeholders in validation processes.

under this Technical Cooperation. All reports, databases, software, and materials 
produced under the project will be considered public goods and will be owned by 
the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), in accordance with the Bank‚Äôs 
intellectual property policies and procedures. Integrity clauses will be applied as 
per standard Bank agreements.

section_title: Objectives and Justification of the TC
section_text:
II. Objectives and Justification of the TC 
2.1 The objective of this TC is to contribute to improve agricultural productivity and climate 
resilience of small and medium landholder farmers by promoting climate-smart 
agricultural practices through digital technologies related to weather and soil 
management. The activities proposed will be implemented in Bolivia, Peru and 
Colombia, with a focus on gender and diversity with the goal of identifying the best 
approaches to scaling up access to these digital services. 
2.2 Latin America's diverse topography, ranging from mountains to coastlines, introduces 
complexities in predicting local weather patterns (WMO, 2022). Seasonal rainfall 
patterns are variable and further complicated by phenomena such as El Ni√±o and La 
Ni√±a (Parente de Souza et al, 2021). Climate change will exacerbate this uncertainty, 
with variation in daily precipitation increasing by 4-5% and temperature variability 
increasing by 10-15 percent per degree Celsius of warming (Pendergrass et al., 2017; 
Bathiany et al., 2018), increasing farmers‚Äô production risks and affecting agricultural 
productivity (WMO, 2022). In the context of increased weather variability, better 
forecasts can benefit farmers through reduced losses, increasing yields and farmer 
income, particularly if these forecasts are carefully crafted to be relevant to farmers, 
including women and ethnic groups.
2.3 There is evidence that farmers adapt farming practices and investment decisions in 
response to weather information. Randomized control trials in Benin and Colombia 
estimate annual benefits of $103-$356 per farmer ( Yegbemey et al., 2023; Camacho 
and Conover, 2019). In Ghana, India, and Pakistan, farmers in communities that 
received forecasts altered their planting and investment behavior.
2.4 New technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), allow for more accurate and 
location specific weather forecasts to be generated and provided to farmers to help 
them optimize their agricultural decisions. But the benefits of the AI revolution in 
weather forecasting are yet to be experienced in LAC. Much of the focus of the AI 
developments in forecasting has been on commercial applications in wealthy countries 
or technological demonstrations by major technology corporations. Forecasts 
produced in many LAC countries, typically by national meteorological services are 
often at an unsuitable time scale or cover too broad of a geographic region to inform 
farmers‚Äô management decisions. AI-based weather forecasting models can generate 
accurate short- and medium-term forecasts at fine spatial and temporal scales and 
can be optimized to provide the information that is most important for farmer decision-
making. These forecasts can be produced more quickly and cheaply than traditional 
forecasts since they require less computational power.
2.5 Farmers need access to soil health and land management information to counter the 
growing effects of soil erosion, degradation, and salinity. Latin America faces 
multifaceted challenges related to soil health. First, soil erosion, driven by 
deforestation, improper land management, and intense rainfall events leads to the 
depletion of crucial topsoil, diminishing fertility and affecting yields (WMO, 2022). 
Second, the excessive use of fertilizers contributes to soil degradation (FAO, 2019). 
Third, soil salinity is a significant challenge in arid and semi-arid regions, where high 
salt concentrations can impede plant growth and limit agricultural productivity (FAO, 
2021). Poor water management practices, such as inefficient irrigation systems and 
inadequate drainage, exacerbate issues related to soil health and compromise overall 
- 4 -
soil health negatively affecting yields (FAO, 2021). Effective soil health management 
can contribute to climate change mitigation efforts and help farmers overcome climate 
challenges thereby enhancing resilience, yields and income, and minimize 
environmental and climate consequences of current agricultural practices (FAO 2015, 
Qiao et al 2022).
2.6 Digitally delivered services, including weather forecasts and soil health data, could 
have significant benefits for farmers in the context of climate change. These services

II. Objectives and Justification of the TC 
2.1 The objective of this TC is to contribute to improve agricultural productivity and climate 
resilience of small and medium landholder farmers by promoting climate-smart 
agricultural practices through digital technologies related to weather and soil 
management. The activities proposed will be implemented in Bolivia, Peru and 
Colombia, with a focus on gender and diversity with the goal of identifying the best 
approaches to scaling up access to these digital services. 
2.2 Latin America's diverse topography, ranging from mountains to coastlines, introduces 
complexities in predicting local weather patterns (WMO, 2022). Seasonal rainfall 
patterns are variable and further complicated by phenomena such as El Ni√±o and La 
Ni√±a (Parente de Souza et al, 2021). Climate change will exacerbate this uncertainty, 
with variation in daily precipitation increasing by 4-5% and temperature variability 
increasing by 10-15 percent per degree Celsius of warming (Pendergrass et al., 2017; 
Bathiany et al., 2018), increasing farmers‚Äô production risks and affecting agricultural 
productivity (WMO, 2022). In the context of increased weather variability, better 
forecasts can benefit farmers through reduced losses, increasing yields and farmer 
income, particularly if these forecasts are carefully crafted to be relevant to farmers, 
including women and ethnic groups.
2.3 There is evidence that farmers adapt farming practices and investment decisions in 
response to weather information. Randomized control trials in Benin and Colombia 
estimate annual benefits of $103-$356 per farmer ( Yegbemey et al., 2023; Camacho 
and Conover, 2019). In Ghana, India, and Pakistan, farmers in communities that 
received forecasts altered their planting and investment behavior.
2.4 New technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), allow for more accurate and 
location specific weather forecasts to be generated and provided to farmers to help 
them optimize their agricultural decisions. But the benefits of the AI revolution in 
weather forecasting are yet to be experienced in LAC. Much of the focus of the AI 
developments in forecasting has been on commercial applications in wealthy countries 
or technological demonstrations by major technology corporations. Forecasts 
produced in many LAC countries, typically by national meteorological services are 
often at an unsuitable time scale or cover too broad of a geographic region to inform 
farmers‚Äô management decisions. AI-based weather forecasting models can generate 
accurate short- and medium-term forecasts at fine spatial and temporal scales and 
can be optimized to provide the information that is most important for farmer decision-
making. These forecasts can be produced more quickly and cheaply than traditional 
forecasts since they require less computational power.
2.5 Farmers need access to soil health and land management information to counter the 
growing effects of soil erosion, degradation, and salinity. Latin America faces 
multifaceted challenges related to soil health. First, soil erosion, driven by 
deforestation, improper land management, and intense rainfall events leads to the 
depletion of crucial topsoil, diminishing fertility and affecting yields (WMO, 2022). 
Second, the excessive use of fertilizers contributes to soil degradation (FAO, 2019). 
Third, soil salinity is a significant challenge in arid and semi-arid regions, where high 
salt concentrations can impede plant growth and limit agricultural productivity (FAO, 
2021). Poor water management practices, such as inefficient irrigation systems and 
inadequate drainage, exacerbate issues related to soil health and compromise overall

soil health negatively affecting yields (FAO, 2021). Effective soil health management 
can contribute to climate change mitigation efforts and help farmers overcome climate 
challenges thereby enhancing resilience, yields and income, and minimize 
environmental and climate consequences of current agricultural practices (FAO 2015, 
Qiao et al 2022).
2.6 Digitally delivered services, including weather forecasts and soil health data, could 
have significant benefits for farmers in the context of climate change. These services 
have very low marginal costs when operated at scale since once a digital services 
system is set up the cost of an additional user is minimal.  This makes digital services 
highly cost-effective (Fabregas et al. 2019; Cole and Fernando 2020). Many 
governments are already providing digital services to farmers, as are the private sector 
and non-governmental organizations. However, current efforts are highly fragmented 
within and across countries and there is significant scope to improve and expand 
digital services for agriculture. Since weather and soil health information are very 
relevant for farmers, these are good starting points to build and evaluate digital 
platforms. Once the basic elements of these platforms are built, there is the potential 
to dynamically expand them in terms of thematic coverage, types of users, and number 
and types of service providers.

III. Description of activities/components and budget 
3.1Component I: Country assessment of technical assistance needs and digital 
readiness with a gender and diversity approach (US$130,000). This component 
aims to analyze small and medium landholder farmers‚Äô main needs in terms of weather 
and soil health information and asses the current capacity and needs of agricultural 
extension services to support farmers on these topics, with a focus on women and 
ethnic communities.  For this, the component will finance background research, focus 
groups and expert interviews in each country to elaborate: (i) an assessment of farmer 
priorities, including main crops and animals raised, input use, irrigation systems, etc., 
to identify the most valuable weather and soil information; (ii) an appraisal of 
agricultural extension services from the public and private sector to determine the 
reach and effectiveness of such systems in each country, including an assessment of 
governments‚Äô digital agriculture priorities to determine if/where digital agricultural tools 
and systems fit; (iii) a mapping of ongoing programs and projects (including IDB's) that 
aim to modernize agricultural extension through the use of digital tools, with a focus 
on the provision of weather and soil-related recommendations for farmers, iii) an 
assessment of farmers‚Äô and extensionists‚Äô access to mobile technologies and 
connectivity, considering farmers typology by land size and age, indigenous 
populations, afro-descendants and gender, (iv) a mapping of available databases with 
farmer contacts, georeferenced location, and other relevant characteristics, and (v) a 
proposal of local value chains to prioritize as part of the pilots to be implemented, with 
a solid justification. 
3.2Component II: Country assessment of weather forecasting and soil data 
management capacities with a gender and diversity approach (US$90,000). This 
component aims to assess local government capacity for generating accurate and 
timely weather forecasts and soil health management recommendations, as well as 
the degree of digital readiness available to digitally provide weather and soil 
management information to small and medium landholder farmers at the country level. 
For this, the component will finance background research, focus groups, expert 
interviews and the application of relevant assessment tools (e.g. from the World 
Meteorological Organization, WMO) in each country to: (i) assess weather forecasting 
capacities (including the use of AI), potential gaps in existing forecasting systems, in 
particular for weather risks that are relevant for the agriculture sector in the country; 
(ii) assess the existing data on soil quality and land degradation, as well as the 
generation and use of soil data as part of extension services; and (iii) map existing 
digital agriculture platforms and digital solutions in the areas of weather and soil that 
focus on local farmers‚Äô main information needs, and their penetration level.
3.3Component III. Strengthen local capacities to produce and disseminate 
improved weather and soil-related recommendations (US$60,000). This 
component aims to train relevant government technical staff in the production and 
dissemination of improved farmer-centered weather forecasts (e.g. through the use of 
- 7 -
AI) and soil health management recommendations, as well as to recommend policy 
innovations in this field. The component will finance: (i) virtual and in-person training 
activities that can target professionals from agrometeorology agencies, agricultural 
research agencies, extension agencies and other relevant institutions; and (ii) the 
production of relevant policy papers. 
3.4Component IV. Pilots design with a gender and diversity approach (US$210,000). 
This component aims to design the pilot research projects to be implemented in 
prioritized value chains in each country, using as inputs the assessments conducted 
as part of components 1 and 2. Pilot value chains will be selected in consultation with 
local stakeholders. Criteria such as market orientation, size, farmer gender and 
belonging to indigenous communities will be considered. The design of the pilots will 
consider current IDB operations and dialogue in the respective countries, as well as 
national rural development strategies. These pilots could be designed as part of hybrid 
(in person plus digital) extension initiatives or systems. It will finance in each country: 
(i) the design of the pilots, including targeted value chains, objectives and timeline; (ii) 
the design and development of a digital solution for dissemination (or the use of an 
existing solution) in line with the delivery channels ‚ÄìSMS, Whatsapp, etc.- that are 
considered the most adequate for each setting, and (iii) the production of  farmer-
centered information products (recommendations, alerts, forecasts) related to 
agrometeorological conditions and soil health management (including content, format, 
target farmers and triggers), which will require detailed agronomic research, focus 
groups and key informant interviews. Differentiated needs and barriers faced by 
women and minority groups will inform the content, delivery channels, and user 
engagement strategies of the digital information products. Also, according to OP-619-
4, an ITE specialist is part of the project team and will be consulted related to the 
procurement of digital solutions. 
3.5Component V: Pilots implementation, evaluation and dissemination 
(US$210,000). This component will focus on the implementation and evaluation of the 
three pilot projects in Colombia, Peru and Bolivia, as well as the dissemination of main 
findings.  This component will finance: (i) the implementation of the pilots, which will 
include feedback loops where farmers can provide input on the usefulness and 
accuracy of the weather forecasts in real time to improve the system‚Äôs adaptability and 
precision; (ii) the design of the pilots‚Äô evaluation schemes (A/B testing, impact 
evaluations) in order to learn the most effective ways to improve the adoption of 
recommended practices and increase farmers‚Äô resilience and income; (iii) the 
implementation of the evaluations, which includes data collection, data  analysis, 
development of data privacy guidelines, and the production of policy papers or 
research articles; (iv) the production of guidelines to design, implement and evaluate 
digital agriculture extension platforms that allow the dissemination of relevant weather 
and soil-related information products to smallholder farmers  at scale in the three 
countries ; and (v) dissemination activities.
3.6 The total proposed budget for this TC is US$700,000 financed by the Multidonor Fund 
AgroLAC 2025 (MAG). There will not be counterpart funding. The disbursement period 
will be 36 months.

3.7Expected results. The expected impact is inducing behavior change that has a 
positive impact on farmers' agricultural productivity and climate resilience, which will 
be tested through the evaluations of the pilots, included in component V. The use of 
digital tools makes evaluations easier and cheaper to implement since digital delivery 
and interaction facilitate data collection.
3.8 The expected outcomes are: (i) three country proposals with gender and diversity 
approach completed (based on country assessments covering farmers' needs, 
weather forecasting, soil data use and ag extension capacities); (ii) at least 10,000 
farmers beneficiaries of pilots of digital agricultural services provision implemented; 
(iii) at least 30 local technicians trained on weather forecasting, soil health data use 
and digital dissemination; (iv) three pilots implemented with evaluations completed; (v) 
three country policy guidelines to design, implement and evaluate digital extension 
platforms focused on weather and soil information that will serve to guide future 
policies and projects on digital agricultural extension.

services required for the execution of the operation. The beneficiary institutions of the 
TC will provide technical input in line with their priorities and strategic approaches to 
the design of the terms of reference that will be produced and will participate in the 
review of the products obtained, the approval of which is the responsibility of the Bank. 
This will promote continuous coordination with the beneficiaries involved, which will 
facilitate monitoring of the expected achievements of the TC. The Bank‚Äôs Technical 
Cooperation Monitoring and Reporting System (OP-1385-4) will also be used to 
properly monitor the operation.

ethnic communities.  For this, the component will finance background research, focus 
groups and expert interviews in each country to elaborate: (i) an assessment of farmer

agricultural extension services from the public and private sector to determine the 
reach and effectiveness of such systems in each country, including an assessment of 
governments‚Äô digital agriculture priorities to determine if/where digital agricultural tools 
and systems fit; (iii) a mapping of ongoing programs and projects (including IDB's) that 
aim to modernize agricultural extension through the use of digital tools, with a focus 
on the provision of weather and soil-related recommendations for farmers, iii) an 
assessment of farmers‚Äô and extensionists‚Äô access to mobile technologies and 
connectivity, considering farmers typology by land size and age, indigenous 
populations, afro-descendants and gender, (iv) a mapping of available databases with 
farmer contacts, georeferenced location, and other relevant characteristics, and (v) a 
proposal of local value chains to prioritize as part of the pilots to be implemented, with 
a solid justification. 
3.2Component II: Country assessment of weather forecasting and soil data 
management capacities with a gender and diversity approach (US$90,000). This 
component aims to assess local government capacity for generating accurate and 
timely weather forecasts and soil health management recommendations, as well as 
the degree of digital readiness available to digitally provide weather and soil 
management information to small and medium landholder farmers at the country level. 
For this, the component will finance background research, focus groups, expert 
interviews and the application of relevant assessment tools (e.g. from the World 
Meteorological Organization, WMO) in each country to: (i) assess weather forecasting 
capacities (including the use of AI), potential gaps in existing forecasting systems, in 
particular for weather risks that are relevant for the agriculture sector in the country; 
(ii) assess the existing data on soil quality and land degradation, as well as the 
generation and use of soil data as part of extension services; and (iii) map existing 
digital agriculture platforms and digital solutions in the areas of weather and soil that 
focus on local farmers‚Äô main information needs, and their penetration level.
3.3Component III. Strengthen local capacities to produce and disseminate 
improved weather and soil-related recommendations (US$60,000). This 
component aims to train relevant government technical staff in the production and 
dissemination of improved farmer-centered weather forecasts (e.g. through the use of 
- 7 -
AI) and soil health management recommendations, as well as to recommend policy 
innovations in this field. The component will finance: (i) virtual and in-person training 
activities that can target professionals from agrometeorology agencies, agricultural 
research agencies, extension agencies and other relevant institutions; and (ii) the 
production of relevant policy papers. 
3.4Component IV. Pilots design with a gender and diversity approach (US$210,000). 
This component aims to design the pilot research projects to be implemented in 
prioritized value chains in each country, using as inputs the assessments conducted 
as part of components 1 and 2. Pilot value chains will be selected in consultation with 
local stakeholders. Criteria such as market orientation, size, farmer gender and 
belonging to indigenous communities will be considered. The design of the pilots will 
consider current IDB operations and dialogue in the respective countries, as well as 
national rural development strategies. These pilots could be designed as part of hybrid 
(in person plus digital) extension initiatives or systems. It will finance in each country: 
(i) the design of the pilots, including targeted value chains, objectives and timeline; (ii) 
the design and development of a digital solution for dissemination (or the use of an 
existing solution) in line with the delivery channels ‚ÄìSMS, Whatsapp, etc.- that are 
considered the most adequate for each setting, and (iii) the production of  farmer-
centered information products (recommendations, alerts, forecasts) related to 
agrometeorological conditions and soil health management (including content, format, 
target farmers and triggers), which will require detailed agronomic research, focus 
groups and key informant interviews. Differentiated needs and barriers faced by 
women and minority groups will inform the content, delivery channels, and user 
engagement strategies of the digital information products. Also, according to OP-619-
4, an ITE specialist is part of the project team and will be consulted related to the 
procurement of digital solutions. 
3.5Component V: Pilots implementation, evaluation and dissemination 
(US$210,000). This component will focus on the implementation and evaluation of the 
three pilot projects in Colombia, Peru and Bolivia, as well as the dissemination of main 
findings.  This component will finance: (i) the implementation of the pilots, which will 
include feedback loops where farmers can provide input on the usefulness and 
accuracy of the weather forecasts in real time to improve the system‚Äôs adaptability and 
precision; (ii) the design of the pilots‚Äô evaluation schemes (A/B testing, impact 
evaluations) in order to learn the most effective ways to improve the adoption of 
recommended practices and increase farmers‚Äô resilience and income; (iii) the 
implementation of the evaluations, which includes data collection, data  analysis, 
development of data privacy guidelines, and the production of policy papers or 
research articles; (iv) the production of guidelines to design, implement and evaluate 
digital agriculture extension platforms that allow the dissemination of relevant weather 
and soil-related information products to smallholder farmers  at scale in the three 
countries ; and (v) dissemination activities.
3.6 The total proposed budget for this TC is US$700,000 financed by the Multidonor Fund 
AgroLAC 2025 (MAG). There will not be counterpart funding. The disbursement period 
will be 36 months.

IV. Executing agency and execution structure 
4.1Executing Agency. The Bank will be the Executing Agency (EA). IDB activities will 
be carried out by the Agriculture and Rural Development Division (PTI/ARD), in close 
coordination with the ARD and CSD/DRM specialists in Bolivia, Peru and Colombia. 
- 9 -
The main responsibilities of the IDB will be to: (i) develop the work plan and monitor 
the schedule of activities; (ii) perform the financial administration of the project; (iii) 
coordinate the preparation of the Terms of Reference for procurement of goods and 
the selection and contracting of consulting services following IDB regulations, policies 
and procedures; (iv) prepare/review progress reports; (v) prepare and update the 
Procurement Plan; and (vi) coordinate the contracting of independent external 
consultants.
4.2 The execution structure is justified by the Bank's experience in the preparation and 
development of regional activities that require a high degree of coordination among 
countries and are highly technical, such as those proposed in this operation. Regional 
coordination is needed to ensure consistency in the analysis and product quality that 
will result from the implementation of the TC. Also, a regional perspective will be 
important to evaluate the potential to share digital solutions across TC countries 
(adjusted to local contexts as needed) and to propose solutions beyond pilots. This 
regional coordination will be achieved through: i) a team leader and co-team leader 
that will lead all TC's activities in the three countries; ii) the continuous involvement of 
ARD and CSD/DRM specialists in the three countries; and iii) keeping CAN's regional 
coordinator informed and involved as appropriate. 
4.3Procurement. The activities planned within the framework of this TC have been 
included in the Procurement Plan (Annex IV) and will be contracted in accordance with 
the applicable Bank policies and regulations as follows: (i) Hiring of individual 
consultants, as established in the Complementary Workforce Standard (AM-650) and 
(ii) Hiring of services provided by consulting firms in accordance with the Institutional 
Procurement Policy (GN-2303-33) and its Guidelines. The consultants and consulting 
firms hired will be from member countries of the Bank. The execution and technical 
supervision of the TC products will be carried out by PTI/ARD. 
4.4 The monitoring of the TC will be carried out by the Bank and will be based on the 
comparison between the planned and actual procurements and the products planned 
in each consultant's work plan and the products delivered.
4.5 The execution costs of the TC will be covered by the administrative budget of the Bank 
staff who are part of the project team.

5.1 The work involving several countries requires close coordination between consultants, 
and/or, firms, as well as the IDB team in different Country offices, and the respective 
country entities involved.1 In this context, difficulties in coordination might arise. To 
mitigate this risk, a core team of specialists from PTI/ARD has been assembled to lead 
and supervise the implementation of this TC and this team will maintain close coordination 
with the Country Offices throughout the execution of the TC to ensure alignment with national 
priorities and ongoing Bank operations.

each country before field research activities are conducted.

remains disruptive to traditional operating practices, some institutions may encounter 
resistance to the adoption of digital tools or a lack of willingness to scale the results.

relevant agencies of the Ministries of Agriculture (extension, agricultural research,

knowledge and digital assets generated will align with regulations AM-331 and AM-325.

II. GENERAL JUSTIFICATION AND OBJECTIVES  
2.1 Background and justification.  Jamaica has effectively managed the economic 
challenges posed by the COVID -19 pandemic, demonstrating prudent 
macroeconomic strategies. Notable achievements include reductions in public 
debt, inflation, and external deficits, as well as the implementation of a Fiscal 
Responsibility Law and the adoption of inflation targeting.1 However, fiscal space 
remains limited  to absorb future shocks or increase expenditure in priority areas  
such as infrastructure, education,  or health. D ebt service represen ts 48% of the 
2024 public expenditure .2 The second highest expenditure is t he wage bil l, which  
in 2024  represented 43% of public expenditure ,3 higher than  the regional average 
of 28%.4 Given such limited fiscal space , achieving spending efficiency  is 
paramount .  
2.2 The Government of Jamaica has room  to improve policy implementation.5 Even in 
its best perform ing sectors, like  education -PISA scores close to the regional

average (377 vs. 374) -, there are  opportunities for efficiency gains. Jamaica's 
learning- adjusted years of schooling are 10 % lower than expected  for its level of 
development, expenditure in education and population size.6 Improved strategic 
human resource management could suggest, for example, m echanisms to tie 
salary increases to performance or the implementation of workforce planning that 
could allow  for the reallocation of teachers  within  education levels without 
increasing costs .7  
2.3 The Government of Jamaica has demonstrated a commitment to increasing the 
efficiency and effectiveness of the public sector. The policy authority  for these 
efforts  is the Public Sector Master Rationalisation Plan, which was tabled in 
Parliament in 2010 , which remains in effect . Recently, with IDB support, it 
completed the execution of the Public Sector Transformation Programme (PSTP) ,8 
with achievements including: (i) the implementation of a cross -government online 
transactional human resources management tool (MyHR+) in 55 Ministries, 
Departments, and Agencies (MDAs), encompassing over 50% of public officers; 
(ii) supporting the restruc turing of the Government of Jamaica compensation 
scheme, including a reduction from 325 different salary scales to 16; and (iii) the 
implementation of four digital services .9 This work was spearheaded by the 
Transformation Implementation Unit (TIU) of the Ministry of Finance and the Public 
Service (MoFPS). During the same period, the TIU also began work towards the 
rationalization of public bodies - comprising companies, agenc ies, and statutory 
bodies ‚Äì to eliminate duplicated functions and close entities that had achieved their 
mandates.  The TIU facilitated the reduction of the number of public bodies from 
190 in 2017 to 152 in 2023. In parallel to PSTP, the government , with IDB support,  
undertook the creation of a national  identification system , which will allow for 
simpler citizen interactions with public institutions, among other benefits.  A 
precursor to PSTP  was the Public Sector Efficiency Programme (PSEP) , which 
supported improvements in public sector human resource management , use of 
information and communications technologies in government, procurement 
processes , and budget oversight.  The current project aims to build on the 
successes of PSTP  and PSEP to address remaining challenges in the efficiency 
of public sector operations.  For example, the shared services activities described 
under Component 1 are direct continuations of activities begun under PSTP.  
2.4 Main problem.  The main problem this project will address is the inefficient 
management of public sector human, financial, and organizational resources .10 
The specific problems related to the general problem are:  
2.5 Specific problem 1. Duplication and inefficiency in government support 
functions.  The main support functions, including payroll, finance and accounts,

management operate in a manual, decentralized way, without strategic direction, 
across most of the 190 Government of Jamaica Ministries, Departments and 
Agencies  (MDAs) , impeding the effective implementation of government 
priorities .11 This fragmentation leads to heterogeneous execution due to the lack 
of cohesive and standardized policies, guidelines, and procedures. For example, 
payroll processes are executed at each MDA, some of which have paper -based 
processes, leading to irregular payment schedules , payroll errors,  and a general 
inability to assess the efficiency of payroll execution. In the case of finance and

2.6 Specific problem 2. The multiplicity of  public bodies13 weakens oversight  
and efficiency.  The IMF has repeatedly cited the fact that the finances  for the 
public bodies are managed off budget  and the resulting difficulty in exercising 
prudent fiscal management as a risk to the government‚Äôs overall fiscal position.14 
The latest incorporation of public bodies into reporting systems is an improvement that needs consolidation.
15 This difficulty is compounded by a lack of oversight: 
under 60% of public bodies regularly submit their annual reports to Parliament as 
required under law. Lastly, out of a total of 152 public bodies, 50 are dormant , 
meaning that they exist legally and are subject to corporate governance 
requirements  but do not have active personnel or produce any output. However, 
they persist in consuming budgetary resources, totaling around US$211,000 per 
year. These funds  cover  expenses such as  board of directors ‚Äô fees , auditing, and 
corporate secretarial services when required, among others.

management in Jamaica is characterized by inefficient, primarily transactional 
functions, and heterogeneous implementation across MDAs. This is evidenced in

implemented in 2022- 2024; (iii)  scattered sources of information on job openings 
in the Government of Jamaica ; (iv) limited information and tools to facilitate internal 
mobility within the public sector; and (v) the employee perfor mance management 
framework is inconsistent with the compensation restructuring implemented in

2.8 Gender and diversity considerations. In 2022, women represented 62% of the 
public sector workforce and held 62,1% of managerial positions in Jamaica.17

operation is included in the Operational Program Report 2024 (GN -3207) . Lastly,

resources. This overall  objective will be accomplished through the following 
specific development objectives: (i) enhancing the management of core 
government support functions ; (ii) optimizing the structure of the s tate; and 
(iii) strengthening the public sector‚Äôs human  capital .

its best perform ing sectors, like  education -PISA scores close to the regional

information and communications technologies in government, procurement

successes of PSTP  and PSEP to address remaining challenges in the efficiency

2.1 Background and justification.  Jamaica has effectively managed the economic 
challenges posed by the COVID -19 pandemic, demonstrating prudent 
macroeconomic strategies. Notable achievements include reductions in public 
debt, inflation, and external deficits, as well as the implementation of a Fiscal 
Responsibility Law and the adoption of inflation targeting.1 However, fiscal space 
remains limited  to absorb future shocks or increase expenditure in priority areas  
such as infrastructure, education,  or health. D ebt service represen ts 48% of the 
2024 public expenditure .2 The second highest expenditure is t he wage bil l, which  
in 2024  represented 43% of public expenditure ,3 higher than  the regional average 
of 28%.4 Given such limited fiscal space , achieving spending efficiency  is 
paramount .

its best perform ing sectors, like  education -PISA scores close to the regional

Departments, and Agencies (MDAs), encompassing over 50% of public officers;

information and communications technologies in government, procurement 
processes , and budget oversight.  The current project aims to build on the 
successes of PSTP  and PSEP to address remaining challenges in the efficiency 
of public sector operations.  For example, the shared services activities described 
under Component 1 are direct continuations of activities begun under PSTP.

functions (US$ 45 million). This component will finance: (i) the development of

supported improvements in public sector human resource management , use of 
information and communications technologies in government, procurement 
processes , and budget oversight.  The current project aims to build on the 
successes of PSTP  and PSEP to address remaining challenges in the efficiency 
of public sector operations.  For example, the shared services activities described 
under Component 1 are direct continuations of activities begun under PSTP.

in the Government of Jamaica ; (iv) limited information and tools to facilitate internal 
mobility within the public sector; and (v) the employee perfor mance management 
framework is inconsistent with the compensation restructuring implemented in

cross- cutting issues of digital transformation and strengthening of institutions.

specific development objectives: (i) enhancing the management of core 
government support functions ; (ii) optimizing the structure of the s tate; and 
(iii) strengthening the public sector‚Äôs human  capital .

functions (US$ 45 million). This component will finance: (i) the development of 
shared corporate services for government, including, inter alia:  HR & payroll

upskilling for public officers transitioning to new roles as a result of the shared 
services transition; and (iv) change management interventions  to support the 
adoption of shared services .

component will finance the following activities: (i) the creation of a catalog of public 
services; (ii) the design and implementation of a  methodology to analyze 
opportunities for efficiency in public bodies as a means to identify the bodies that 
will be prioritized for intervention24; (iii) the rationalization of public bodies, including  
the closure of those which are dormant (approximately 3 0 of 50) , as well as 
potential  divestment, incorporation into a ministry, and fusion with other public 
bodies ; and (i v) the conceptual, legal, and procedural development of alternative 
service delivery models .25

(US$16 million). This component will finance (i) implementation of the new 
Government of Jamaica  human resources management operating model with a 
gender and diversity perspective26; (ii) implementation of a tool that will connect 
public servants interested in new government jobs with relevant vacancies and 
trainings necessary to fill skills gaps; (iii) implementation of an online recruitment 
platform  accessible for persons with disabilities ; (iv) restructuring of the job 
classification system; (v) automation of the job evaluation process; and 
(vi) implementation of an improved performance management system .

US$4 million that will be used for covering PEU contractor compensation , audit, 
and monitoring and evaluation.

2.17 Execution. The executing agency will be the Ministry of Finance and the Public 
Service, through the TIU. The TIU has a proven track record of successfully 
executing IDB -financed programs, including the Public Sector Transformation 
Programme ( 4374/OC -JA, US$50 million), which concluded execution in February 
2024. Furthermore, the Bank previously invested U$65 million in building the 
institutional capacity of the Ministry of Finance through an investment loan 
operation 2658/OC -JA, which concluded in 2018. An analysis of the Ministry of 
Finance and the Public Service (including the TIU ) institutional capacity to 
implement the project will be conducted using the Bank‚Äôs Institutional Capacity Analysis Platform (ICAP) and the results will be fully incorporated in the 
development of the operation. Moreover, the results will inform the risk analysis, 
the areas for improvement, the detailed execution arrangements, and the fiduciary 
actions needed to be in place for the program's successful execution.  
2.18 Financial instrument.  The operation will be an investment loan under the modality 
of specific investment loan of ordinary capital with a six -year disbursement period, 
executed by the Government of Jamaica through the Transformation 

- 7 - 
 
Implementation Unit (TIU) of the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service. This 
loan modality will allow for specific investments in hardware, software, advisory, 
and training, the financing of the personnel of the TIU as the Project Execution Unit 
to su pport implementation, and for continuous IDB technical and fiduciary support.  
2.19 Complementarity with other operations in development.  This project will 
benefit from complementarity with the Government Digital Transformation 
Programme (in preparation) and Strengthening Cybersecurity in Jamaica (in 
preparation). The Government Digital Transformation Programme will finance 
investments in cross -government digital capability, allowing for the more efficient 
delivery of transactional public services for citizens and firms. Taken together, will 
significantly reduce the cos ts institutions face  to manage their non -core business, 
such as building their online presence and managing the administrative support 
functions. Strengthening Cybersecurity in Jamaica will result in greater protection 
against cyberattacks on government digital assets, which will increase with the 
new operations . Furthermore, the Government Digital Transformation Programme 
will also be executed by the TIU, facilitating coordination between the two projects 
and generating economies of scale in programme administration.  
2.20 Coordination.  Most of the programme will benefit different units within the Ministry 
of Finance and the Public Service (e.g. the Strategic Human Resources Management Division and the Office of Public Procurement), where the TIU is also 
located, thus facilitating coordi nation. Component 3 (talent) will also require 
coordination with the Office of the Services Commissions, which holds several responsibilities for human resources management. This would be conducted 
through the working groups established for the purposes of the public sector 
compensation review completed under PSTP.

of 28%.4 Given such limited fiscal space , achieving spending efficiency  is 
paramount .

its best perform ing sectors, like  education -PISA scores close to the regional

efforts  is the Public Sector Master Rationalisation Plan, which was tabled in

simpler citizen interactions with public institutions, among other benefits.  A 
precursor to PSTP  was the Public Sector Efficiency Programme (PSEP) , which 
supported improvements in public sector human resource management , use of 
information and communications technologies in government, procurement 
processes , and budget oversight.  The current project aims to build on the 
successes of PSTP  and PSEP to address remaining challenges in the efficiency 
of public sector operations.  For example, the shared services activities described 
under Component 1 are direct continuations of activities begun under PSTP.
