II. Objectives and Justification of the TC
2.1Investment in economic and social infrastructure in the region has been insufficient 
and inefficient to date. Alongside the development of an agenda that implies efficiency 
improvements to public investment processes, there is a need to develop mechanisms 
that encourage more active private sector participation. The infrastructure gap in Latin 
America and the Caribbean (LAC) is estimated to be 3.12% of the region's GDP in 
terms of investment effort relative to the size of the economy. This figure represents 
- 2 -
over a 70% increase compared to the current level of investment.1 Additionally, there 
are investment needs in social infrastructure. For hospitals, the estimated investment 
required in the sector is around USD 153 billion, which is designated solely for new 
hospital construction and the modernization of existing facilities and equipment.2
2.2Infrastructure investment has a direct impact on economic growth as part of gross fixed 
capital formation, and an indirect impact to increase productivity.3 Investing in resilient 
infrastructure has an estimated net benefit of four dollars for every dollar spent. 4 
Although developing infrastructure and delivering related services can be costly and 
carry certain risks, failing to invest has negative repercussions not only on GDP growth 
but also disproportionately affects the poorest individuals in the income distribution. 3
2.3Public investment in LAC has been insufficient to address the region's infrastructure 
gap. Historically, the public sector has contributed two-thirds of total infrastructure 
investment, with some economies experiencing a more significant involvement from 
the private sector. However, public investment in infrastructure has proven to be highly 
inefficient. According to studies by the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), the 
efficiency of infrastructure spending in LAC is below the international average. The 
region effectively wastes one out of every two dollars allocated to public infrastructure 
investment due to issues such as cost overruns, time delays, and poor planning, 
among other factors (Su√°rez-Alem√°n, Serebrisky, and Perelman 2019; IDB 2020). 
This inefficiency is especially challenging given the current fiscal constraints.5
Closing infrastructure gaps and achieving growth goals cannot rely solely on increased 
public investment. Instead, a more effective approach focuses on improving the 
efficiency of public spending while promoting active and diversified participation from 
the private sector. Well-structured and properly implemented Public-Private 
Partnerships (PPPs) offer a valuable opportunity to address both of these issues. By 
enhancing innovation and efficiency in infrastructure development and service 
delivery, PPPs can ultimately drive economic growth and productivity.
2.4Recognizing the positive impact of upstream interventions on mobilizing private 
resources for public infrastructure development ‚Äì and subsequently on economic 
growth, productivity, and competitiveness ‚Äì6the PPP Unit has been actively supporting 
the enhancement of enabling environments for the implementation of PPPs in three 
key areas:

PPP, which involves two key components: (i) the regional Infrascope, a tool

among other factors (Su√°rez-Alem√°n, Serebrisky, and Perelman 2019; IDB 2020). 
This inefficiency is especially challenging given the current fiscal constraints.5
Closing infrastructure gaps and achieving growth goals cannot rely solely on increased 
public investment. Instead, a more effective approach focuses on improving the 
efficiency of public spending while promoting active and diversified participation from 
the private sector. Well-structured and properly implemented Public-Private 
Partnerships (PPPs) offer a valuable opportunity to address both of these issues. By 
enhancing innovation and efficiency in infrastructure development and service 
delivery, PPPs can ultimately drive economic growth and productivity.
2.4Recognizing the positive impact of upstream interventions on mobilizing private 
resources for public infrastructure development ‚Äì and subsequently on economic 
growth, productivity, and competitiveness ‚Äì6the PPP Unit has been actively supporting 
the enhancement of enabling environments for the implementation of PPPs in three 
key areas:
2.4.1The diagnosis of the enabling environment for identifying and implementing 
PPP, which involves two key components: (i) the regional Infrascope, a tool

trillion in 2008 to nearly USD 5.8 trillion after the pandemic‚Äîalmost double that amount. This represents 117% of the 
region's GDP and up to 140% of the GDP of its five largest economies. Public debt soared to over 70% in 2020, but due to 
fiscal adjustment efforts in the region, it is now decreasing and approaching pre-pandemic levels of around 60% of GDP in 
2023. However, these levels remain high, as prudent debt levels for the region are estimated to be between 46% and 55% 
of GDP.  The elevated debt levels in many countries are also hindering growth. The IDB's flagship report, "Dealing with 
Debt" (2023), indicates that peaks in debt are associated with significant reductions in growth, with the impact being 
especially pronounced during more prolonged periods of high debt. This situation can lead to increased financing costs and 
a decrease in both public and private investment.

investments. World Bank Document

developed by the IDB and Economist Impact to assess the capability of Latin 
American and Caribbean countries in implementing efficient PPP, which 
encompasses 26 member countries of the IDB and has been updated and 
published biannually since 2009, and (ii) the subnational adaptation of the 
Infrascope, currently being piloted in Brazil for the first time, with results expected 
to be presented in 2025.7 This has been complemented not only with country 
specific diagnosis for each of the 26 IDB member countries, but also with sector 
based PPP diagnosis, such as ports, airports, hospitals, environmental assets, 
water or sanitation, among others currently in development (railways, roads, 
schools).  
2.4.2The development of solutions primarily through the Network for Analysis 
and Best Practices in PPP (PPP Network). This initiative has effectively 
systematized knowledge and experiences that were previously scattered across 
the Region. To date, it has produced a wide range of analytical outcomes and 
methodological tools that have contributed to generating evidence and best 
practices for the regulatory, institutional, and planning enhancement of 
infrastructure development through PPPs in the region. In 2023, the PPP Network 
shifted its focus to the evaluation of PPP policies, programs, and projects, following 
the recommendation from the Infrascope report. This report highlighted that LAC 
is missing an opportunity to learn from its experiences due to the lack of systematic 
ex-post evaluation. From 2024 to 2025, the newly formed PPP Evaluation Network 
has been collaborating with Peru, Brazil, and Colombia8, as well as regional 
universities and think tanks, to improve their capacities for conducting ex post 
evaluations. Concurrently, the Network is implementing performance evaluations 
of programs and projects in each country.9
7 Brazil has been selected as the first pilot for the implementation of the subnational Infrascope since majority of the PPPs 
and concession are being developed at the state level and most of the states have its one institutional and regulatory 
framework with differences in performance that make it worth to analyzes and learn from. The methodology of the regional 
Infrascope is being adapted to the subnational level and could be use in the future to analyze other countries with similar 
characteristics.  
8 The selection of Peru, Brazil and Colombia on how advance the PPP programs are in those countries, the availability of 
data and the support of the government to the evaluation initiative 
9 In 2020, the IDB. with the support of governments and research institutions across Latin America and the Caribbean, 
successfully established the Network for Analysis and Best Practices in Public-Private Partnerships (PPP Network). This 
initiative was recognized as a Regional Public Good, aimed at enhancing infrastructure development in the region by 
improving quality and efficiency. Prior to its creation, valuable knowledge and experiences related to public-private 
partnerships were scattered throughout Latin America and the Caribbean. Since then, the PPP Network has conducted 
three annual cycles. These cycles involve identifying key public policy issues in the area of PPPs that require practical, 
applied knowledge. This identification process is carried out through public consultations with regional governments and is 
organized into five thematic categories: 1) regulation and institutional framework; 2) preparation of sustainable projects; 3) 
project financing; 4) risk management, monitoring, and supervision; and 5) evaluation, impact, and performance. The 
Network has launched open calls for proposals, inviting knowledge institutions capable of addressing these challenges. It 
has also produced more than twenty analytical documents and methodological tools, contributing to the generation of 
evidence and best practices for strengthening regulatory, institutional, and planning frameworks related to infrastructure 
development through PPPs in the region. The Network has established a strong community of practice, comprising over 
2,000 participants. Additionally, it has launched the First Knowledge Portal on PPP Analysis and Best Practices 
(www.reddeapps.org) for Latin America and the Caribbean. Initiated under Technical Cooperation RG-T3545, this initiative 
has been recognized as a success, both in terms of its impact and scope. It has not only motivated engagement from 
numerous stakeholders but has also laid the groundwork for a Technical Assistance agenda focused on Upstream PPP, 
which includes enhancing regulatory and institutional frameworks, and project planning. Notable examples of this agenda 
include TC RG-T4199, CH-T1285, and CH-T1326. Moreover, the efficient use of resources has been demonstrated, with 
analytical outcomes nearly tripling expectations. Recently, the PPP Network has concentrated on evaluation initiatives, 
leading to the creation of the PPP Evaluation Network, funded by RG-T4644.
The work of the PPP Network is currently active with a focus on evaluation of PPP projects in Latin America and the 
Caribbean through the technical cooperation RG-T4344.

2.4.3 The implementation of PPP Upstream technical assistances to LAC 
countries, with more than 20 technical assistance solutions across 15 economies 
in the region encompassing both mature environments, such as Brazil, Peru, 
Colombia, and Chile, and those with relatively less experience, like Guatemala, 
Trinidad and Tobago, Paraguay, and Belize. In mature economies for instance, 
following the diagnosis and recommendations from the Infrascope, the Chilean 
government with IDB support has been actively working to enhance its project 
preparation process aimed at mobilizing sustainable financing for concession 
projects. Meanwhile, in less experienced economies as an example, the IDB has 
supported the Belizean government in developing its PPP policy, which was 
approved in 2021 and is now being utilized to attract private investment in the 
transport sector.
2.5 Results so far and challenges. The latest edition of Infrascope 2023/202410 
highlights significant progress. Investment in infrastructure PPPs across LAC has 
reached $160 billion in the period 2014-2023, marking a 14% increase from $141 
billion during the 2011-2020 period analyzed in the previous edition. Additionally, the 
number of PPP projects has grown by over 25%11. Although most of these projects 
are concentrated in the transport (37%) and energy sectors (52%), there is a notable 
increase in interest and activity in areas such as water and sanitation (6%) and social 
infrastructure (4%).12 In the inaugural edition of the Infrascope in 2009, only one 
country had a developed regulatory and institutional framework for the preparation, 
implementation, and supervision of PPP.13 By 2024, the majority of the countries 
analyzed have established some regulatory framework to facilitate PPP 
implementation, and 13 of these countries have fully operational PPP units in place.
2.6On a country level, Brazil and Chile continue to excel, followed by more established 
countries like Colombia, Uruguay, and Peru. Other nations are also making progress; 
for instance, Panama is strengthening its regulatory framework and improving its PPP 
project preparation process. Jamaica has demonstrated outstanding leadership in 
developing resilient PPPs, while Ecuador has made recent advances in planning and 
prioritizing PPP projects. Paraguay has seen positive developments in its PPP 
program as well. Additionally, countries like Belize and Suriname are working on 
establishing a PPP regulatory framework, showcasing a growing commitment from 
smaller and emerging markets.
2.7However, and despite the overall positive trends in the region, challenges and 
disparities still exist. Infrascope‚Äôs results indicates that there is still considerable room 
for improvement, which could significantly benefit their citizens, especially in 
developing economies.
2.7.1Regulations and Institutions - Strengthening institutional capacity: The ability of 
institutions involved in the PPP process to effectively support project identification, 
preparation, and implementation is a critical and ongoing challenge across the

region. Currently, only half of the 26 countries in the region have fully operational 
PPP agencies, 27% have a PPP Unit but with limited activity and the rest of the 
countries don‚Äôt have a formal unit. The situation with the availability of dedicated 
resources to facilitate project preparation or to assist with the associated costs is 
even more complicated with only 11 countries having such facilities. As an 
example, Guatemala needs to improve their capacity for contract management and 
monitoring and their coordination mechanisms between the different institutions 
involved in the PPP process (EI, IDB, 2024).14 
2.7.2Planning and Preparation - Improving project structuring: The percentage of 
tendered PPP that have achieved successful financial closure is under 60%. The 
primary obstacles include increasing financing costs, deficiencies in risk 
management, and insufficient project preparation. As an example, Dominican 
Republic needs to enhance its planification process and technical capacities for 
project preparation aiming to improve the success rate of their PPP (EI, IDB, 
2024).15.
2.7.3Monitoring and Evaluation ‚Äì Developing Performance and impact measurement 
capabilities: Many countries in the region are not actively learning from past 
experiences, which limits their ability to create impactful projects. As an example, 
Ecuador has a mandate to perform evaluations of PPP process, but these are not 
being conducted, losing the opportunity to include the lessons learned into the 
projects under preparation (EI, IDB, 2024).16 
2.8Recognizing these challenges and building on the success of previous technical 
cooperation projects ( RG-T3545, RG-T4199, RG-T4344), the aim of this initiative is to 
enhance the enabling environment for PPP in the 26 IDB countries. This will support 
regional economic growth, productivity, and competitiveness by fostering the 
development of efficient infrastructure. To achieve this, the initiative will be structured 
around a solid diagnostic approach at regional, country and sectorial levels to keep 
track of the advance of the challenges presented above and identify new ones. This 
will lead to the identification of specific areas for improvement in each country and 
regional needs that will guide our agenda for development of evidence and tools.  As 
illustrated in the previous examples, the Infrascope provides detailed information 
through 106 specific indicators that assess how countries can effectively develop PPP 
by enhancing regulatory, institutional, planning, and evaluation frameworks. This 
information will establish roadmaps for potential improvement in each of the 26 IDB 
countries. This updated diagnosis will serve as the basis for implementing technical 
assistance through this Technical Cooperation.
2.8.1Regional, Country-level, and Sector PPP Diagnosis: The Infrascope is the 
primary diagnostic tool for LAC countries to assess the enabling environment for 
PPP. Continuing to implement the Infrascope at regional and subnational levels, 
as demonstrated in the pilot case in Brazil, is a priority since this approach not only

provides ongoing recommendations to public officials in the region‚Äîhelping to 
strengthen enabling environments over the past 15 years‚Äîbut also enables the 
tracking of regional development through the collection of comparable data. 
2.8.2Development of evidence and tools to strengthen regulatory, institutional, 
planning, and project preparation PPP frameworks: We are focusing our efforts 
on two major challenges identified by the Infrascope. The first challenge is to 
enhance the region's capacity for ex-post evaluation practices. These practices 
aim to learn from past experiences in order to improve future PPP. The second 
challenge involves a deeper analysis of the capabilities of PPP Units in the region. 
This analysis will help us assess whether these units are utilizing their resources 
efficiently, which is crucial for the successful implementation of PPP.
2.8.3Implementing PPP Upstream Technical Assistance, aiming to enhance the 
regulatory, institutional, planning and project preparation frameworks and 
processes in emerging PPP programs in Latin America and the Caribbean. This 
will be based on the findings from regional and country-specific diagnostic 
exercises (Component 1), and through the application of best practices and 
evidence generated in Component 2.17
2.9 Strategic Alignment
2.9.1 This TC aligns with the IDBG Institutional Strategy ‚Äì IDB Impact+ (2024-2030) 
(CA-631), which prioritizes Public-Private Synergies as a key component of our 
value proposition, positioning the Group as the partner of choice for our borrowing 
member countries and clients. Specifically, this initiative is aligned to the goal of 
enhancing sustainable regional growth by developing a robust institutional, legal, 
and regulatory framework for implementing PPPs. This framework is essential for 
mobilizing private capital for infrastructure projects and developing more efficient 
infrastructure that positively impacts economic growth. In terms of operational 
focus, the TC is connected to the sustainable, resilient, and inclusive development 
of infrastructure. By creating and strengthening the enabling environment for PPP 
implementation, we can help countries close their infrastructure gap in both 
quantity and quality. Furthermore, this initiative is aligned with the operational 
focus on productive development and innovation through the private sector. The 
proposed activities aim to foster the development of more efficient infrastructure 
that enhances productivity. 
2.9.2 The recently approved IDB Group Synergies Framework (GN-3159-3) recognizes 
that PPP are crucial for enhancing IDB Group synergies. To support this initiative, 
the Bank has established a dedicated team to implement PPPs in the region. This 
approach has proven effective in helping countries develop strong institutional, 
legal, and regulatory frameworks to attract private investment in infrastructure 
through transactional advisory services and transparent procurement processes. 
This TC will help maintain the successful trajectory of the PPP Unit by focusing on 
strengthening regulatory and institutional capacities in the countries involved and 
developing valuable knowledge products. This proposal also aligns with the IDB 
Infrastructure Strategy (GN-2710-5), which underscores the importance of 
enhancing countries' abilities to establish public-private partnerships. It also

emphasizes the need to create a well-defined portfolio of substantial and high-
quality infrastructure projects, supported by a clear and predictable regulatory 
framework. 
2.9.3 Additionally, this TC aligns with the ONE Caribbean Regional Strategic Framework 
(GN-3201-5). The Caribbean region presents both opportunities and challenges in 
developing effective PPP for economic and social infrastructure. Infrascope 
indicates that while Caribbean countries vary significantly from one another, there 
is potential to strengthen their PPP programs in several key areas, including policy 
development and project preparation. This TC aims to facilitate large-scale 
investments to bridge the infrastructure gap through PPPs. The PPP unit has 
already collaborated with One Caribbean Management to identify specific 
opportunities for upstream interventions. PPP interventions play a special role in 
the One Caribbean implementation, and the development of a regional Project 
Preparation Facility, which states how "Strengthening technical capabilities and 
institutional capacity will contribute, among other issues, to building the local 
technical expertise necessary to implement impactful projects in the Caribbean".
2.9.4 It is also aligned with America en el Centro Program that mentions that building on 
the supported provided to several program‚Äôs beneficiary countries, the Bank will 
increase its support for PPP project preparation in Central America, Panam√° and 
Dominican Republic (CAPDR), with a focus on integration-infrastructure projects 
aligned with Am√©rica en el Centro. To achieve this, technical assistance resources 
will be used to finance increased upstream and downstream PPP support, 
considering each country's challenges and PPP-market development stage. 
Alternative mechanisms for strengthening project preparation capacity will also be 
considered, such as supporting or creating PPP Project Preparation Facilities at a 
national level.
2.9.5 Finally, the TC aligns with the Window 2 of the Ordinary Capital Strategic 
Development Program (W2F) priority area, inclusive economic growth.  This TC 
aims to create opportunities for public-private partnerships in economic and social 
infrastructure within Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC). Additionally, it 
focuses on improving the quality and performance of infrastructure services, 
sharing lessons learned in the sector, and promoting best practices in 
infrastructure. The development of more and better infrastructure and the 
improvement of the quality of the services due to the efficiency and innovation that 
the private sector can bring have a direct impact on economic growth and the 
reduction of inequality.

III. Description of components and budget
3.1 Component 1: Regional, Country-level, and Sector PPP Diagnosis ‚Äì U$S 700,000
3.1.1 The development of the 2025/2026 edition of Infrascope for the 26 IDB member 
countries will follow a similar structure to previous editions. This component‚Äôs 
resources will fund the collaboration with Economist Impact, which will be 
responsible for data collection, application of the methodology, and publication of 
the results for the new edition. Economist Impact will gather information with the 
assistance of local specialists in public infrastructure and PPP. The data collected 
for each country will be shared with the respective governments for review and 
feedback before publication. This edition will also feature the development of a 
regional key funding report, along with country profiles and case studies available 
in English, Spanish, and Portuguese.
- 8 -
3.1.2 The development of the 2026 edition of the Subnational Infrascope in Brazil is 
underway. Continuing the subnational initiative of the Infrascope, which has been 
implemented in Brazil since 2024 and will have its results published in 2025, this 
technical cooperation (TC) will provide funding for engagement with Economist 
Impact. This collaboration will involve the collection of data, the application of the 
methodology, and the publication of results for the new edition of the Subnational 
Infrascope for Brazil.
3.2 Component 2: Development of evidence and tools to strengthen regulatory, 
institutional, planning, and project preparation PPP frameworks - U$S 400,000
3.2.1 The PPP Evaluation Network ‚Äì currently active in Brazil, Colombia, and Peru ‚Äì is 
being expanded to include evaluations of the PPP programs in three additional 
LAC countries that have established PPP programs with projects that are either 
finalized or in advanced operational stages, which have sufficient and comparable 
historical data, necessary for effective evaluation exercises. These evaluations will 
include analyses such as ex-ante versus ex-post assessments of investment 
decisions, procurement methods, contract characteristics, performance, and 
impact. According to our Infrascope results, the eligible countries that meet these 
criteria include Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Uruguay, Peru, Jamaica, Panama, Mexico, 
Ecuador, Costa Rica, Guatemala, the Dominican Republic, Paraguay, and 
Argentina. Notably, Ecuador has officially expressed interest in joining the PPP 
Evaluation Network and benefiting from a comprehensive evaluation of its PPP 
program, as well as an in-depth assessment of its port sector. This will help gather 
evidence for future projects in that sector. The selection of the other two beneficiary 
countries will be based on the presence of an active PPP program, the 
advancement of PPP projects, the availability of information, and the government's 
commitment to pursuing the evaluation agenda.
3.2.2 Resources will be utilized to collaborate with universities and think tanks in the 
region. This collaboration aims to support the collection of data regarding the 
country's performance during the preparation, procurement, and implementation 
of PPP. Additionally, the TC will work on developing indicators to analyze the 
effectiveness of PPP programs and projects. The main lessons learned from the 
analysis will be published in collaboration with the participating countries, as these 
insights can benefit other countries in the region.
3.3 Component 3: Component 3: Implementing PPP Upstream Technical Assistance 
- U$S 200,000
3.3.1 The TC aims to provide technical assistance for the development of regulatory and 
institutional frameworks, as well as to enhance planning processes for nascent 
PPP programs in Latin America and the Caribbean, based on the diagnosis 
implemented in Component 1, and applying evidence and best practices identified 
in Component 2. The resources from the TC initiative will enable us to strengthen 
our technical assistance teams across various disciplines, including legal, 
technical, economic, financial, social, and environmental areas, addressing each 
country's specific needs. This will allow us to effectively offer public policy 
recommendations aimed at improving upstream PPP frameworks in LAC. Notably, 
Dominican Republic and Guatemala has expressed interest in improving their 
enabling environments, through enhanced regulations and capacities for the 
prioritization, preparation, management, and monitoring of PPP project (including 
development of manuals, guidelines and tools as well as specific capacity building 
- 9 -
exercises). While initial candidates have been identified as beneficiaries of this 
component, other countries identified as emerging and nascent according to the 
Infrascope assessment18 could be eligible, if officially requested and proven to act 
on the implementation of best practices to overcome their particular PPP 
challenges. 
Indicative Budget
3.4The total amount of funding needed to achieve the expected outcomes is U$S 
1,300,000 of non-reimbursable resources to finance through the ordinary capital of the 
Bank - SDP Window 2 - Economic Growth.

countries will be based on the presence of an active PPP program, the 
advancement of PPP projects, the availability of information, and the government's 
commitment to pursuing the evaluation agenda.

section_text:
II. Objectives and Justification of the TC  
2.1 Haiti benefits from a diversity of ecosystems due to variations in altitude, soil type and 
exposure to prevailing winds, representing an opportunity for national agricultural 
production. The agricultural sector accounted for 15,7% of Haiti's GDP (BRH, 2022) 
and employs between 50% and 60% of the active population (WB, 2024). Its growth 
rate has been respectively -5% in 2018 and 2% in 2019 (FAOSTAT, 2021). However, 
according to a study conducted by the IDB on agricultural productivity in Latin America 
and the Caribbean (1961-2021), Haiti experienced declines in agricultural productivity, 
while most other countries made significant progress. For instance, Dominican 
Republic achieved a productivity growth rate of approximately 2%, aligning with the 
rate observed in Andean Community (CAN) countries. Meanwhile, Haiti‚Äôs productivity 
growth remains close to zero, like Jamaica, which shows a comparable trend. 
2.2 The Haitian agricultural sector is highly vulnerable to climate change. Haiti is in a very 
high-risk position with respect to the occurrence of adverse climatic phenomena such 
as hurricanes, tropical storms, waves and tropical currents. Measured through the ND-
GAIN index, its degree of exposure is 35.5 in 2021 (position 169 out of 185 countries). 
Over the period 1981 to 2020, the country was hit on average, by 2.1 tropical storms 
and 0.8 major hurricanes per year (Karnauskas, 2022), causing significant material 
damage and loss of human life (CIAT, 2012).  Climate models for Haiti predict 
temperatures to increase up to 2.3¬∞C by 2060, precipitation to decrease up to 20% in 
the mid-2030s, and frequency and intensity of extreme weather events to increase. 
This implies important adaptation challenges for the agricultural sector.
2.3 Moreover, Haiti is a country in a fragile situation, with low-income levels, socio-
economic challenges, high insecurity context and political upheaval. Haiti is ranked 
10th out of 178 countries on the Fragile States Index (2023). It is expected that the 
fragile and conflict-affected states (FCS) will disproportionately suffer from climate 
change, including because of their geographical location and dependence on 
agriculture and drought will increase hunger, from already high levels (IMF, 2023). 
This could contribute to both malnutrition and increased dependence on imports to 
meet food security needs. According to the IPC Acute Food Insecurity Analysis, 
covering the period from August 2024 to June 2025, nearly 5 million people‚Äî
approximately half of the analyzed Haitian population‚Äîare facing high levels of acute 
food insecurity. Of these people, 6,000 experience catastrophic levels of hunger and 
livelihood collapse, classified as IPC phase 5 (catastrophe). The impacts of climate 
change, criminal violence, and political instability exacerbate this challenge by 
reducing agricultural productivity and undermining families' ability to secure their 
livelihoods. According to CNSA data from August 2024, the Haitian economy 
experienced a general inflation rate of 48.3% in 2022, with an increase of more than 
47% in the prices of essential food items. 
- 3 -
2.4 In this context, the Government of Haiti aims at addressing part of the challenges that 
impact the agricultural productivity in the context of climate change through PAPAIR 
operation. In this sense, the project includes investments in infrastructure for fisheries 
and transportation, as well as direct support to farmers to promote agricultural 
technology transfer. Impact evaluations of the current PAPAIR project and former 
PITAG operation (HA-L1107) are currently under way to assess their effects on 
agricultural productivity, resilience to climate change, and food security.
2.5 The current Bank strategy for Haiti includes agricultural sector as a major pilar for 
economic and social stability, and the Government of Haiti and the Bank agreed to 
increase investment efforts in this sector through new financing opportunities based 
on lessons learned from past and ongoing operations. In that context, the Government 
of the Republic of Haiti requested the Bank's technical and financial support through 
a non-reimbursable technical cooperation to support the execution of the PAPAIR 
operation (HA-J0002) and explore new sustainable investment opportunities to 
improve agricultural productivity in Haiti. PAPAIR operation has been delayed for 
several reasons such as lack of competent staff for procurement processes, delayed 
importation of civil works equipment for rural roads, and some weaknesses in overall 
project planning and operational management.
2.6 The objective of this Technical Cooperation (TC) is to support the Ministry of 
Agriculture efforts to promote sustainable agriculture, food security and resilience to 
climate change in the northern region of Haiti.  The specific objectives are to: (i) 
strengthen the Ministry‚Äôs capacity to implement HA-J0002 (PAPAIR) operation; (ii) 
elaborate on lessons learned from past and current operation in execution, including 
financing mechanisms implemented through public and private sector initiatives and, 
(iii) support the design of new strategies and investments to boost agriculture 
productivity, sustainability and resilience to climate change.
2.7 The TC is consistent with the Updated IDB Group Institutional Strategy: Transforming 
for Scale and Impact (CA-631) and aligns with the objectives of: (i) reducing poverty 
and inequality; and (ii) addressing climate change, as it will strengthen the capacity of 
the Ministry of Agriculture (MARNDR) to implement the PAPAIR operation (HA-J0002) 
and to identify new sustainable initiatives aimed at improving agricultural productivity 
and resilience in Haiti‚Äôs northern region. The TC is aligned with the following 
operational focus areas: (i) biodiversity, natural capital, and climate action; (ii) 
sustainable, resilient, and inclusive infrastructure; and (iii) productive development and 
innovation through the private sector. It is also aligned with the Country Engagement 
Note for Haiti 2024‚Äì2026 (GN-3199-2), specifically with the strategic axis: ‚ÄúImproving 
the business climate to enhance productivity‚Äù, as it will contribute to strengthening the 
quality of agricultural support services, thereby promoting agricultural productivity, 
increasing household income, and combating food insecurity. In addition, the TC 
contributes to two cross-cutting themes of the Country Engagement Note that are 
essential for the sustainability of development outcomes: First, supporting the most 
vulnerable segments of society, especially women, youth, and internally displaced 
persons, who face multiple forms of discrimination, violence, and exclusion. Second, 
increasing Haiti‚Äôs resilience to external shocks, such as earthquakes, climate-related 
hazards, pandemics, and economic crises, by investing in prevention, preparedness, 
and mitigation measures to avoid future losses. The TC is also aligned with the

III. Description of activities/components and budget
3.1Component 1: Support to PAPAIR‚Äôs implementation (US$108.000). This 
component aims at providing technical assistance to the MARNDR project‚Äôs team to 
strengthen the ministry‚Äôs capacity to implement PAPAIR project and other initiatives in 
a more efficient way. The support will be provided through the contracting of consulting 
services that will focus on: (i) procurement and contract management, (ii) rural 
infrastructure management (civil engineering); (iii) monitoring & evaluation, (iv) gender 
and diversity, among other aspects. Consultants will be recruited to assist the Ministry 
project team in these fields to provide coaching, training and assistance to foster 
project management processes, based on an action plan validated by the Ministry and 
the Bank. The main expected result of this component is the improvement of the 
execution path of PAPAIR operation, measured through the Bank‚Äôs PMR system.
3.2Component 2: Lessons learned (US$15.000). This component will finance: (i) 
qualitative assessment of the effectiveness and efficiency impact of incentive 
mechanisms, subsidy programs, and technical assistance provided in the framework 
of several past and on-going operations (HA-L1059; HA-L1107; HA-L1096; HA-
J0002). Consultants will be hired to analyze the support provided by these instruments 
to smallholder farmers and agro-industries, identify gaps and inefficiencies in the 
current subsidy system, and formulate recommendations to improve access to modern 
equipment and technologies; (ii) Previous and ongoing experiences from the agro-
industrial private sector in creating market linkages with small and medium size 
farmers in the north will also be assessed; (iii) identification of alternative incentive 
models suited to beneficiaries and local context. The main result of this component 
will be a shared vision of the Ministry of Agriculture about instruments and 
methodologies to support agriculture production in the northern region of Haiti.
3.3Component 3: identification of new strategies and investments (US$177.000). 
This component will finance consulting services for the following activities: (i) 
identification of key investments for the development of sustainable value chains, 
including technology transfers, resilient and innovative infrastructure, equipment, and 
agro-processing units. The assessment will also explore technical assistance 
mechanisms that can support sustainable agricultural growth, address institutional and 
regulatory challenges affecting investments, identify opportunities for public-private 
partnerships and innovative financing, and propose strategies to enhance resilience 
to climate change, economic fluctuations, and food insecurity. Particular attention will 
be given to high-potential value chains identified as strategic by local stakeholders to 
guide investments toward sectors with strong growth and sustainability potential. The

IV. Executing agency and execution structure
4.1 Upon request of the Government of Haiti, the Bank will execute the TC through the 
Agriculture and Rural Development Division of the Productivity, Trade and Innovation 
Department (PTI/ARD). The main beneficiary and counterpart will be the Ministry of 
Agriculture, Natural Resources and Rural Development (MARNDR), the public entity 
responsible for sectoral policy, which will participate throughout TC implementation. 
The MARNDR will provide, among other contributions: (i) the information required for 
the preparation of the expected outputs; (ii) support for potential field visits and 
interviews; and (iii) the convening of relevant stakeholders in the sector.
4.2 According to OP-619-4, the execution by the Bank can be justified by the fact that the 
beneficiary has limited operational capacity to duly and timely execute the activities 
provided in the respective project. In particular, the MARNDR‚Äôs current limited capacity 
stems from the country‚Äôs prevailing social and political instability. Under these 
conditions, TC activities would be at risk of delays or inadequate implementation, 
jeopardizing the achievement of the objectives. Additionally, the current unstable 
political and institutional situation deter firms and consultants from participating in local 
public procurement processes or signing contracts with the Haitian public 
administration. Direct execution by the Bank will ensure that procurement processes, 
- 6 -
including the contracting of consultants, proceed without delays or uncertainties 
associated with government execution mechanisms. Furthermore, financial execution 
will not depend on the availability of public budget funds. Part of the consultancy is 
essential to provide timely technical inputs and public policy recommendations, which 
will support the preparation of a new investment operation planned for 2026. To 
mitigate these risks and ensure the timely and effective completion of the TC 
objectives, the MARNDR has formally requested that the Bank act as the Executing 
Agency. 
4.3 PTI/ARD will be responsible for TC implementation, with support from the Haiti Country 
Office (CID/CHA), which will serve as the Disbursement Unit (UDR).
4.4 Final terms of reference of the consultancies and all technical outputs will be prepared 
in dialogue with the Haitian Ministry of Agriculture and Natural Resources. A technical 
focal point will be appointed in the Ministry to facilitate coordination with the Bank‚Äôs 
team. The Bank‚Äôs team and the Ministry of Agriculture focal point will meet at least 
monthly to monitor the execution of the TC and take the relevant decisions to ensure 
that the technical staff and consultants in charge will deliver in a timely manner.
4.5 The activities to be executed under this operation will be included in the Procurement 
Plan and will be executed in accordance with the Bank's established procurement 
methods, namely: (i) hiring of individual consultants, as established in the 
Complementary Workforce Document (AM-650); and (ii) contracting of services 
provided by consulting firms in accordance with the Institutional Procurement Policy 
(GN-2303-33) and its associated guidelines.
4.6 The knowledge products generated within this technical cooperation will be the 
property of the Bank and may be made available to the public under a creative 
commons license.
4.7 There are no conditions to be fulfilled prior to first disbursement nor for the execution 
of the TC.

section_text:
I. Background
Despite being one of the larger English-speaking Caribbean nations, Trinidad and Tobago 
attracted only 1.4% of the 26 million international tourists in the region in 2019. The sector 
was already facing a slowdown before the COVID-19 pandemic, with only 388,000 
international arrivals in 2019, reflecting stagnation since 2010 and a growth rate of just 0.16% 
annually compared to 3.4% in the Caribbean. The pandemic exacerbated these issues, 
causing arrivals to plummet to 95,000 in 2020 and resulting in a -43.8% contraction in tourism 
GDP, dropping from 7.9% to 4.8% of the total economy. Recovery has been slow, with 
tourism's GDP contribution still 30% below pre-COVID levels in 2021 and international arrivals 
42% below 2019 figures in 2022. Tobago, in particular, relies heavily on tourism for economic 
stability, with many residents and businesses depending on it. However, the island faces 
challenges from national and sub-national crises, as well as the broader impact of global 
events on travel trends.
Recent unforeseen events, such as the unprecedented oil spill off Tobago's Atlantic coast in 
February 2024 and a shark attack involving a British visitor, have prompted tourism and 
emergency management authorities to reassess and enhance their crisis management 
protocols for the island. This reassessment is crucial in the post-pandemic era, where global 
travelers are particularly sensitive to perceived risks and require a strong sense of safety and 
security. Currently, Tobago‚Äôs tourism crisis management is coordinated between the Tobago 
Emergency Management Agency (TEMA) and the Division of Tourism, Culture, Antiquities, 
and Transport (DCAT). However, the roles and responsibilities between these agencies are 
not formally defined, and TEMA‚Äôs crisis management functions are not specifically tailored to 
the tourism sector. This oversight may result in gaps in essential protocols related to visitor 
relations and destination communications. Additionally, the absence of a comprehensive, 
tourism-specific crisis management policy or plan represents a critical vulnerability. To 
address these challenges effectively, it is imperative for Tobago to establish robust, well-
defined policies and planning frameworks. Engaging with a mature tourism destination that 
already has established, effective protocols and procedures for tourism crisis management 
would provide valuable insights and best practices. Such collaboration could enhance 
2Tobago's preparedness and response capabilities, thereby mitigating potential damage to its 
reputation in the global tourism market.
 
The Bahamas is recognized as a leading example of effective tourism crisis management in 
the Caribbean due to its comprehensive and well-structured approach. This effectiveness is 
demonstrated through the development of robust crisis management plans and protocols 
specifically tailored to the tourism sector, as well as the seamless coordination among 
government agencies, tourism stakeholders, and emergency services. For instance, the 
Bahamas Ministry of Tourism and Aviation collaborates closely with the National Emergency 
Management Agency (NEMA) to ensure a unified and efficient response to crises. 
Additionally, the Bahamas excels in crisis communication, with established systems for 
providing timely and transparent updates to both tourists and the global public. This 
commitment to clear communication helps maintain traveler confidence during emergencies. 
Further supporting these efforts is the Visitor Relations Unit, established in 1972, which 
addresses visitor complaints promptly and provides hospitable assistance to those facing 
challenges while visiting the destination. These well-coordinated practices collectively 
underscore the Bahamas' proactive and effective approach to managing tourism-related 
crises.
It follows then, that this knowledge exchange hopes to achieve the following: 
ÔÇ∑To examine first-hand the factors and lessons learned from the Ministry of Tourism 
and Aviation of The Bahamas as a successful and longstanding example of sound 
tourism destination crisis management in the Caribbean;
ÔÇ∑To equip participants with knowledge to enhance existing tourism destination crisis 
management strategies;
ÔÇ∑To engage in knowledge exchange and networking with technical experts from state 
enterprises relative to tourism destination crisis management.

section_text:
IV. EXECUTION STRUCTURE
4.1 The Government of Suriname, through the Ministry of Finance and Planning, has 
formally requested that the Inter-American Development Bank execute this 
Technical Cooperation directly. This request reflects the Government's recognition 
that the specialized nature of required interventions and the urgency of addressing 
implementation bottlenecks necessitate direct Bank management of technical 
resources.
4.2 The rationale for Bank execution stems from three critical factors. First, the 
technical expertise required (i.e., international specialists in laboratory biosafety 
infrastructure and complex irrigation engineering) exceeds current market 
availability in Suriname and requires procurement through specialized 
international networks where the Bank maintains established relationships. 
Second, the compressed timeline for delivering solutions before the June 2028 
deadline for SU-L1020 and November 2026 for SU-L1052 demands streamlined 
procurement processes that Bank execution enables through more efficient 
contracting mechanisms, avoiding the 90-day average processing delays currently 
experienced through government systems. Third, the coordination complexity of 
managing consultants across two separate loan operations with different executing 
arrangements benefits from unified Bank oversight, ensuring consistent technical 
standards and integrated delivery of complementary solutions.
4.3 LVV acknowledges that while IICA serves effectively as the Program Execution 
Unit for fiduciary management, the institution lacks the specialized technical 
capacity and procurement agility required for rapid deployment of highly 
specialized consultants. The Ministry's request for Bank execution represents a 
strategic decision to leverage IDB's technical expertise and procurement efficiency 
for targeted problem-solving, while maintaining LVV's substantive engagement 
through technical review, validation of deliverables, and participation in all 
consultant activities. This arrangement ensures optimal use of limited TC 
resources while building sustainable capacity within national institutions through 
structured knowledge transfer embedded in consultant terms of reference.
4.4 Thus it is established that this TC will be executed by the Inter-American 
Development Bank (IDB), based on a request by the beneficiaries, in accordance 
with the Bank‚Äôs Technical Cooperation Policy (GN-2470-2) and the Procedures for 
the Processing of Technical Cooperation Operations and Related Matters (OP-
619-4), through the Division of Agriculture and Rural Development (ARD).
4.5Procurement. All procurement to be executed under this Technical Cooperation 
have been included in the Procurement Plan (Annex IV) and will be hired in 
- 12 -compliance with the applicable Bank policies and regulations as follows: (a) Hiring 
of individual consultants, as established in the regulation on Complementary 
Workforce (AM-650) and (b) Contracting of services provided by consulting firms 
in accordance with the Corporate procurement Policy (GN-2303-33) and its 
Guidelines. 
4.6Execution and Disbursement Period. The Technical Cooperation will be 
executed over 24 months from the date of approval, with full disbursement 
expected within this period. This timeline aligns with the critical implementation 
phases of both associated loans: supporting SU-L1020's laboratory construction 
activities through its June 2028 completion date and accelerating SU-L1052's 
infrastructure works before its November 2026 closure. Consultant mobilization will 
occur within 30 days of TC approval to maximize impact during the 2025-2026 
construction season, with Component I activities concentrated in months 1-12 to 
expedite laboratory procurement, and Component II interventions spanning 
months 1-18 to support the full irrigation infrastructure construction cycle. The 24-
month execution period provides sufficient time for delivering all technical products 
while ensuring knowledge transfer and capacity building activities achieve 
sustainable institutional strengthening.
4.7Monitoring, Reporting, and Supervision. The Agriculture and Rural 
Development Division (CSD/RND) specialist assigned to the Country Office in 
Suriname (CSU) will serve as focal point and responsible for technical execution. 
Semi-annual progress reports will be submitted through the Technical Cooperation 
Monitoring and Reporting System (TCM) tracking outputs and financial execution 
against the Results Matrix and disbursement projections. Monthly coordination 
meetings with LVV, IICA, and IDB will review progress and address challenges. A 
completion report documenting results and lessons learned will be submitted within 
60 days of closure.

V. POTENTIAL RISKS
5.1 The primary risk facing this Technical Cooperation stems from the limited resource 
envelope relative to the magnitude of implementation challenges across both loan 
operations. With only US$200,000 available to address bottlenecks affecting 
US$24.6 million in undisbursed funds, the TC faces inherent constraints in scope 
and duration of interventions. This resource limitation may restrict consultant 
deployment to brief diagnostic missions rather than sustained implementation 
support, potentially resulting in technically sound recommendations that lack the 
hands-on accompaniment necessary for successful execution. The mitigation 
strategy requires rigorous prioritization of interventions based on impact potential 
and implementation readiness, focusing on bottlenecks where targeted technical 
inputs can unlock multiple downstream activities. Additionally, consultant terms of 
reference will emphasize practical tools and frameworks that extend impact 
beyond direct technical assistance periods, creating multiplier effects through 
replicable solutions.
5.2 The availability of specialized expertise presents significant execution risks given 
the narrow technical requirements for laboratory biosafety infrastructure and 
coastal irrigation engineering. The global shortage of consultants combining 
- 13 -technical depth with practical experience in Caribbean small island contexts may 
result in recruitment delays or compromised selections that affect deliverable 
quality. Furthermore, short-term consultant engagements risk producing generic 
solutions insufficiently adapted to Suriname's institutional and market constraints. 
Risk mitigation includes initiating recruitment processes immediately upon TC 
approval to maximize candidate pools, establishing framework agreements with 
specialized firms for rapid expert deployment, and requiring demonstrated 
experience in similar developing country contexts as primary selection criteria. 
Consultant contracts will mandate in-country presence during critical phases to 
ensure solutions reflect ground realities rather than theoretical approaches.
5.3 Technical complexity of the infrastructure involved poses risks to successful TC 
outcomes, particularly given the sophisticated nature of laboratory biosafety 
requirements and hydraulic engineering for coastal agricultural systems. 
Inadequate technical specifications could result in procurement failures, 
construction defects, or operational deficiencies that emerge only after TC 
completion. The risk compounds when considering that current LVV staff lack 
experience managing such specialized infrastructure, potentially 
misunderstanding or incorrectly implementing consultant recommendations. 
Mitigation requires selecting consultants with proven track records in similar 
facilities, mandating detailed technical documentation with step-by-step 
implementation guidance, and including validation mechanisms where draft 
specifications undergo peer review before finalization. Technical products will 
incorporate quality assurance protocols and commissioning procedures to identify 
and address deficiencies before infrastructure acceptance.
5.4 Finally, sustainability risks emerge from the temporary nature of TC interventions 
without established mechanisms for maintaining enhanced capacity beyond 
consultant departure. Solutions developed through external technical assistance 
may not become institutionalized within regular operations, resulting in gradual 
regression to previous implementation constraints. This risk intensifies given 
uncertain government budget allocations for maintaining coordination positions or 
technical functions created through TC support. The mitigation approach embeds 
knowledge transfer requirements throughout consultant engagements with verified 
capacity building milestones, development of institutional tools integrated into 
mandatory operational procedures, and seeking formal government commitment 
to sustain critical positions using loan savings from improved execution efficiency. 
Documentation of all technical products in user-friendly formats ensures 
institutional memory persists beyond personnel changes, while establishing 
communities of practice creates peer support networks that reinforce new 
competencies.
